articles.title: Empire State University, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Lecturer - The Harry Van Arsdale Jr. School of Labor Studies

The Harry Van Arsdale Jr. School of Labor Studies at Empire State University (SUNY Empire) seeks to hire a lecturer based at its New York City location, where the majority of the Labor School's students attend face-to-face classes. The department invites candidates from a range of social science disciplines - including sociology, political science, anthropology, economics, and geography - with a commitment to participatory labor education and historical and/or contemporary research relevant to the labor movement, broadly defined to include unions, worker centers, and other social justice organizations.

The successful candidate will have expertise in Labor Studies and will teach, develop curriculum, and mentor/advise students in programs offered both in person and online. They will also design and develop high-quality online Labor Studies courses from existing curricula, working collaboratively with faculty and staff to translate course outcomes, readings, assignments, and assessments into engaging, accessible learning experiences within the university's learning management system. Central to the faculty role is helping adults from diverse cultural backgrounds design and complete degrees that meet their personal and professional goals. SUNY Empire faculty provide advising from entry through graduation to students in the Labor Studies academic program. Working in cooperation with faculty and staff, the successful candidate will provide high-quality educational services to students, pursue relevant scholarly interests, participate in University life, and enhance the University and HVASLS's reputation and impact within the community.

The Harry Van Arsdale Jr. School of Labor Studies (HVASLS) is one of the founding programs of Empire State University. It currently serves approximately 1,000 students through partnerships with various labor organizations in New York City, and it offers in-person, as well as online and residency programs to members of partner organizations from across the country. Its labor-centered liberal arts program was inspired by Harry Van Arsdale Jr., a major twentieth century labor leader and a tireless promoter of life-long education for members of his union, IBEW Local 3, and all working people.

The Van Arsdale program offers associate and bachelor's degrees in Labor Studies as well as non-degree certificate programs. The program seeks to build a broad and inclusive labor and community-centered approach to help develop solutions to the most pressing challenges that our society is facing today, including issues related to economic, racial, and gender inequalities, globalization, technological change, industrial and financial restructuring. The courses are designed to provide the knowledge, awareness, and skills needed for our students to become leaders in the labor movement and in their communities.

Required Qualifications:

  • Master's degree in labor studies or related social science disciplines such as sociology, political science, anthropology, economics, and geography.
  • Demonstrated experience designing, developing, and teaching online courses in a learning management system, including building courses from existing curricula, organizing course content, developing learning activities and assessments, and supporting student engagement in an online environment.
  • Experience with labor education, the labor movement, and social justice movements.
  • College-level teaching experience.
  • Experience teaching and/or advising non-traditional students from diverse backgrounds.

Preferred Qualifications:

  • PhD. in Labor Studies, or related social science disciplines such as sociology, political science, anthropology, economics, and geography.
  • Experience teaching courses in Labor Studies or courses on labor topics in related fields.
  • Demonstrated commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion in higher education and/or through community-based work.
  • Demonstrated commitment to a participatory pedagogy.
  • Research interests in issues related to working people, labor organizations, and social movements.
  • Familiarity with the D2L Brightspace learning management system.

Special Information:

  • Candidates should include with their application a statement on their teaching philosophy and methods.
  • Occasional travel will be required to fulfill university-wide obligations, including biannual travel to Saratoga Springs, New York.
  • Office hours will vary in accordance with student needs. Periodic evening and weekend engagement will also be required.
  • Applicants must be currently authorized to work in the U.S. on a full-time basis. VISA sponsorship is not available for this position.
  • SUNY Empire provides employees with robust remote and flexible work options to meet the needs of students, faculty, and staff in a dispersed work environment.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: Applications accepted until position is filled.

articles.title: Johannes Kepler University Linz, Austria
articles.body_html:
Job title:Graduate Teaching Assistant (must hold a Diploma/Master's degree) for a full-time, four-year position

On the one hand, the newly founded Department of Environmental and Transformation Sociology deals with the reciprocal relationship between society and the natural environment, which includes, for example, social metabolism, dealing with environmental problems, and debates about sustainability, energy transition, and environmental justice (classical environmental sociology). On the other hand, the department investigates how societies deal with the increasing transformation requirements of the global climate and biodiversity crisis (newer transformation sociology). The focus is often on how natural uses and environmental problems are mediated by the North-South relationship. It analyzes from an intersectional perspective the extent to which it has been possible to shape the desired transformation in a fair way, what unintended consequences and contradictions arise in the process, and how this affects internal and international inequalities.

  • Participation in administrative and organizational tasks in the department and at the institute, especially concerningcommittee work, publications and knowledge transfer
  • Conducting independent and collaborative research on sustainability and the challenges and asynchronies of socio-ecological transformation in different world regions
  • Writing a doctoral dissertation in the department's field of study
  • Assuming teaching responsibilities at the institute
  • Presentation of scientific results at national and international scientific conferences
  • A completed bachelor's or master's degree in sociology or a related social science discipline
  • Professional competencies in the field of environmental and transformation sociology, in particular debates on social inequalities and socio-ecological transformation
  • Experience in empirical social research and related methodological knowledge
  • Ability to independently plan, carry out, and document research projects; initial experience with submitting grant proposals is an advantage
  • Didactic competence and a commitment to the further development of innovative university teaching
  • Very good knowledge of German and English (level C1), knowledge of Spanish is an advantage
  • Ability to work in a team and interest in international networking; international experience is desirable
  • Interest in inter- and transdisciplinary cooperation; experience in cooperation with civil society actors is an advantage
  • On the basis of full-time employment (40 hours/week) the minimum salary in accordance with the collective agreement is € 3,776.10 gross per month (14 x per year, CA Job Grade: B1)
  • Stable employer
  • Attractive campus environment with good public transportation connections
  • Attractive continual educational opportunities
  • State-of-the-art research infrastructure
  • Dynamic research environment
  • Broad range of on-campus dining services/healthy meals (organic food at the cafeteria)
  • Exercise and sports classes (USI)
  • Collaboration in a new department at the Institute of Sociology
  • Collegial interaction
  • Family-friendly and, on request, flexible working hours (by arrangement)
  • …and much more

For further information please click here.

articles.title: New York University, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Clinical Assistant Professor - Economics

Liberal Studies at New York University invites applications for a Clinical Assistant Professor position to begin September 1, 2027, pending administrative and budgetary approval. The Liberal Studies Core is a dynamic liberal arts curriculum that provides a global and interdisciplinary foundation for nearly 100 NYU majors. The Global Liberal Studies Bachelor of Arts is an innovative global studies major grounded in the spatial, conceptual, and temporal understandings of a highly interconnected world, with a program of study that is distinguished by experiential learning, study away, and independent research focused in an interdisciplinary concentration. In both the LS Core and the GLS major, small, seminar-style classes and close faculty-student interaction provide students with the benefits of a liberal arts college within a large urban research university. The coordinators are especially interested in hiring qualified candidates who can contribute their research, teaching, and service to the diversity and excellence of Liberal Studies and NYU.

Candidates should be able to teach introductory microeconomics and macroeconomics in a liberal arts context from both mainstream and heterodox perspectives. The coordinators seek colleagues who, as needed, will teach intermediate and advanced courses in the listed fields of specialization in the Economy and Society Concentration (E&S) of Global Liberal Studies. Candidates should emphasize interdisciplinary and global connections in their teaching and research. They must apply theoretical analysis to real-world events in lectures and show a commitment to fostering an inclusive, collegial classroom environment.

Minimum qualifications: PhD by the date of appointment; three years of college-level teaching experience; and demonstrated excellence in teaching. The coordinators are especially interested in qualified candidates who share Liberal Studies’ commitment to equity, inclusion, and belonging, and who can contribute to the diversity of intellectual life in LS and NYU. Candidates must present demonstrated experience and commitment to interdisciplinarity, intersectionality, and a teaching approach informed by global perspectives. articles.title: Skidmore College, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Assistant Professor, Economics and Asian Studies

The Department of Economics at Skidmore College jointly with the Asian Studies Program invite applications for a tenure-track position at the assistant professor rank, beginning in the fall of 2027. This is the Frances Young Tang ’61 Professorship in Economics and Asian Studies. Applicants must possess a strong desire to teach and pursue research in a liberal arts environment in a department and program with a reputation for excellent teaching. The successful candidate will teach both electives and required courses in economics and Asian studies.

Applicable JEL Fields:

  • E [macroeconomics and monetary economics],
  • O11 [Macroeconomic Analyses of Economic Development],
  • O53 [Economywide country studies: Asia including middle east],
  • P5 [Comparative Economic Systems],
  • Z13 [Other special topics: Economic Sociology • Economic Anthropology • Language • Social and Economic Stratification]

Responsibilities:

  • Teach 18 credits per academic year in Economics and Asian Studies
  • Contribute to interdisciplinary offerings such as the First-Year experience or relevant College general education programs
  • Develop a coherent research stream and maintain a vigorous, ongoing research agenda that produces peer-reviewed publications in high-quality outlets.
  • Advise students and participate in departmental service activities.
  • Play a critical role in continuing to build the Asian Studies program through service.

Qualifications:

  • A minimum of a Ph.D. degree in Economics (advanced ABDs with dissertation defenses scheduled prior to the start of the fall semester 2027 will be considered).
  • Research interest and teaching capability in economics and Asian studies relating to China and Asia.
  • Evidence of teaching experience and promise and/or a teaching statement.
  • Three reference letters are required as part of the application.
  • One research paper to serve as evidence of scholarly promise is also required.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 30 November 2026

articles.title: University of Massachusetts Amherst, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Assistant Professor - Department of Economics

The Department of Economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst invites applications for an Assistant Professor appointment expected to start on September 1, 2027.

Preference will be given to innovative analytical methods, both empirical and theoretical, in a core area such as microeconomics, industrial organization, international trade and finance, and economic history, although economists in all fields are encouraged to apply. UMass Economics has a history and commitment to fostering a wide range of alternative perspectives and rigorous analytic methods for addressing economic challenges in innovative ways.

The teaching load is 2/2. Candidates will be judged on their scholarly research, as well as high quality and enthusiastic teaching. A completed Ph.D. in Economics or a closely related field is required by time of appointment. Current or previous external funding, or experience seeking external grants, is a plus.

Under exceptional circumstances, highly qualified candidates at other ranks may receive consideration.

Please find more info here.

Review of applications will begin on November 15, 2026, and continue until the position is filled. Preference will be given to applications received on or before November 15, 2026.

articles.title: University of Southern Denmark, Denmark
articles.body_html:
Job title: Tenure-Track Assistant Professor(s) Position in Economics

The Department of Economics at the University of Southern Denmark invites expressions of interest for applications for one or more tenure-track Assistant Professor positions in Economics. The department particularly welcomes applications in microeconomics (including applied microeconomic theory), macroeconomics, and econometrics and data science, including machine learning and computational methods for analyzing economic data. The department also welcomes applications from candidates specializing in economic history or environmental and resource economics.

Qualifications

Individuals must hold a PhD or equivalent qualification in Economics or a related field at the time of appointment and demonstrate strong potential for high-quality research, research-based teaching, and external research funding.

Responsibilities

  • Conduct top-tier research resulting in publications in prestigious international academic journals.
  • Engage in research-based teaching and supervision (including examination duties).
  • Engage in fundraising and grant writing activities.
  • Participate in course development and pedagogical initiatives.
  • Maintain and develop relationships with appropriate stakeholders.
  • Perform academic, knowledge dissemination/outreach, and administrative tasks.

The working language of the department is English. SDU offers free Danish language courses to support successful candidates in contributing to teaching and supervision in Danish. Language-learning needs and expectations will be assessed individually, taking account of any existing proficiency in Norwegian or Swedish.

For more information about the position, please contact Head of Administration Astrid Holm Nielsen or Head of Department Lone Grønbæk Jørgensen.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 6 December 2026

articles.title: Vienna University of Economics and Business (WU), Austria
articles.body_html:
Job title: Tenure-track assistant professorship in Economic History

You want to understand how things are connected and make a fundamental impact? The institute for Economic and Social History offers an environment where you can realize your full potential. At one of Europe’s largest and most modern business and economics universities. On a campus where quality of work is also quality of life.

A qualification agreement will be concluded at the start of the employment (§ 27 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement). Pursuant to WU’s Personnel Development Plan, this position can only be fixed-term for up to six years. Once all objectives agreed upon in the qualification agreement have been fulfilled, the employment relationship can be made permanent. Employees who have successfully completed a qualification agreement are classified as associate professors. From an organizational regulation perspective they belong to the group of professors. Three years after successful completion of the qualification agreement, they are entitled to apply for promotion to full professor according to the By-Laws of WU § 43a.

The institute is inviting applications for an Assistant Professor position (tenure track) in the field of Economic History to join our institute. This tenure track assistant professor position offers the opportunity to advance an independent research profile, publish internationally, acquire funding and gain substantial teaching experience while working collaboratively within a close-knit group of colleagues who share a strong interest in the field. Join an ambitious, internationally connected academic environment to take the next step in your academic career.

What to expect

  • Development of an internationally oriented research profile
  • Publications in relevant high-quality outlets and presentations at relevant international conferences
  • Teaching at BSc and MSc level (usually 4h/week per semester, 8h/week after tenure), collaboration in the development of the institute’s teaching portfolio
  • Collaboration and independent supervision of BSc and MSc theses
  • Participation in teaching and research administration within the academic self-administration at WU
  • Independent or collaborative preparation of applications for third-party funded research projects.

What you have to offer

  • PhD/doctorate in Economic and/or Social Sciences (including Economic History).
  • Proven research focus on topics relating to Economic History; applications from all areas of quantitative economic history are welcome.
  • Excellent command of quantitative empirical methods of the economic and social sciences; the use of modern use of modern econometric and/or data science methods is expected
  • Ability to develop and work with relevant datasets for the aforementioned research focus
  • Publication(s) and/or forthcoming articles in leading journals and/or monograph(s) with academic publishers.
  • Demonstrated active engagement with the international academic community, for example, through collaboration with international coauthors, research visits at other universities, or presentations at leading academic conferences.
  • Candidates must have completed their PhD at a university other than WU or have at least two years of postdoctoral working experience at another university. It is an advantage if they demonstrate international academic experience—such as a PhD from a non-Austrian university or postdoctoral work at a non-Austrian academic institution for at least two years.
  • Excellent spoken and written English skills; German skills are not required, but knowledge and/or willingness to acquire them will be an advantage, as they improve flexibility in teaching.
  • Experience in university teaching, preferably in the announced area of expertise, ability to teach in English and commitment to excellence in teaching
  • Experience in applying for competitive research grants is not strictly required, but will be of advantage
  • Willingness to engage in interdisciplinary research and teaching collaborations within the Department of Socioeconomics and at WU.

What the institute offers you

  • Flexible working hours
  • Training opportunities
  • A wide range of benefits, from an in-house medical officer to athletic activities and a meal allowance to a variety of employee discounts
  • Meaningful work in an open-minded, inclusive, and family-friendly environment
  • A modern campus with spectacular architecture in the heart of Vienna
  • Inspiring campus life with over 2,400 employees in research, teaching, and administration and approximately 21,500 students
  • Excellent accessibility by public transportation
  • Living and working in one of the world’s most livable cities.
  • Tax incentive for eligible international researchers moving to Austria.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 18 November 2026

articles.title: Call for Applications: New Competition School Award for Best Commentary
articles.body_html:
The New Competition School (NCS) is a community of academics, members of civil society, practitioners and journalists seeking to address rising concentrations of private corporate power and the economic, political and societal dangers that flow from it. Members have teamed up with Tech Policy Press (TPP), to launch the New Competition School Award for Best Commentary.

The Award aims to recognise and platform outstanding work by students interested in competition law, economics and policy. The organizers are looking for lively, practical contributions with a touch of ingenuity, which have the potential to shift the Overton window within competition law and policy. Entries to the award should be complete drafts of a short article suitable for publication in TPP between 800 and 1500 words, themed around one of the two topics for this year: breakups and acts of economic aggression (for more info, see link below). It should be accessible to a policy-literate, but non-specialist audience.

Entries must be written in English and submitted before the 30th of November (subject to extension). Entrants must be enrolled in a university degree, or have completed such a degree in the last three years (not including career breaks for caring responsibilities etc -- please get in touch if you are unsure). Co-authorship is encouraged, especially where it facilitates interdisciplinarity, providing all authors are eligible.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 30 November 2026

articles.title: Call for Applications: UW/H Young Scholar Award for Outstanding Research in PPE
articles.body_html:
Witten/Herdecke University invites applications and nominations for the UW/H Young Scholar Award for Outstanding Research in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE). The award recognises outstanding early-career researchers whose work makes original and rigorous contributions to PPE and related interdisciplinary fields.

Three prizes will be awarded:

  • First Prize: €2,500
  • Second Prize: €1,500
  • Third Prize: €1,000

The prize money is generously funded by the UH/H-Stiftung.

The Award is open to early-career scholars working in PPE or a closely related field, for example political science, economics, political theory, social theory, public policy, institutional analysis, ethics or law.

As a general guide, candidates should normally be within six years of the successful defence or official acceptance of their doctoral dissertation. The organizers take career interruptions and other justified exceptions into account. Submitted work should be written in English or German. Work in other languages may be considered with a substantial English summary.

The Award is not tied to a single method. Theoretical, normative, empirical, historical and formal work is as welcome as qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods approaches. What counts is the contribution to PPE. Many topics are conceivable, from democracy and justice to sustainability and inequality, technological change, public health and global order.

Please combine the following documents in a single PDF file:

  • Curriculum vitae
  • List of publications
  • A statement (maximum two pages) on what the research contributes to PPE and why it matters for the field
  • Confirmation of the successful defence or official acceptance of the dissertation, including the date of completion
  • Two or three representative research outputs (journal articles, working papers or dissertation chapters)
  • For nominations: a short nomination letter
  • Optional: one academic reference or supervisor's statement

Submit applications to Jan-Christoph Heilinger.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 15 February 2027

articles.title: Call for Nominations: ESHET Awards 2027
articles.body_html:
The ESHET Council is inviting nominations for the Awards that will be announced at the next annual Conference in Athens, Greece, 3-5 June 2027. Nominations should be sent as soon as possible, but not later than 30 December 2026 to the Chair of the relevant panel. Self-nominations are not accepted for any of the prizes. Subsequently each nominee will be asked to submit to the Council three publications on which s/he wishes to be judged.

Best Monograph Award

The Best Monograph Award is for the best book (not necessarily written in English) in the history of economic thought published during 2025 or 2026. The author can be from any part of the world. The winner will be invited to attend the Society Conference that follows the announcement of the prize to deliver the Jérôme-Adolphe Blanqui Lecture. Note that, in supplement, the Council can also give a Scholarly Edition Award.

Chair: Erwin Dekker

History of Economic Analysis Award

The History of Economic Analysis Award is for the best article (not necessarily written in English) in the history of economic thought, published in the issue of a scientific journal during 2025 or 2026. Candidates can be from any part of the world. The winner will be invited to attend the Society Conference that follows the announcement of the prize and will receive an award of 500 euro.

Chair: Nathalie Sigot

ESHET Young Researcher Award

This prize recognizes scholarly achievements of historians of economic thought who are at an early stage of their career. The prize is awarded to scholars below the age of 40 at the time of the annual conference in recognition of outstanding publications in the history of economic thought. The winner will receive an award of 1,000 euro and have their conference fee waived in the year following the announcement of the prize.

Chair: Renee Prendergast

Gilles Dostaler Award

The Gilles Dostaler Award is an award created in the memory of Gilles Dostaler, thanks to the generosity of his widow Marielle Cauchy. This prize recognizes scholarly achievements of young research fellows working on one of Gilles Dostaler’s many fields of interest — e.g., Marx and classical political economy; Keynes; Hayek; critical approaches to free market theories; and relationships between economics, politics, philosophy and ethics. It is awarded to scholars below the age of 35 at the time of the annual conference in recognition of an outstanding article not necessarily already published or published within the two previous years. The winner will receive an award of 500 euro and have their conference fee waived in the year following the announcement.

Chair: Michel Zouboulakis

Nominations for the book and article prizes should include:

  1. Full bibliographic details of the book or article.
  2. A short statement (in English) of why the book or article merits being considered for a prize.
  3. An electronic copy of the book or article, if this is available.

Nominations for the Young Researcher Award should include:

  1. A short resume stating the achievements of the candidate.
  2. A CV including a list of publications.

articles.full_text: The ESHET Council is inviting nominations for the Awards that will be announced at the next annual Conference in Athens, Greece, 3-5 June 2027. Nominations should be sent as soon as possible, but not later than 30 December 2026 to the Chair of the relevant panel. Self-nominations are not accepted for any of the prizes. Subsequently each nominee will be asked to submit to the Council three publications on which s/he wishes to be judged. Best Monograph Award The Best Monograph Award is for the best book (not necessarily written in English) in the history of economic thought published during 2025 or 2026. The author can be from any part of the world. The winner will be invited to attend the Society Conference that follows the announcement of the prize to deliver the Jérôme-Adolphe Blanqui Lecture. Note that, in supplement, the Council can also give a Scholarly Edition Award. Chair: Erwin Dekker History of Economic Analysis Award The History of Economic Analysis Award is for the best article (not necessarily written in English) in the history of economic thought, published in the issue of a scientific journal during 2025 or 2026. Candidates can be from any part of the world. The winner will be invited to attend the Society Conference that follows the announcement of the prize and will receive an award of 500 euro. Chair: Nathalie Sigot ESHET Young Researcher Award This prize recognizes scholarly achievements of historians of economic thought who are at an early stage of their career. The prize is awarded to scholars below the age of 40 at the time of the annual conference in recognition of outstanding publications in the history of economic thought. The winner will receive an award of 1,000 euro and have their conference fee waived in the year following the announcement of the prize. Chair: Renee Prendergast Gilles Dostaler Award The Gilles Dostaler Award is an award created in the memory of Gilles Dostaler, thanks to the generosity of his widow Marielle Cauchy. This prize recognizes scholarly achievements of young research fellows working on one of Gilles Dostaler’s many fields of interest — e.g., Marx and classical political economy; Keynes; Hayek; critical approaches to free market theories; and relationships between economics, politics, philosophy and ethics. It is awarded to scholars below the age of 35 at the time of the annual conference in recognition of an outstanding article not necessarily already published or published within the two previous years. The winner will receive an award of 500 euro and have their conference fee waived in the year following the announcement. Chair: Michel Zouboulakis Nominations for the book and article prizes should include: Full bibliographic details of the book or article. A short statement (in English) of why the book or article merits being considered for a prize. An electronic copy of the book or article, if this is available. Nominations for the Young Researcher Award should include: A short resume stating the achievements of the candidate. A CV including a list of publications.

articles.title: A Critical History of Double Entry Accounting 1150–1800
articles.body_html:
By Alan Sangster | 2025, World Scientific

The English language accounting history of double entry accounting before 1800 has reached an impasse. The doors to its reawakening are fiercely guarded by combination locks powered by confirmation bias and adherence to a priori wisdom requiring vast amounts of supportive scholarship to make public the smallest contribution to what is known and understood of the first 600 years of its use. To open those doors, a foundation is needed upon which scholarship can begin anew — a framework of reference that can be used to justify the validity and relevance of scholarship and discovery in this field. That is the purpose and role of this book.

It does not focus on the technical. It focuses on the environment and context of use of the method, and its function. It considers 'why' and consequences. It asks who, when, where, and what, along with 'how'. It adopts the perspective that the reason for the bookkeeping drove how it was adopted, not the availability of parchment or paper, nor the emergence of the concept of the technology — the book — in which it was recorded. Rather its use was driven by a need of the person who wrote the record, or by the needs of those who wished a record to be kept.

A critical traditional historical method is adopted. Explanations are sought and identified utilising knowledge of the environment and context of practice that, to this point, rarely if ever feature in the antiquarian historiography this book ideally seeks to replace. The approach adopted is multi-disciplinary and the sources used are multi-disciplinary and multi-lingual. This book is essential reading for anyone with an interest in accounting's past.

Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: Fighting for the American Dream: From Blue-Collar Kid to Maverick Economist, The Battle to Defend Working Families
articles.body_html:
by Charles J. Whalen | September 2026, Bloomsbury

Explores the decades-long erosion of the American Dream from the author's perspective: a working-class kid who became a celebrated economist dedicated to advancing the interests of struggling workers, while also caught in the same currents of job insecurity and downward mobility as the people he aimed to defend.

Worker insecurity, increasing inequality, and downward mobility in our current era contrast sharply with expanding prosperity and opportunity in the first three decades after World War II. What happened? And what can we do to revitalize the American Dream, reduce worker precarity, and foster broadly shared prosperity?

In this historical account of a protracted and expanding national crisis, intertwined with a personal story about growing up in a work-obsessed family and pursuing a career devoted to addressing that crisis, Charles J. Whalen grapples with the social forces that sever the link between hard work and employment success. He exposes the obstacles that mar the path of many people seeking job opportunities and traces the fading of the American Dream, ultimately encouraging readers to take a fresh look at the current economic situation and championing a more constructive set of public policies to shape the future.

He exposes the obstacles that mar the path of many people seeking job opportunities and traces the fading of the American Dream, ultimately encouraging readers to take a fresh look at the current economic situation and championing a more constructive set of public policies to shape the future. articles.title: Governance of the Local Co-creation of the Green Transition: A Global Perspective
articles.body_html:
Edited by Christopher Ansell, Eva Sørensen and Jacob Torfing | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This book provides an innovative theoretical framework for studying the governance of the local co-creation of environmental solutions. Expert contributors comparatively analyse a series of international case studies to discern similarities and differences across local collaborations between public, private and civic actors working towards the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Focusing on local sustainability transitions from a broad spectrum of socio-political regimes, contributors examine key questions concerning the role of community capital, cultural context, conflict mediation and public sector capacity. They discuss empirical findings from the GOGREEN Project, exploring factors which support and challenge activists in their efforts to co-create sustainability transitions. Chapters assess the impact of private entrepreneurs initiating and facilitating green co-creation, as well as conflict resolution in sustainable energy projects.

International in scope and perspective, this is an essential read for researchers and graduate students of public policy, environmental studies and sustainable governance. Policymakers and practitioners working in environmental governance and regulation, as well as those focusing on implementing the SDGs, will likewise benefit from its novel and timely analysis.

articles.title: Macroeconomics Has No Clothes: A New Treatise of Macroeconomics
articles.body_html:
by Zuoshi Xie | 2026, Sheer Echonomics

This book will change the way you think about macroeconomics for good.

It strips away the blackboard abstractions and exposes what's really driving economic outcomes. Read it once, and you'll never misread the economic climate again. Early on, the book introduces pseudo-GDP—an original concept developed by Professor Xie—to cut through the illusion of false prosperity and challenge core assumptions behind government intervention. It goes further, arguing that GDP accounting has no real logic of production behind it, and that among its three components, only investment truly drives growth. From this foundation, Professor Xie offers a bold new explanation for why China's system of public land ownership has fueled its extraordinary economic growth.

This book dismantles the conventional separation of aggregate supply and demand, treating them instead as two sides of the same coin. Recessions, it argues, stem from erroneous production—not insufficient effective demand, as conventional theory holds. This single insight renders the textbook AS-AD model obsolete. Building from first principles and plain common sense, the book reveals how exchange rates really adjust: real exchange rates move either through nominal rates or through wages and prices—turning exchange rate theory into a practical lens for understanding today's global economy. It offers fresh, original perspectives on the income gap and optimal tariffs, departing sharply from conventional wisdom. Nearly every page rewards careful readers with a new way of seeing familiar problems. This isn't another theory added to the pile. It's a unified framework that finally connects the dots.

articles.title: Marx’s Capital
articles.body_html:
by Ben Fine and Alfredo Saad-Filho | 2026, Pluto Press

‘This expert guide to the political economy of Marx’s Capital has always been the very best available’ – David Harvey

Now it its 7th edition.

Whether you are a student of economics, a political activist, or merely trying to make sense of a world in upheaval, Marx’sCapital is a beginner’s guide to one of the most influential and eye-opening critiques of capitalism.

In today’s world of deep inequality, recurring financial meltdowns, and the climate crisis, understanding Marx’s ideas is more important than ever, but reading him alone can be daunting.

In this updated seventh edition, Ben Fine and Alfredo Saad-Filho strip away the jargon, guiding readers through the essential pillars of Marxian political economy: from the Labour Theory of Value and the secret of Primitive Accumulation to the internal contradictions that trigger systemic crises and potentially lead to revolution.

articles.title: Money Beyond Borders: Global Currencies from Croesus to Crypto
articles.body_html:
By Barry Eichengreen | 2026, Princeton University Press

Doubts about the international dominance of the dollar are only growing amid worries about tariffs, political dysfunction, and fraying international alliances. Will the dollar continue to reign supreme? In Money Beyond Borders, the leading authority on international currencies, Barry Eichengreen, puts the dollar’s prospects in deep historical perspective by chronicling the entire history of cross-border currencies, from the invention of coins in the seventh century BCE to the cryptocurrencies of today and the central bank digital currencies of tomorrow.

Money Beyond Borders recounts how Greek and Roman coins became the first true international currencies. It tells how the Florentine gold florin became the “greenback of the Renaissance,” and how it was succeeded by Spanish silver and a Dutch fiat currency. The book explains why the British pound dominated the international economy in the nineteenth century, why the dollar rose to the top during World War II, and why the dollar has survived predictions of the imminent loss of its preeminence since the 1970s.

The long history of international currencies shows that the same factors that encourage their widespread use eventually lead to their abandonment. Money Beyond Borders makes a powerful case that the dollar is now on the downside of this cycle, and it considers who the winners and losers will be when there is flight away from the greenback. Revealing important patterns in the life cycles of international currencies over the past 2,500 years, the book offers valuable lessons and insights about how currencies rise—and why they fall.

articles.title: Neoliberal Fascism: The Crisis of Capitalism and the Rise of the Far-Right
articles.body_html:
By Alfredo Saad-Filho | 2026, Pluto Press

From the rise of Trump and the MAGA movement to the strongman politics of Modi and Bolsonaro, a new wave of spectacular authoritarianism is sweeping the globe.

Alfredo Saad-Filho argues this is no accident, but the inevitable structural outcome of fifty years of neoliberalism hollowing out democracy and intensifying inequality. This emerging political form, ‘neoliberal fascism,’ marries the ruthless defense of free-market interests with the exclusionary violence of classic fascism. By mobilizing mass resentment against fabricated enemies like immigrants and the so-called deep state, these regimes distract from economic devastation to build a totalitarian state far more resilient than traditional dictatorships.

Neoliberal Fascism offers a path for resistance, urging a struggle for a renewed, inclusive democracy that transcends the failures of the past.

articles.title: Radical Expectations: How the New Left Changed Economics
articles.body_html:
by Tiago Mata | 2026, Cambridge University Press

In the 1970s radical economists campaigned to reform their discipline and their universities. They became journalists and activists, moving beyond academia, to forge new models of public engagement and collaborative knowledge in economic life. Radical Expectations tells the story of how these economists set out to make economics more democratic. It traces their campaign to bring protest movements to the campuses, triggering the emergence of an alternative understanding of expertise directed at validating and empowering the perspectives and voices of women, Black Americans, labor activists, and the urban poor. It shows how a radical identity formed and how radicals helped reform disciplinary institutions. Furthermore, it argues that the radical economics' legacy was the development of a language and models of expert–lay collaboration that empowers direct action in economic affairs. The book is about the community of radical economists who championed the promise of change and what came of it.

  • Provides the first real history of radical economics
  • Integrates science studies (knowledge and society co-production) with the history of economics
  • Takes a novel approach to the crisis of expertise plaguing our political moment

articles.title: Rebellion and Reconnection for Sustainable Futures: A critical framework for practical politics
articles.body_html:
By Robert Biel | 2026, UCL Press

We stand at a point of crisis for human society and life on Earth, with sustainability a constant theme in global discourse. Governments, industries and individuals attempt to take constructive action, but their steps are everywhere countered by the habits and relationships built over 300 years of capitalism, while right-wing populism and climate denial openly hold them back. Rebellion and Reconnection for Sustainable Futures proposes an urgent change of direction.

Grounded in the critical and theoretical tradition of political ecology, the book calls for a practical politics that rebels against the dominance of nature, resists fascist populism and reconnects with human tradition. Robert Biel argues that two forms of ‘remembering’ are needed, first that we embrace humanity’s past connection with socio-ecological change through deep time, and second that we assimilate still-valuable socialist traditions such as dignity and creativity of work. From this basis, he proposes a novel synthesis between complex systems research, Indigenous one-ness with nature, the ‘good Anthropocene’, and Marxist perspectives on nature. This unlocks a broad interrogation of the COVID experience by drawing on notions of biopolitics and queer theory, while also re-framing theories of imperialism to critique the central role of racism. Written in an engaging style, the book builds a compelling case for a new practical and actionable politics based on reclaiming what we have lost.

articles.title: Should Money Be Obsolete?
articles.body_html:
by A.S. Gailey | 2026, Self-Published

What if money-the tool built to make life easier-has become the force quietly keeping humanity from thriving?

In Should Money Be Obsolete?, Dr. A.S. Gailey challenges one of the deepest assumptions of modern life: that money-based trade is not only necessary, but the best system available. Drawing from history, economics, psychology, politics, health care, food systems, media, industry, and government, Gailey examines how money creates conflicts of interest between buyers and sellers, citizens and institutions, workers and employers, and even patients and the industries meant to heal them.

Rather than simply criticizing capitalism or calling for socialism or communism, Gailey asks readers to think beyond familiar ideological categories. Could private enterprise still exist without money? Could innovation, motivation, and resource distribution function in a system no longer driven by profit? And could such a transition happen peacefully, gradually, and practically?

For readers ready to question the economic foundation of everyday life, this book offers a bold invitation: imagine what society could become if money were no longer at its center.

articles.title: Stablecoins: Law, Regulation and Technology
articles.body_html:
By Erica Stanford | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

Combining legal analysis with technical and commercial insight, this essential Practical Guide explains what stablecoins are, how they are used and why they matter. Erica Stanford responds to the rapidly changing laws, risks and technology surrounding stablecoins as they transition from crypto markets to the core of finance, payments and regulation. Chapters address key topics from issuance, reserves, design and innovation to redemption and custody, financial crime, taxation and due diligence.

Key Inclusions:

  • How stablecoins differ from cryptoassets, tokenised deposits and central bank digital currencies
  • Real-world applications for crypto markets, payments, remittances, financial inclusion, humanitarian finance, insurance, gig work and in tokenisation and agentic payments and the machine economy
  • Case studies and practical frameworks necessary for assessing stablecoin arrangements with both commercial realism and legal discipline
  • The crucial features of major and emerging stablecoin regimes, such as those in the EU, UK, Switzerland, the USA and UAE, as well as offshore jurisdictions
  • Risks, enforcement and mitigation tools including blockchain analytics, tracing, freezing and asset forfeiture

Stablecoins is an essential resource for legal practitioners, in-house counsel and law firms advising on stablecoins, cryptoassets, finance and banking law and corporate law. Compliance and money laundering reporting officers and those working in anti-fraud services will also benefit from discussions on the risks of stablecoins and how they can be used in digital economic crime.

articles.title: Sustainable Finance Beyond Market Utopias
articles.body_html:
edited by Ulrich Klüh, Lisa Knoll, Daniel Mertens & Silke Ötsch | 2026, Metropolis (Ökonomie und Gesellschaft (38))

Towards a Sociopolitical Approach

Politics and the economic mainstream have placed great expectations on sustainable finance. The disclosure of climate-related financial risks and moderate incentives for private capital are intended to direct financial assets into sustainable investments - so far with limited success.

The contributions in this volume examine the activities, strategies, and positions of actors from finance, regulation, civil society, and the real economy. They show why sustainable finance strategies fall short of their claims: their theoretical assumptions prove to be incorrect, and they operate within a narrowly defined political framework.

From sociological, political science, and heterodox economic perspectives, the volume considers sustainable finance in its social context. It analyzes the possibilities and limits of a financial sector that is supposed to contribute to socio-ecological transformation and asks how sustainable finance can be rethought and realigned beyond market-centered governance approaches.

You can download the PDF-Version free of charge from the publishers website (link below).

articles.title: The Original Error: Why Macroeconomics Keeps on Failing
articles.body_html:
By Mathew Coakley | 2026, Atmosphere Press

Critiques of mainstream macroeconomics have identified problems in its omissions, behavioural assumptions and theoretical structure. The Original Error makes a different case: that some of the deepest difficulties originate in the standard theory of production itself. It argues that this mistake helps generate persistent puzzles about recessions, profits, firms, investment, bargaining and why similar workers can earn radically different wages depending on where they live. The proposed remedy is not another refinement within modern DSGE modelling – another friction, heterogeneity or auxiliary assumption – but a replacement theory of production. The book develops Asset Theory as that alternative foundation, and then uses it to revisit a range of persistent mismatches between economic theory and observed reality.

articles.title: The Social Economy: Things and People
articles.body_html:
By David Reisman | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

In The Social Economy David Reisman argues for a social economics that centres on the role of human choice and behaviour. Rejecting the reduction of the economy to the efficient allocation of scarce goods and services, he proposes that it be examined as the meaningful interaction of real-world people engaged in production, consumption, distribution and exchange.

Arguing that the economy is the whole as well as the part, the book advocates a broader understanding of economics. From the sovereign individual to the social organism, Reisman demonstrates that economic activities are governed by norms, values, rights and duties, as well as being dependent on habits, heuristics and bounded rationality. He emphasises that without our memories and ideologies there would be no economic processes to meet our needs and wants. He supports his contention with reference to areas such as work and creativity, shared institutions, social capital and the economics of envy.

Interdisciplinary in scope, The Social Economy is an essential resource for scholars and students of economic theory, economic sociology, institutional economics and the history of economic thought. Practitioners and social policymakers will also find value in its comprehensive coverage of current debates.

articles.full_text: By David Reisman | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing In The Social Economy David Reisman argues for a social economics that centres on the role of human choice and behaviour. Rejecting the reduction of the economy to the efficient allocation of scarce goods and services, he proposes that it be examined as the meaningful interaction of real-world people engaged in production, consumption, distribution and exchange. Arguing that the economy is the whole as well as the part, the book advocates a broader understanding of economics. From the sovereign individual to the social organism, Reisman demonstrates that economic activities are governed by norms, values, rights and duties, as well as being dependent on habits, heuristics and bounded rationality. He emphasises that without our memories and ideologies there would be no economic processes to meet our needs and wants. He supports his contention with reference to areas such as work and creativity, shared institutions, social capital and the economics of envy. Interdisciplinary in scope, The Social Economy is an essential resource for scholars and students of economic theory, economic sociology, institutional economics and the history of economic thought. Practitioners and social policymakers will also find value in its comprehensive coverage of current debates. Please find a link to the book here .

articles.body_html:
by Joanna Sullivan | 2026, Routledge

Through over 50 personal interviews with women leading high-profile organisations, this book reveals emerging trends and highlights innovative strategies uniquely crafted by women. These trailblazing experts and pioneers in European Union policymaking are pushing the boundaries of sustainability, offering invaluable insights for a greener, fairer future beyond 2030. Their stories serve as powerful examples to inspire the next generation of young women pursuing careers in sustainability. This book showcases the effectiveness of their initiatives and the growing movement for change inspired by their actions.

Women Leading Sustainability: The Feminine Shift is an empowering resource designed to inspire and uplift current and future women leaders, as they work towards shaping a more sustainable world, offering powerful lessons to established changemakers and young men and women starting their sustainability careers. The seven strengths of ‘the Feminine Shift’ are at the heart of future leadership.

articles.title: Högbom-Cocozza Foundation: Two research fellowships in economic history at Linköping University
articles.category: Heterodox Graduate Programs, Scholarships and Grants
articles.body_html:
The Högbom-Cocozza Foundation invites applications for two three-year postdoctoral research fellowships in economic history. The Foundation aims to contribute to the development of a strong research environment in economic history at Linköping University and to support early-career researchers with high scientific potential. The fellow will be affiliated to the Division of Economics at the Department of Management and Engineering at Linköping University.

Focus of the fellowships

Two fellowships will be awarded in economic history, broadly defined as the study of how economies and the material conditions of life have developed over the long run, and how economic processes have interacted with institutions, technology, politics, and society. The field draws on both the analytical tools of economics and the source-based methods of history.

We welcome projects on any aspect of the field. These might address, for example, economic growth and development, living standards and inequality, labour, demography, trade and globalisation, institutions and the state, technology and innovation, or entrepreneurship and business. Projects using quantitative methods applied to historical databases, register data, or other historical sources are particularly encouraged, but we also welcome applications using qualitative or mixed-method approaches.

Terms

The fellowships cover three years of full-time research, with a planned start in mid-2027 or by agreement.

Each fellowship is awarded as a tax-free stipend amounting to a total of SEK 1,965,000 for the entire three-year period and is paid semi-annually in advance directly to the fellow. The stipend is intended to cover living expenses, personal insurance (life, accident, and health insurance), and pension contributions.

To be eligible, applicants must hold a doctoral degree in economic history or a closely related field (for example economics, economic geography, economic demography, statistics or history) awarded no more than five years before the application deadline.

The fellow is expected to conduct their research at Linköping University, Campus Valla, and to be resident and registered as living in the Municipality of Linköping during the fellowship period.

Application

The application must include:

  • Curriculum vitae.
  • List of publications.
  • Research plan (max. 5 pages including reference list).
  • A brief statement of why the fellowship is being sought.
  • Contact details for two referees.

The application should be submitted as a single PDF file to economics.nek@iei.liu.se. Please state the reference PD-EH-2026 in the subject line of the email and in the application.

Application deadline: 1 December 2026.

For further information please click here.

articles.title: The Levy Economics Institute's Graduate Programs in Economic Theory and Policy
articles.category: Heterodox Graduate Programs, Scholarships and Grants
articles.body_html:
The Levy Economics Institute's Graduate Programs in Economic Theory and Policy are accepting applications for 2027—2028.

Levy's Master of Arts (MA) and Master of Science (MS) in Economic Theory and Policy combine a rigorous course of study with the exceptional opportunity to participate in advanced economics research at the Levy Economics Institute, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank with 40 years of economic experience. The curriculum provides a solid foundation in both neoclassical and heterodox economic theory, policy, and empirical research methods.

The institute offers several academic scholarships in honor of our Distinguished Scholars, including Hyman Minsky and Wynne Godley. The programs are housed at Bard College, a cultural nexus for the arts and progressive intellectual thought in the Hudson Valley of New York State.

For a complete description of the program and how to apply, please visitLevyGrad.Bard.edu.

Contact Karley Sullivan at ksullivan@levy.org with any questions.

Apply here.

Early Decision Deadline: 15 January 2027

Regular Decision Deadline: 15 April 2027

articles.title: Democratizing Work Newslettter #19
articles.body_html:
Democratizing Work is a global academic consortium born in May 2020 from a collective call to action: to democratize firms, decommodify work, and remediate the environment. Sparked by an op-ed published simultaneously in 43 newspapers and signed by over 6,000 scholars from 700 institutions worldwide, the movement has grown into an international network of researchers rethinking the role of work in our societies. Through research, dialogue, and collaboration with different stakeholders (policy makers, trade unionists, business leaders, NGOs), #DemocratizingWork seeks to build an economic future that is democratic, dignified, and sustainable — where people and the planet, not profit, are at the center.

The intitative puts out a monthly Newsletter. The current Issue of the Democratizing Work Newsletter for example features Information on the Conference: AI: Worker Voice as Critical Internal Conditionand a global Workshop series.

You can follow the Democratizing Work Newsletter here.

articles.title: Launch of the Garegnani Archive
articles.body_html:
Centro Sraffa is pleased to announce that the Garegnani Archive website is now online at www.garegnaniarchive.it. Its launch marks an important step in our work to preserve Pierangelo Garegnani’s scholarly legacy and make it more widely accessible. The editors believe that the archive will be a valuable research resource, and hope that its opening will give fresh impetus to studies contributing to the revival of the theoretical approach of the Classical economists, to which Garegnani made a fundamental contribution.

The website hosts the catalogue of the documents held in the archive. Searches by word or phrase allow users to identify both archival units, corresponding to the folders of documents originally assembled by Garegnani, and individual documents within them whose titles contain the search terms.

The editors should, however, point out that the catalogue still contains some inaccuracies, particularly in the transcription of archival unit titles and the cataloguing of certain documents. The economists involved in the project have begun reviewing the catalogue. However, to make the website available as soon as possible and meet the deadlines associated with the project’s public funding, we decided to launch it before completing this review, which will be concluded in due course. The editors would therefore particularly welcome reports of inaccuracies and errors from researchers using the website.

A large proportion of the documents described in the catalogue can be consulted at Centro Sraffa.

Finally, Centro Sraffa would like to remind you that the event “Capital, Distribution and Growth. Garegnani Archive Inaugural Conference” will take place in Rome at Roma Tre University on 19 and 20 November 2026. For the conference programme see here or the Centro Sraffa website.

articles.title: Open Invitation to Participate in the Decolonial Digital Social Sciences Network (DDSSN)
articles.body_html:
The Decolonial Digital Social Sciences Network (DDSSN), a free, voluntary and non-hierarchical international network for researchers, students and practitioners interested in critical social sciences and humanities, shares an open invitation to participate.

The network welcomes work on critical political economy, class, labour, capitalism, coloniality, decolonial and postcolonial theory, feminist and antiracist scholarship, Indigenous perspectives, media and culture. A focus on digital technologies is not required.

Participants may exchange research, initiate collaborations and help shape activities collectively. There are no membership fees or mandatory duties. Participation in the network is separate from any editorial or scientific advisory board appointment.

Please find more info here.

Please find the participation group here.

issues.title: Heterodox Economics Newsletter #366
issues.editorial_html:
The production of this Newsletter issue was slightly overshadowed by the disruptive impact of AI on our shared computer and internet infrastructure 😅. Critical PHP vulnerabilities, brought to light with AI assistance (see here or here), forced us to take our background machinery down for a while. Our busy-bee editorial team was sadly stalled by this exogenous disruption 😢. However, emergency rescue was quick and efficient – much applause goes to bendlas for first-class and fun emergency intervention services, jointly with the head editor 🎉🚀😂. Still somewhat stressful, though.

In any case, one might say that this disruption served a useful purpose: exposing the bugs and fixing them should make our shared infrastructure safer. In our case, disruption did not turn into destruction – luckily, we were quick enough to shut down our exposed servers with our mobile phones 🤪. However, there are many instances where AI and the way we use it can be destructive in a narrower sense, with ecological costs, undermined learning and the degradation of our shared information environment (here, here or here) being key concerns. As I nonetheless believe that a reflective attitude towards AI is possible (students use it anyway, so why not at least give it a try?), I have prepared a somewhat idiosyncratic, and hopefully fun, guide on how to use AI for my students. If you wanna have a look, you can check it out here.

In more practical terms, without infrastructure there is also no Newsletter, and it would have been a true pity to withhold the current issue from you, which is really rich in opportunity and substance. Aside from the more beaten paths, I cherished hearing about an updated version of the DIY Macroeconomic Model Simulation site (which was already super-impressive without the update 😅), two fresh calls for Erasmus Mundus MA programmes with a strong heterodox component (see here and here), a Special Issue on ‚The Euro at 25‘ in the Review of Evolutionary Political Economy (see here and below) and the Wealth Cap initiative, with its timely proposals on a key question in (heterodox) economics: how to actually put the “wealth of nations” to good use…

Alongside all this good news, there is also sad news: in recent weeks, Perry Mehrling and Anwar Shaikh have left us. Both were giants in heterodox economics in their own, idiosyncratic and impressive ways, and the lasting imprint of their work ensures that we will never forget them. Below, we have collected the tributes that reached the editorial office: a statement from the History of Economics Society for Perry and an obituary by Nikolaos Chatzarakis for Anwar.

All the best,
Jakob

articles.title: 16th Annual Workshop on Growth, History and Development (Odense, March 2027)
articles.body_html:
12 March, 2027 | Odense, Denmark

Workshop theme: A History of (Women’s) Work - Work, Gender and Economic Development

The Historical Economics and Development Group (HEDG) at SDU invites submissions for the 16th Annual Workshop on Growth, History and Development. All are welcome, but junior faculty and graduate students are particularly encouraged to apply.

Who counts as a worker, and whose work counts? How have technology and social change reshaped the work of women and men?

This year’s workshop explores the history of work and its relationship with economic development, with particular attention to women’s experiences. We welcome papers on paid and unpaid work, labor-force participation, wages, and occupational segregation, as well as the role of technology, institutions, and social norms in shaping opportunities. Historical and contemporary perspectives are encouraged, including new sources and methods that reveal work overlooked in conventional statistics.

Submissions on all topics relating to growth, history, and development are welcome, but those exploring the workshop theme will be prioritized.

Prospective speakers should submit an extended abstract (max. 1000 words), including methodology and main results, to Sophie Yiwen Li (soli@sam.sdu.dk), who is also the contact for inquiries.

The workshop is a one-day event. There is a registration fee of 600 DKK (ca. €80). Refreshments, lunch, and dinner are provided.

Submission Deadline: 15 January 2027

articles.title: 16th International Conference on Political Economy: "Geopolitical Shifts, Green Transitions, and the New Global Order" (Istanbul, Feburary 2027)
articles.body_html:
23 - 24 Feburary | Istanbul, Turkey

The International Conference on Political Economy (ICOPEC) is delighted to announce its 2027 edition, themed “Geopolitical Shifts, Green Transitions, and the New Global Order.” This year’s conference seeks to delve into the most pressing challenges and transformations shaping our world today, exploring the multifaceted intersections of global power realignments, ecological imperatives, and the evolving global economic landscape.

The contemporary world is witnessing seismic shifts in the political and economic order. Rising geopolitical tensions, the decline of unipolarity, and the resurgence of regional alliances are reshaping the frameworks of international governance and cooperation. Simultaneously, the urgent need for sustainable development in the face of climate crises is driving an unprecedented green transition, which is redefining industries, labour markets, and trade systems. These transformations are further complicated by the rapid advancement of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, which are both empowering and disrupting societies globally.

Against this backdrop, persistent inequalities in wealth, opportunity, and environmental burdens highlight the necessity of addressing questions of social justice. Vulnerable populations, marginalised communities, and the Global South often bear the brunt of economic disruptions, environmental degradation, and migration crises, underscoring the need for inclusive solutions to these challenges. At the same time, grassroots movements, innovative policies, and interdisciplinary research offer hope for equitable and sustainable transitions.

ICOPEC invites scholars, policymakers, and practitioners to critically engage with these intertwined dynamics and explore pathways to a resilient and inclusive global order. This year’s theme seeks to address key questions:

  • How are shifting geopolitical alliances shaping the global response to climate change and sustainability?
  • What are the political, economic, and ethical implications of the green transition across nations, regions, and industries?
  • How do global trends in technology, health, urbanisation, and trade interact with the pursuit of equity and sustainability?

By integrating perspectives from economics, sociology, political science, environmental studies, law, philosophy, and other disciplines, this conference aims to foster a vibrant dialogue on the challenges and opportunities of this critical moment in history. Papers addressing theoretical, empirical, and interdisciplinary approaches are encouraged, as are those offering innovative methodologies or proposing actionable solutions to these global issues.

Abstract Deadline: 12 January 2027

For further information please click here.

Papers addressing theoretical, empirical, and interdisciplinary approaches are encouraged, as are those offering innovative methodologies or proposing actionable solutions to these global issues. articles.title: 62nd ITH Conference: Gender and Labour after WWII: Political Rights, Social Justice, and Welfare Politics (Linz, September 2027)
articles.body_html:
16 - 18 September 2027 | Linz, Austria

The ITH invites submissions for a conference which explores how social movements and political institutions engaged with women’s – paid and unpaid – work, and gendered ideas and practices of work and labour in the aftermath of WWII.

The period between 1945 and the 1960s was marked by major turning points for workers’ rights, political engagement, and the development of social welfare systems and saw the struggle for the advancement of political and social rights of women around the world.

Key contexts shaping the struggles on gender and labour in this period included border-crossing population movements and racialized diversity, changing patterns of international governance and social movement internationalism, post-WWII reconstruction, the economic boom, late colonial rule and decolonization, state-socialist catch-up development, and global sociopolitical competition. In different world regions and on the international stage, these contexts impacted on the engagement with gender and labour to various degrees.

The conference seeks to advance our understanding of gender and labour in the post-1945 decades from a global perspective. It moves beyond historical narratives of the post-WWII era which have considered the establishment of new political regimes in or after 1945 as an unblemished break with the past, or construed the post-WWII period, alternatively, as the historical moment of women's integration into society as equals to men or as a mere prequel to the global changes after 1968.

We invite scholars to submit papers that critically examine the interplay of gender and labour in social movements and the politics of work and explore how this interaction influenced and was influenced by the shifting political, social, and economic landscapes of the post-war period.

We are interested in women’s and men’s gendered demands and organizational practices, the nexus of masculinities and labour, and in papers employing cross-regional and transnational perspectives. We are looking for new answers to the question of how to conceptualize a gendered “aftermath” of WWII, in regional and global perspective.

Conference Themes:

1. How to Conceptualize an Aftermath?

Historical studies have referred to the end of WWII as marking the beginning of a new epoch. The immediate aftermath of the war has been described as an ‘hour zero’, as the era of ‘reconstruction’ after massive destruction or (colonial) exploitation caused by the war, and as a period of (coming) fundamental regime change in formerly Nazi-ruled territories, Eastern Europe and the Global South.

We invite applications that engage critically with the interpretative frameworks historians have applied to the aftermath. Questions addressed in this theme include:

  • How does this epoch compare to other watershed moments of postwar eras?
  • How did labour activists themselves understand the impact of (the end of) WWII, the gendered (post)war labour regimes and the “new” world order of the Cold War?
  • Which concepts can capture the immediate post-WWII years when considering regional differences, and putting gendered labour organizing and labour regimes centre stage?

2. Political Rights and the Long Shadow of Wartime Labour Mobilization and (Far-)Right-Wing Politics

The rise of far-right ideologies during the interwar period, political oppression of labour movements, and wartime labour mobilization which included elements of coerced labour left a lasting imprint on the labour movement.

In the post-war period, labour movements had to rebuild from this legacy of repression while confronting lingering far-right sentiments and, in some places, new elements of mobilization into work.

We aim to explore how labour movements fought for gendered political rights and social justice, while also confronting repression and strong-armed labour mobilization. This session invites scholarly contributions that explore the long-term impacts of gendered wartime politics on labour movements.

The following research questions can be discussed in this section:

  • How did the repression of labour under fascist and right-wing authoritarian regimes affect post-war labour organization and activism?
  • How did labour movements advance workers’ political rights in the aftermath of the war?
  • To what extent did labour movements confront or reconcile with former collaborators or sympathizers of far-right ideologies?
  • How were conceptions of masculinity renegotiated within labour movements as they transitioned from wartime and fascist repression and coercive policies of labour mobilization to peacetime activism and changed political landscapes?
  • To what extent did wartime repression of labour activism under different political regimes around the world shape forms of labour mobilization and political organizing in the post-war period?

3. Mass Displacement and Migrant Work

Mass displacement and large-scale population movements are one of the characteristics of the aftermath of war. WWII and its aftermath saw people fleeing conflict zones, becoming refugees, prisoners of war, and subject to sometimes forced relocation and detention.

The early Cold War saw massive political confrontation over the right to migration and governments’ control over citizens’ movement across borders. Displaced persons, people on the move, and people barred from free movement often faced discrimination, economic hardship, and exploitation, including in domestic work.

In this theme, the intersection between labour movements and labour regimes, the state, gender, and migration could be explored through topics such as:

  • How did labour movements and labour administrations address the needs and rights of displaced or detained women and migrant women workers?
  • What forms of discrimination did these workers face, and how were or weren’t these challenges overcome?
  • How did the inclusion (or exclusion) of migrant women’s labour shape post-war economies and labour politics in countries of origin and receiving countries?

4. Discrimination Against Women Workers and Multiply Marginalized Workers and Communities

The post-war period saw both advancements and setbacks for women workers, including multiply marginalized women workers and their communities.

While labour movements and organizations were central to advancing workers’ rights, they often failed to challenge gender, racial, and ethnic discrimination.

In this section, the following questions can be examined, among others:

  • How did labour movements and organizations react to or challenge the discrimination faced by women, workers of color, and marginalized groups in the workforce?
  • What role did reference to multiple marginalization play in shaping labour movements’ and organizations’ policies and goals in the post-war era, if any?
  • In what ways did multiply marginalized (women) workers organize for their rights within or outside of traditional labour structures?
  • Were there explicit discourses on masculinities and femininities in the labour movement and labour organizations?

5. Labour and Other Social Movements and the Struggles for Post-War Welfare Politics

One of the most significant legacies of post-WWII labour and other social movements is their role in the creation of welfare and universalist, socially inclusive labour politics.

Labour unions and socialist and social democratic parties have been described as key players in advocating for state-led social security systems, healthcare, unemployment benefits, and pension schemes. Many of these policy schemes and advancements were deeply gendered. They tackled women as a special category of workers and engaged, implicitly or explicitly, with the gendered and racialized division of paid and unpaid work.

As current research shows, the establishment of welfare politics in countries such as Great Britain and the Netherlands was made possible partly through revenues from their colonial territories.

Against this background, we encourage papers which engage with questions such as:

  • How did labour movements and organizations and other social movements influence the establishment of gendered post-war welfare and inclusive labour politics?
  • What were the key political, economic, and social strategies employed by labour movements and organizations in these reforms?
  • How did welfare programmes transform the relationship between labour, the state, and society, and what were the long-term consequences for the labour and other social movements?
  • How did international and national labour organizations and other movements interact in shaping governmental strategies aimed at improving women workers’ lives, mobilizing them into the labour force, or remoulding their role in the community?
  • How did labour movements and labour activists interact with states, their agents (bureaucrats) and international experts?

Dedline Submission of proposals: 31 January 2027

Dedline Full Paper: 15 August 2027

For further infromation please click here.
