articles.title: ASE @ WSSA Conference 2027 (Denver, March/April 2027)
articles.body_html:
31.03 – 03.04.27 | Denver, Colorado, USA

The Association for Social Economics (ASE) invites submissions for in-person sessions at the World Social Science Association (WSSA) conference. Individual papers on any aspect of social economics are welcome, as are complete session proposals of three to four papers organized around a coherent theme. Individual submissions require the presenting author’s contact information, a paper title (max. 20 words), JEL codes and an abstract of up to 250 words. Session proposals should provide this information for each paper and author, plus a brief rationale of two to three sentences and, if available, a proposed chair or discussant. Submissions can be e-mailed to Iris Buder (ASE Session Organizer for WSSA 2027) at irisbuder@isu.edu or made through the WSSA conference website under “Economics (Association for Social Economics)”. The ASE may provide up to 500 USD in travel support for a graduate student; if several graduate students present, the award is divided among them.

Further information can be found here.

Submission deadline: 15.01.27

articles.title: Association for Institutional Thought (AFIT) 2027 Conference (Denver, March/April 2027)
articles.body_html:
31.03 – 03.04.27 | Denver, Colorado, USA

The 48th Annual Meeting of the Association for Institutional Thought (AFIT) will take place March 31 - April 3, 2027, in Denver, Colorado, USA, in conjunction with the 69th Annual Conference of the World Social Science Association (WSSA)

Venue

Hilton Denver City Center
1701 California St.
Denver, CO 80202, USA

Theme

Institutions in a New Gilded Age: Technology, Reproduction Crises, and Collective Action

This year’s theme examines how emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, intersect with intensifying capitalist extraction and exclusion across the political, economic, social, and ecological spheres. It explores the challenges of AI-driven displacement and reorganization of work, the crises of social reproduction, and the challenges of building sustained collective action in hyperpolitical times.

As capitalist encroachment on sites of social reproduction accelerates, wealth and power are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a minority. This concentration evokes a new Gilded Age in which the majority faces growing barriers to democratic participation in decisions shaping their social and economic livelihood. Amid the heightened concerns about the effects of mega-corporations deployment of AI on employment and livelihoods, these barriers raise urgent questions about who directs technological change, who benefits from it, and who bears its costs.

Mass political parties, labor unions, and grassroots organizations have historically provided institutional foundations for popular resistance. As many of these organizations have weakened, heightened politicization and resentment expressed in public discourse and episodic protests have often struggled to translate into sustained collective action. The theme asks how popular resistance can build durable institutions capable of challenging concentrated capitalist power and also expanding democratic participation.

We encourage papers that tackle this theme’s questions. In addition, we encourage papers that explore structural, class, gender, ecological, and societal dynamics and employ institutional, multi-disciplinary, and historical perspectives that broaden our understanding of these current systemic crises and overall economic and social provisioning.

Among the topics that we encourage:

  • Impact of artificial intelligence on the economy/labor market and social provisioning
  • The political economy of evolving trade and global production restructuring
  • Modern monetary theory, neo-chartalism, and constitutional money
  • New development questions and challenges in the Global South
  • Market structures, supply chains, and monopoly power
  • Issues in social reproduction and women's rights
  • The political economy of macroeconomic policies
  • Democracy, political extremism, neoliberalism, geopolitical conflict and inequality
  • Urban economies, spatial justice, and land use
  • Comparative systems and alternative models of development & progress
  • Chinese economy as a regional and emerging global leader
  • Immigration, migration, globalization and climate change
  • History of Institutional and Economic Thought and Economic History
  • Unequal access to justice in vulnerable communities and criminal justice reform
  • Climate Change and environmental justice
  • Culture and religion
  • The political economy of digital currency/cryptocurrencies
  • Income and Wealth Inequality
  • Emerging Pedagogical Challenges and Practices
  • Pedagogy, Panels, and Roundtables

AFIT welcomes proposals for complete panels and roundtables on pedagogy, critical institutional methods, and recently published books—particularly by AFIT members. We also encourage conversations between scholars and activists engaged in commons-based practices.

Student Participation & Paper Competition

AFIT strongly encourages undergraduate and graduate student submissions.

  • Outstanding student papers are eligible for the AFIT–AFEE Student Scholars Award, recognizing work rooted in institutionalist, heterodox, and pluralist traditions.
  • Deadline for full student paper submissions: December 20, 2026
  • Details:
  • Students submitting to the competition are also encouraged to apply for a travel grant.
  • AFIT is committed to supporting students’ intellectual development and presence at the conference.

Regarding submissions and questions about the student paper competition, please contact the student paper competition coordinator: Jenica Kramer: jenicamariekramer@gmail.com

Call for Mentors

AFIT invites faculty, postdoctoral scholars, and senior graduate students to serve as mentors for the student paper competition. Mentors will provide constructive feedback to student authors ahead of the conference and, if possible, attend student sessions to support discussion and engagement. This initiative is part of AFIT’s long-standing commitment to the development of emerging scholars and the reproduction of heterodox institutional traditions.

If you are willing to mentor one or more student authors, please contact the section coordinator:

Ahmad A. Borazan – aaborazan@mail.fresnostate.edu

Submission Guidelines

To participate in the 2027 AFIT Conference, you may submit one of the following:

  • An individual paper
  • A panel of papers
  • A roundtable
  • A workshop, demonstration, or professional development event

You must submit your proposal via the WSSA website:

https://wssaconference.com

First, choose the section that best fits your contribution. To be included in AFIT programming, select: Economics – Association for Institutional Thought

Submissions made to other sections cannot be moved, and proposals submitted elsewhere will not be reviewed by AFIT.

How to Register and Submit

1. If you have not registered on the WSSA website, use this link:

https://wssaconference.com/

2. Once registered, click “Submit Abstract” to log in and access the submission form.

3. Complete the form and be sure to select Economics – Association for Institutional Thought as your section.

Submission Format Definitions

  • PAPER: A single paper submitted to one section. It may have multiple authors but represents only one paper.
  • PANEL: A set of papers organized by a submitter to form a unified session. All papers, authors, and titles must be included at the time of submission.
  • ROUNDTABLE: An open session on a specific topic with no formal papers. All discussants must be listed, and a description of the topic must be provided.
  • WORKSHOP / DEMONSTRATION / PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT EVENT: A teaching, training, or skills-building session you will design and lead. These may include lectures, demonstrations, or interactive professional development formats.

Submission Deadline

All submissions must be received by January 15, 2027. No proposals will be accepted after this date.

Abstracts must be no longer than 250 words.

Membership & Conference Registration

To present in AFIT sessions, all participants must:

  • Hold current AFIT membership:
  • Register for the 2027 WSSA conference:

Important Registration Dates:

  • Early Bird Registration Ends: November 30, 2026
  • Final Registration Deadline: See WSSA website

Publications & Partnerships

Presenters are encouraged to submit their work to AFIT-affiliated journals and partners:

  • Journal of Economic Issues
  • Money on the Left: History, Theory, Practice
  • International Journal of Pluralism and Economics Education (especially for pedagogical work)

Contact

For questions about submissions, mentoring, or participation:

AFIT 2027 Program Chair Ahmad A.Borazan – aaborazan@mail.fresnostate.edu

articles.title: Call for Essay Proposals: The Routledge Handbook of Social Science History
articles.body_html:
Rebecca Jean Emigh (Professor of Sociology, UCLA) is editing The Routledge Handbook of Social Science History and invites proposals for essays. The handbook is under contract with Routledge and is to comprise 60 to 65 essays on topics in social science history. It is intended as a cutting-edge research tool and will be published online and in print (hardcover and paperback). Contributors can send initial ideas, after which a specific topic is agreed or a list of possible topics is provided by the editor.

Essays are to be synthetic reviews of a topic that serve as an introduction to the material as well as a research guide. They should cover a long historical period and have global coverage as far as possible, both temporally and regionally. The main body is limited to 3,000 words, the bibliography to 1,000 words, and each essay requires an abstract of no more than 200 words. Authors have six months to write the essay. After receiving the editor’s comments, they have three months to submit the final version. Proposals are to be sent by e-mail to emigh@soc.ucla.edu. Further information can be found here.

articles.title: Historical Materialism Conference: "Liberation, Now: The Death of Liberal Order and the Fight for Another World" (Sydney, Feburary 2027)
articles.body_html:
11-12 February | Sydney, Australia

Liberalism is dead. In Australia and elsewhere, the social contracts, agents, and institutions of capitalism formed in the early 20th century are collapsing under the weight of contradiction. The temporary shackles and shock stabilisers have lost their hue of permanence. In the imperial core the morbid symptoms grow. Governments determinedly fail to square the circle of genocide in the name of freedom. Ecological disaster forms the backdrop to growing indignities for an ever-increasing proportion of the population. Naming and understanding this conjuncture is a fraught process; we appear to be adrift within a newly unfolding and not yet solidified political-economic order. But one thing is clear: the authoritarian wing of capital is ascendant. The world historical defeat of labour that defined the neoliberal counterrevolution has resulted in a steady decline in the old institutions of the left. Progressive forces across the world are fragmented, defensive and struggling to mount a meaningful challenge to capitalism and imperialism.

And yet liberation cannot wait. Ruthless critique must be accompanied by praxis. Actions speak louder than words. We invite participants of Historical Materialism Sydney 2027 to consider action, agency and new forms of struggle in their analysis of this conjuncture. How do we take action even in moments of extreme uncertainty? Which tactics, strategies, cultural and institutional forms are emerging, and what can we learn from past failures of the socialist left? How do we build sustained solidarity, political commitment and ethical protocols for action in an era marked by social fragmentation, political nihilism, and widespread indifference? What does it mean to ‘show upʼ even as the bases of socioecological reproduction are steadily eroded? How can we build counter hegemony in the face of state repression and a media landscape flattened by the concentration of capital and the dehumanising effects of AI? And how might we maintain our movement histories and aspirations, safeguarding them for a future where other possible worlds may be even harder to imagine than they are now? In short, what can be built from the expanding wreckage, in this place and elsewhere?

Questions for consideration include but are not limited to:

  • What is this current political economic order? Where in history are we? How useful are historical analogies for making sense of the current conjuncture?
  • How do we fight? What are the tactics, organisational forms and goals of socialist strategy in the 21st century?
  • What kind of internationalist visions does this moment demand of us, and how might we actualise it in an age of bordering and resurgent nationalism?
  • Where are the key agents and sites of social transformation emerging in an era marked by climate breakdown, war, genocide and rising authoritarianism?
  • How do we build new and defend existing progressive cultural institutions from attacks by the state and the far right?
  • How can we shape, in turn, the production of culture, art, and literature towards the ends of liberation rather than the end of liberation?
  • What can we learn from the successes and failures of socialist revolutions (in the past and ongoing)?

Abstract Deadline: 15 November 2026

For further infromation please click here.

articles.title: Imperialisms in the 21st Century Conference (Amiens, June 2027)
articles.body_html:
9-10 June, 2027 | Amiens, France

Conference theme: Imperialisms in the 21st Century

The conference is organized by the Université de Picardie Jules Verne, including the LEFMI, with the sponsorship of the journal Recherches Internationales.

The global landscape is undergoing a profound transformation, marked by the transition from a unipolar world dominated by a single superpower to a multipolar order, further characterized by the rise of multiple centers of influence: multinationals, certainly, but also GAFAM, NATU, major investment funds, major global AI operators, mafia regimes, dictatorial regimes, etc. This transition is accompanied by the emergence of new forms of inequality and predatory behavior, fundamentally altering power dynamics, the distribution of wealth, and global governance. This results, in the current period, in an antagonism between capital and nature that renders the dynamics of accumulation unsustainable and intersects with economic and geopolitical rivalries.

A new geopolitical configuration of states: from unipolarity to multipolarity Throughout history, the international order has been characterized by dominant powers exerting influence on world affairs. For decades, the post-Cold War era saw the emergence of a unipolar world, largely shaped by the hegemonic dominance of the United States, which exerted unparalleled influence in the political, economic, and military spheres, shaping international relations and geopolitical dynamics. Since the collapse of the USSR (1991), the United States has dominated the global economy politically and economically, with its Western allies (European Union, Great Britain) and others (Japan) within its sphere of influence, relying on the hegemony of the dollar, while facing a growing challenge, particularly from China. This has allowed the US to inflate the value of the dollar and to seize the wealth of the global economy, including that of the European Union and the mineral and other resources of countries in the Global South. The emergence of new centers of power, including China and, to some extent, India and Brazil, coupled with the resurgence of Russia and the assertion of regional powers, has brought an end to the unipolar order. A new era of intense rivalry has begun, the contours of the global landscape are shifting, and new actors are poised to shape world politics and secure their futures in various regions. Tim Marshall, in his book "The Power of Geography: 10 Maps to Understand the World's Issues ," demonstrates how, in the context of the rise of bipolarity, regions and states navigate power dynamics between dominant poles—whether geopolitical, economic, or ideological—and how the strategic position and resources of these states shape their alliances, conflicts, and influence. He examines, in particular, five regions: the Pacific, with a focus on Australia; Africa, with a focus on the Sahel and Ethiopia; Europe, with a focus on the United Kingdom, Turkey, Greece, and Spain; the Middle East, with a focus on Iran and Saudi Arabia; and also highlights the growing importance of outer space in politics. And a major challenge of this new imperialist configuration of states is the management of migrations. New predatory imperialist agents are gaining ground over states. Large multinational corporations are reshaping the world with their supply chains; they are breaking down production barriers here and there, reducing industrial companies most often to forms of subcontracting (furthermore, outsourced here and there according to changes in labor costs) and contract work, with a ruthless plundering of wealth for their own profit through financial companies . The economic power of these multinational corporations rivals that of nation-states. These multinational corporations are increasingly embedded in the functioning of the military-industrial system that has taken shape within the major powers (C. Serfati, 2026). Within this complex international landscape, new global players such as GAFAM (Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon, Microsoft), NATU (Netflix, Airbnb, Tesla, Uber), BlackRock, Vanguard, without forgetting China’s BATX companies (Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent, and Xiaomi), have acquired considerable influence, particularly through new technologies, illustrating the rapid and profound changes in the global economy and governance. These large companies and investment funds, BlackRock and Vanguard in particular, are among the world's largest asset managers, controlling colossal sums of money invested in various businesses and economic sectors. Their investment decisions have a significant impact on financial markets, the global economy, and corporate governance. And then come the major global operators of Artificial Intelligence in the wake of the Multinationals, the GAFA and others, such as Open AI (ChatGPT), Google DeepMind & Alphabets (Google Gemini), Microsoft Azure, Nvidia, Meta AI, Amazon Aws, Anthropic, as well as Chinese companies (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, DeepSeek).

These three new components of the global economy (large multinational corporations, new international players, and major global AI operators) are interconnected and interrelated, positioning themselves as a future solution, replacing state governance. Faced with the potentially devastating consequences of AI on employment, some AI gurus, such as Sam Altman (OpenAI) and Dario Amodei (Anthropic), anticipate a new global governance based on capital taxation, universal basic income, and reduced working hours, replacing the projected shortcomings of states (Le Monde, May 10, 2026).And we cannot forget, in this global disorder, the arrival of dictatorial states and mafia networks. What analyses of neo-imperialisms at work today? At the heart of this new geopolitical dynamic, a new configuration of the world economy is at stake, characterized by an epistemological shift in the foundations of imperialism, and the emergence of new actors. The old fundamental traits of the theories of imperialism, as analyzed by Lenin, Bukharin, Rosa Luxemburg, and others, are situated within a context of capitalism that was then macroeconomically centered on the state and monopolies. According to some, the recourse to global imperialist expansion aimed to counter the tendency of the rate of profit to fall, stemming in part from the overaccumulation of capital by monopolies, while others saw it as a way to create new markets. This ultimately led to inequalities in development and an unequal fragmentation of the global economy. The theoretical contributions of the 1970s-90s ( Baran & Sweezy, AGFrank, G.Arrighi, S.Amin, …) focus on the link between imperialism and the military-industrial complex and on unequal exchange (A.Emmanuel) with unequal development between centers and peripheries. The new foundations of imperialism in this new phase of economic financialization are becoming increasingly complex. New actors, from large multinational corporations (including GAFAM, NATO, and others) to major AI operators, are not only aiming to divide the world horizontally, but are also offering a vertical dynamic of power grabs, to the detriment of states. They are opportunistically allied with them, but with the clear intention of weakening them. The macro- and imperialist functioning of states, in their links to military-industrial complexes here and there, appears compelled to rely on these new actors. The differentiated imperialist game played by these various predatory components, at work in different regions and nations, leads to a chaotic course in the global economy and a weakening of national production systems. This is compounded by the way military-industrial systems operate in different places.

But what new foundations does each actor possess, and how do they combine? And what is the way out of this crisis?

The main themes of the call for papers

  1. What is the contemporary relevance (contributions and limitations) of the classical theory of imperialism (Lenine, Bukharin, Rosa Luxemburg, etc.), and what is the contemporary relevance (contributions and limitations) of the theories of imperialism from the 1970s–2000s (P. Baran & Sweezy, A.G. Frank, G. Arrighi, S. Amin, etc.)? What is the renewed relevance of the theory of unequal exchange (A. Emmanuel) within new international relations and ongoing forms of predation?
  2. What analysis today of the differentiated imperialisms of states: United States, China, Russia, Europe, Japan, or even of related sub-imperialisms (Israel, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, …). What is the analysis of the role of the BRICS in the current game of imperialisms?
  3. What imperialist foundations are linked to the analysis of Large Multinational Firms, GAFFA, and major AI operators? What are the intersections between differentiated imperialisms of States and differentiated imperialisms of new actors (Large Multinational Firms, AI Operators, …) ? What role do the military-industrial complexes at play have?
  4. What analysis of the main imperialist conflicts at work: Ukraine, Iran, Gaza, Sudan, Yemen, Congo/Rwanda, Sahel?

Call for Papers All proposals, in French or English, addressing and aligning with one of the 4 axes mentioned above, are welcome, whether they fall within economic theory, economic philosophy, or interdisciplinary perspectives.

Presented papers may contribute (subject to a peer-review process) to a special issue of the journal to be published in 2028. Proposals (specifying name, institution, a few keywords, and accompanied by an abstract of fewer than 700 words) must be sent to the following address: conferencelesimperialismes2027@gmail.com

Contacts:

Jean Louis Girard,

Christian Palloix

Submission Deadline: 31 March 2027

articles.title: Journal of Entrepreneurial and Organizational Diversity: Special Issue on “Cooperatives in Times of Conflict and War: Robustness, Resilience, and Recovery”
articles.body_html:
The Journal of Entrepreneurial and Organizational Diversity (JEOD) invites contributions to a special issue on cooperatives in times of conflict and war. The guest editors are Marcelo Vieta (University of Toronto), Fiona Duguid (Saint Mary’s University), Yuliya Amelina (Rural Women’s Business Network, Ukraine) and Sofia Burtak and Iryna Volovyk (Cooperative Academy; Rural Women Business Network, Ukraine). The special issue examines how cooperatives sustain communities in acute and ongoing crises, with a particular focus on Ukraine and other war-affected regions. It welcomes theoretical, empirical, practical and policy-oriented contributions. Topics include cooperative resilience during conflict, post-conflict reconstruction and recovery, cooperatives and social cohesion, gendered experiences and the role of women’s cooperatives, policy frameworks and enabling environments, and case studies from Eastern Europe, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East.

Extended abstracts of 1,500 words (excluding references) are to be sent to the JEOD Editorial Office at jeod@euricse.eu, with a reference to the special issue in the headline. Communication on the evaluation of abstracts follows by 31.01.27, and an online information meeting will be held afterwards. Full papers, which undergo double-blind peer review, are due by 31.05.27 via Editorial Manager, and the special issue is scheduled for publication in June 2028.

articles.title: Postgrowth and Degrowth in and beyond the Italian Debate: Contemporary Perspectives and Future Opportunities (Trento, December 2026)
articles.body_html:
10 – 11.12.26 | School of International Studies, University of Trento, Trento, Italy

The Environment Research Cluster at the School of International Studies of the University of Trento invites contributions to a conference on degrowth and postgrowth research in and beyond Italy. Italy was one of the first countries where degrowth ideas became popular, but this has not been matched by a comparable rootedness in academia. The conference aims to take stock of contemporary debates, research opportunities and future directions. It also intends to launch the Italian Degrowth and Post-Growth Research Network as a space for coordination and collaboration among scholars in the field.

The conference language is Italian and English. Submissions in either language should include the paper title, an abstract of approximately 300–500 words, author names and affiliations, contact details and 3–5 keywords. They are to be sent by e-mail to alice.dalgobbo@unitn.it with the subject line “Italian degrowth conference 2026 Trento”. Further information can be found here.

Submission deadline: 30.10.26

articles.title: RE:PRO: International Interdisciplinary Conference (Warsaw, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
26-28 November, 2026 | Warsaw, Poland

Conference theme: Reproduction Resituating Reproduction Across the Semi-Periphery and Global South

The RE:PRO Research Group invites researchers working on gender, reproduction, care, labour, inequality, reproductive justice, activism, and related questions to participate in an international interdisciplinary conference on social reproduction.

Particular attention will be given to perspectives from Central and Eastern Europe, Southern Europe, other semi-peripheral contexts, and the Global South, and to how these perspectives challenge, complicate, or extend dominant approaches developed in Western contexts.

The organizers particularly invite PhD students to apply to present their research. Selected participants will be invited to give a 15-minute presentation of their research, followed by discussion and feedback from invited senior scholars and other conference participants.

Participation in the conference is free of charge. All conference-related costs are covered by funding. Travel and accommodation support will be available to selected participants. Further details will be provided upon acceptance.

More information on the conference here.

articles.title: The Marx Conference 2027: The Current Conjuncture and the Making of Possible Futures (Toronto, August 2027)
articles.body_html:
03 – 05.08.27 | York University, Toronto, Canada

The Marx Centre (MSGAP) at York University invites abstracts for the second Marx Conference, following the inaugural edition in 2025. The conference examines the gap between the maturity of capitalism’s crises and the weakness of left organizing, asking which forms of organization, strategy and mass struggle could rebuild a revolutionary Left. Individual papers, panels and roundtables are welcome, especially those combining theoretical analysis with historical investigation and/or practical experience of socialist organization and struggle. Themes include political economy, ecology and new technologies, the state and democracy, imperialism and militarism, and socialism, culture, strategy and resistance. Individual paper proposals require a title, an abstract of up to 400 words, up to five keywords and the author’s contact details and affiliation. Panel proposals (3–4 papers, roundtables or book discussions) require a panel title, a panel abstract of up to 400 words and contact details for all participants. Notification of acceptance is planned for 15.01.27. Correspondence can be directed to msgap@yorku.ca.

Further information can be found here.

articles.title: URPE @ EEA (Eastern Economics Association) Annual Conference (New York, February 2027)
articles.body_html:
11-14 February, 2027 | New York City, NY, USA

URPE members are invited to submit entire organized sessions or individual papers to URPE for our participation in this year's 53d Eastern Economics Association Annual Conference (see Eastern Economic Association conference website for more information).

In its twentieth year, URPE @ EEA is continuing to provide a forum for URPE members and economists across the heterodox spectrum to meet and engage with each other, and continue to develop the frontiers of radical political economy.

If you have any questions on these meetings, contact Al Campbell.

URPE targets building sessions of 3 papers given the short sessions (1 hour 20 minutes), but they can be 4. (Proposals for sessions with 3 can have a 4th added if URPE receives a related single paper proposal that fits there and nowhere else.)

Given their short length, panels that URPE builds out of individual papers do not have discussants, in order to maximize time available for presentation and discussion by the audience. However, proposals for a fully formed session (i.e., a panel) may have discussants and/or chairs different from the presenters, if those who are organizing such panels feel that would benefit the work being presented and discussed.

Submissions for panels or individual papers to the URPE panels will be made through the portal for the conference at https://eea.meetingsavvy.net/.  

Submission Deadline: 15 November 2026

articles.title: URPE @ WSSA Conference 2027 (Denver, March 2027)
articles.body_html:
31 March - 3 April, 2027 | Denver, CO, USA

URPE will once again organize panels at the World Social Science Association's annual conference. Any topic relevant to radical political economy is welcome. Also encouraged are pedagogy papers and roundtable discussions of books or important issues.

To submit an abstract, roundtable or panel, create an account and go to https://wssaconference.com/2027-submit-abstract

When you submit, the first thing you do is to select a section. This is where you would select Union for Radical Political Economics. You could also select Economics (Association For Institutional Thought) or Economics (Association for Social Economics). URPE generally constructs panels at the WSSA in partnership with AFIT and ASE. In the past, URPE sessions have been cross listed with AFIT and ASE. Do not select Economics (General) unless you want to be part of a mainstream panel.

Along with ICAPE and the Easterns, the WSSA is an excellent conference for heterodox economists. The WSSA is a very left group of social scientists with the largest subgroup working on borderland studies. They always organize events with local activists and a fundraiser for a local food bank. AFIT is also a group with a lot of connections to radical political economy via radical institutionalism and post-Keynesianism.

For questions contact Geoff Schneider.

Submission Deadline: 15 January 2027

articles.title: WINIR Young Scholars Pre-Conference Workshop (São Paulo, May 2027)
articles.body_html:
31 May, 2027 | São Paulo, Brazil

Workshop theme: Innovation, Institutions and Inclusion - Technology and Development in the Global South

The WINIR Conference on Institutions for Innovation, Breakthrough Technologies and Global Challenges with Special Attention to the Global South will be held at FGV EAESP in São Paulo, Brazil, on 1–3 June 2027

The organizers invite early career researchers to submit abstracts for the WINIR Young Scholars Pre-Conference Workshop on Innovation, Institutions & Inclusion: Technology & Development in the Global South that will be held in São Paulo on 31 May 2027. The workshop seeks to create a forum for emerging scholarly voices working across disciplines and jurisdictions, with particular attention to research engaging with the Global South and perspectives that remain underrepresented in mainstreams debates on technology and innovation.

New technologies are transforming markets, states and societies, but their benefits are neither automatic nor evenly distributed. Their effects depend on the institutions within which they operate, and on the power, interests and coalitions that shape those institutions. These questions are particularly important in the Global South, where technological innovation and investment can generate significant opportunities for development but do not necessarily translate into broad-based or inclusive economic or social gains.

The workshop will examine how technological change reshapes economic and political relationships: who participated in benefits from innovation, who may be excluded or disadvantaged, and how states, firms, communities, and civil society influence its direction. We are particularly interested in how law, regulation, markets, and other institutions enable, constrain, and govern innovation, as well as the conditions under which technological change can contribute to development that is socially, environmentally, and economically sustainable.

These questions invite interdisciplinary perspectives. The organizers welcome contributions from economics, law, political science, sociology, geography, history, development studies, and science and technology studies, and we particularly encourage work that crosses disciplinary boundaries. Theoretically grounded empirical research, comparative and historical studies, and conceptual papers are all welcome. Above all, the workshop is intended to provide a space for early career scholars to bring a range of geographical and intellectual perspectives into conversations about the governance and political economy of technological change.

The organizers welcome submissions on any aspect of the political economy and institutions of innovation, including but not limited to the following themes:

  1. Innovation and Development in the Global South: The institutional foundations of productivity growth, structural transformation and inclusive development. This includes the role of states, markets and firms in technological catch-up, and the contribution of experiences from Brazil, Latin America, Africa and Asia to institutional theory.
  2. Technology, Inequality and Intersectionality: The distributional consequences of technological change, including its intersections with race, gender and identity. This includes the institutions that shape access to, participation in and the benefits of innovation.
  3. Law, Regulation and Governance: The governance of AI and other emerging technologies by public and private actors. This includes regulation, property rights and intellectual property, state capacity, and the changing boundaries between state and market authority.
  4. Sustainability and Institutional Change: The relationship between technological change and social, environmental and economic sustainability. This includes institutional responses to climate change and the political economy of just transitions.

Eligibility

Applicants should either be enrolled in a doctoral programme or have graduated no more than three years before 31 March 2027. Scholars based in or working on the Global South are particularly encouraged to apply. Successful applicants will present their research to peers and senior scholars and receive constructive conceptual and methodological feedback. Priority will be given to first-time attendees at WINIR Young Scholars events.

All participants selected for the workshop will be eligible to attend the main WINIR conference, with the conference registration fee waived.

Submission guidelines

Submissions should be made using the ONLINE FORM and should include:

  • Abstract: max 500 words
  • Short professional bio: max 300 words.

Please find more info here.

Please address all inquiries to youngscholars@winir.org.

Submission Deadline: 5 December 2026

articles.title: (Post)Colonial Business History beyond the Classical Empires (Vienna, April 2027)
articles.body_html:
15 – 17.04.27 | University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria

This workshop invites paper proposals on (post)colonial and imperial business history from outside the conventional colonial centres. The call asks whether entrepreneurs and businesses from “smaller” states and from regions such as Central and Eastern Europe, the Balkans or Central Asia can be integrated into the study of (post)colonial business history. Empirical case studies as well as theoretical contributions are welcome, including those on the applicability of (post)colonial concepts beyond the Global South. The workshop is kept small, with approximately 10–12 participants, and selected papers are envisaged for a special issue in a leading journal of global and/or imperial history.

Accommodation and refreshments are generally covered by the organisers. Contributions to travel costs may be possible, with priority for participants from underrepresented backgrounds and from the Global South; applicants who wish to be considered should state this in their submission and give an estimate of the amount needed.

Abstracts of 300–350 words and a brief biographical statement are to be sent to the organisers, Anka Steffen (anka.steffen@univie.ac.at) and Gijs Dreijer (dreijer@eshcc.eur.nl). Applicants will be notified by 10.01.27, and full papers are due by 15.03.27.

Further information can be found here.

Submission deadline: 10.12.26

articles.title: Capital, Distribution and Growth: Garegnani Archive Inaugural Conference (Rome, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
19 – 20.11.26 | Roma Tre University, via Silvio D’Amico 77, Rome, Italy

The inaugural conference of the Garegnani Archive, dedicated to the work and papers of the economist Pierangelo Garegnani, takes place at Roma Tre University. The provisional programme begins with an introduction to the archive and a biographical and intellectual profile of Garegnani. It continues with sessions on the history of economic thought, the surplus approach, capital theory, the Cambridge debates and macroeconomics. Many contributions draw on material from the archive, including Garegnani’s manuscripts, his correspondence and an unpublished 1996 typescript. Speakers include Heinz D. Kurz, Neri Salvadori, Maria Cristina Marcuzzo, Fabio Petri, Franklin Serrano and Sergio Cesaratto.

The inventory of the archive is already available online; it can be found here.

The full provisional programme and further information can be found here.

articles.title: School of Advanced Studies in the Reappraisal of the Surplus Approach - 2027 (Rome, February 2027)
articles.body_html:
22-27 February, 2027 | Rome, Italy

The School’s purpose is to provide participants with a deeper understanding of the surplus approach as taken up and developed by Piero Sraffa and subsequent authors. Participants will therefore be introduced to the analyses of the Classical economists and to the modern research conducted within the reappraisal of their theoretical framework. The activity will embrace different topics, ranging from the theory of value and distribution to the study of economic growth, also dealing with applied analyses and policy issues. In addition, the School aims to stimulate participants into developing their own research by fostering contacts and scientific exchange between young researchers and expert scholars.

Organizing and Scientific Committee:

Roberto Ciccone, Saverio M. Fratini, E. Sergio Levrero, Antonella Palumbo, Daria Pignalosa, Davide Romaniello, Antonella Stirati, Paolo Trabucchi, Attilio Trezzini, Gabriel Zaffari.

Application:

The School welcomes applications by PhD students at any stage of their PhD as well as post-doc researchers. Candidatures by undergraduate and Master students will be considered only if their profile is exceptionally strong. If you would like to attend the School, please fill in the application form by 15 November 2026. Please also send a curriculum vitae to cswinterschool2027@gmail.com. As the effective organization and running of the School require a minimum number of participants, applicants will be informed by 25 November 2026 whether the School will take place on the dates indicated, in which case notifications of acceptance will be sent by the same date, or whether it will be postponed to a later date, to be announced.

Fees and funding awards:

The registration fee is €150 and includes teaching materials, coffee breaks and lunches. Centro Sraffa is providing a limited amount of funding for grants to be awarded to selected participants as a contribution towards travel and/or accommodation expenses. Applicants for financial support are requested to specify whether they are applying for a contribution to travel and/or accommodation expenses, and the country or countries from which they will be travelling, together with a brief description of their research (300-500 words). A reference letter may also be sent to cswinterschool2027@gmail.com, if desired. Since the effective organization and running of the School require a minimum number of participants, applicants are kindly requested to state whether their participation is conditional on financial support from the School.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 15 November 2026

articles.title: System Dynamics Society Economics Special Interest Group Online Seminar (Online, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
18 November, 2026 | Online

Seminar title: Exploring the circuit of capital models through a lens of system dynamics

The Economics Special Interest Group (SIG) of the System Dynamics Society brings together researchers and educators interested in applying system dynamics to economic analysis. With its emphasis on causal feedback, stock–flow relationships, and nonlinear dynamics, this approach offers tools for studying economic processes outside equilibrium. These features provide common ground with heterodox traditions concerned with cumulative causation, institutional change, and endogenous instability.

The SIG seeks to foster dialogue across theoretical perspectives and promote methodological pluralism in economic research and teaching. The Economics SIG Online Seminar Series provides a forum for sharing research and discussing the connections between economic theory and simulation-based modeling.

Upcoming seminar will feature Prof. Hee Young Shin (Wright State University) presenting “Exploring circuit of capital models through a lens of system dynamics” on 18 November 2026. The presentation will be followed by discussion, and researchers, students, and practitioners from different theoretical and methodological backgrounds are welcome.

Please find more info here.

articles.title: UN Economist Network webinar on global inequality report and initiative (Online, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
29 October, 2026 | Online

The organizers are pleased to invite you and the members of your network to the next in the series of UN Economist Network global webinars in association with several leading international academic networks. The featured speaker in this session will be University of Massachusetts Amherst Professor of Economics Jayati Ghosh on the topic of global inequality, including the report of the G20 Extraordinary Committee of Independent Experts on Inequality of which she was a member. That report has inspired efforts to form an International Panel on Inequality (IPI) modelled in part on the IPCC.

The webinar will take place on October 29 from 2 pm to 3:30 pm Paris time. The two discussants will be Paris School of Economics Professor and IPSP Founding Member Marc Fleurbaey and Marta Roig, Chief of Emerging Issues and Trends Section, UN DESA and co-lead of the World Social Report 2025. Prof. Ghosh's opening remarks and the comments by the two discussants will be followed by an interactive discussion with the global webinar audience of UN and academic economists. This session is organized in association with the International Panel on Social Progress and its Global Social Progress Week.

Please register here.

articles.title: Workshop in History and Methodology (Online, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
29 October, 2026 | Online

Workshop theme: Evolutionary and Institutional Economics – Conceptualizations and Contributions: Emergence, “Meso”, Trust, Change, and an Institutional Life Cycle

The next Workshop in History and Methodology meeting will be help on the 29th of October at 17:00 South Africa time. Professor Wolfram Elsner of the University of Bremen (retired) will give a presentation titled: "Evolutionary and Institutional Economics – Conceptualizations and Contributions: Emergence, “Meso”, Trust, Change, and an Institutional Life Cycle".

The presentation will illustrate some way towards Evolutionary-Institutional Economics (EIE) in an Original Institutional Economics (OIE) perspective. Contributions will be epistemological (economics as a contested multiparadigmatic discipline and Kuhnian losses in the mainstream), HET-related (e.g., retrieving Adam Smith’s theory of institutional emergence), and real-world based, as regards regional and industrial networking and policies. Wolfram Elsner will elaborate on institutional emergence, with careful modeling and hermeneutics, on the conceptualization of institutions, on T.B. Veblen’s institutional dichotomy, and critical factors of institutional development. The presentation will touch applied theoretical issues such as general trust, social leverage, embedded organization, and institutional collapse, and fields such as “meso”-economics, the theory of institutional change, and an institutional complexity economics. Value change, policy conceptions, and methodological reflection will be integral to these efforts.

Time: Oct 29, 2026 05:00 PM Johannesburg

articles.title: University of Massachusetts Amherst, US (1)
articles.body_html:
Job title: Assistant Professor - Department of Economics

The Department of Economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst invites applications for an Assistant Professor appointment expected to start on September 1, 2027.

Preference will be given to innovative analytical methods, both empirical and theoretical, in a core area such as microeconomics, industrial organization, international trade and finance, and economic history, although economists in all fields are encouraged to apply. UMass Economics has a history and commitment to fostering a wide range of alternative perspectives and rigorous analytic methods for addressing economic challenges in innovative ways.

The teaching load is 2/2. Candidates will be judged on their scholarly research, as well as high quality and enthusiastic teaching. A completed Ph.D. in Economics or a closely related field is required by time of appointment. Current or previous external funding, or experience seeking external grants, is a plus.

Under exceptional circumstances, highly qualified candidates at other ranks may receive consideration.

Please find more info here.

Review of applications will begin on November 15, 2026, and continue until the position is filled. Preference will be given to applications received on or before November 15, 2026. Selected candidates will be interviewed remotely beginning in December 2026, with campus visits beginning after January 11, 2027.

articles.title: University of Oxford, UK
articles.body_html:
Job title: Post Doctoral Research Associate in Agent-Based Climate Macroeconomics

The University of Oxford is seeking a Postdoctoral Research Associate to contribute to research examining the macroeconomic impacts of UK climate mitigation policies. Based at the Institute for New Economic Thinking (INET), the successful candidate will join the MacroCB7 – Macroeconomics of the Seventh Carbon Budget project, working closely with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) to assess how climate policies affect economic growth, employment, inflation and inequality.

Working with Professor Doyne Farmer, Tom Youngman and Dr. Donal Brown, you will contribute to the development and application of an innovative agent-based macroeconomic model to evaluate the economic and distributional consequences of net zero policies. Research will explore areas including low-carbon heating technologies, government finances, alternative investment scenarios and the potential for social tipping points in climate transitions.

The role combines quantitative research, software development and policy engagement. You will develop and implement new modelling approaches using Python, analyse esults through sensitivity testing and simulation, contribute to academic publications, and present findings to government and policy partners. From June 2027, the research will expand to examine transformative net zero policies across energy, housing, transport and food, with a particular focus on reducing inequality alongside greenhouse gas emissions.

The University of Oxford is seeking candidates who hold, or are close to completion of, a PhD/DPhil in a relevant discipline, with programming experience and a strong understanding of economic theory, particularly macroeconomics and complexity approaches. You should have excellent analytical and communication skills, experience contributing to research publications, and an interest in applying quantitative modelling to climate policy. Experience in agent-based modelling, collaborative coding or policy-engaged research would be advantageous.

The role is based at INET's offices on Manor Road, Oxford. Flexible working arrangements may be considered, subject to discussion and approval, including part-time working at 0.5 FTE or above. A minimum of one day per week in the office during term time is expected.

This position offers the opportunity to develop and apply innovative economic modelling methods to inform UK climate policy, working within an interdisciplinary research team with established government partnerships. This post is offered on a full-time, fixed-term basis for 18 months upon start date. (Part-time arrangements of 0.5 FTE or above may be considered)

What is Offered

As an employer, we genuinely care about our employees’ well-being, and this is reflected in the range of benefits that we offer including:

  • An excellent contributory pension scheme
  • 38 days annual leave
  • A comprehensive range of childcare services
  • Family leave schemes
  • Cycle loan scheme
  • Discounted bus travel and Season Ticket travel loans.

Application Process

You will be required to upload a covering letter with a supporting statement, CV and the details of two referees as part of your online application. In your supporting statement, please explain how you meet each of the selection criteria found in the job description, and why you would like to do this role. See guidance at https://www.jobs.ox.ac.uk/cv-and-supporting-statement.

Any technical questions related to this vacancy can be sent to:recruit@ouce.ox.ac.uk

Application Deadline: 9 November 2026.

For further information please click here.

articles.title: Utrecht University, the Netherlands
articles.body_html:
Job title: Assistant Professor in Economics

The Utrecht University School of Economics (U.S.E.) invites applications for an Assistant Professor position in Economics. The position is embedded in the Applied Economics section.

The Applied Economics section brings together researchers working in a large variety of areas of applied economics (e.g. public economics, behavioral economics, health economics, economics of crime, regional/urban economics, development economics, labour economics, economics of education, and other applied fields) with researchers working on the history, methodology, and/or philosophy of economics. Research and teaching in the section is typically empirical, policy-oriented, and sometimes multidisciplinary.

The position involves teaching in areas where economics is itself the object of study. These areas include the history of economics, economic history, philosophy of economics, and economic/econometric methodology, such as for example the courses “Contemporary Economics in Historical Perspectives” or “Ethical and Historical Reflections”. Candidates should explain in their cover letter how their research connects to these teaching areas.

The position includes 60% teaching time (including 5% governance), and 40% research time.

The candidate’s responsibilities will include:

  • conducting high-quality research in economics or a closely related field;
  • teaching undergraduate and graduate courses within U.S.E.;
  • contributing to courses at U.S.E. in which economics is reflected upon (e.g. history of economic thought, philosophy of economics, economic methodology, or related themes) but also teach at the Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) programme to which U.S.E. contributes;
  • engaging in interdisciplinary collaboration within Utrecht University, for example with the for the History and Philosophy of the Sciences and the Humanities, a university-wide center that promotes critical reflection on academic disciplines, methods, and the role of knowledge in society.

The successful candidate is expected to:

  • hold a PhD, or be close to finishing their degree, in economics or another field related to the position;
  • have a potential for excellence in research, targeting publications in top international peer-reviewed journals;
  • be able to inspire students from undergraduate to graduate levels, and prior teaching experience is a plus;
  • have excellent communication and management skills;
  • have an excellent command of spoken and written English.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 15 November 2026

The Applied Economics section brings together researchers working in a large variety of areas of applied economics (e.g. public economics, behavioral economics, health economics, economics of crime, regional/urban economics, development economics, labour economics, economics of education, and other applied fields) with researchers working on the history, methodology, and/or philosophy of economics. Research and teaching in the section is typically empirical, policy-oriented, and sometimes multidisciplinary. The position involves teaching in areas where economics is itself the object of study. These areas include the history of economics, economic history, philosophy of economics, and economic/econometric methodology, such as for example the courses “Contemporary Economics in Historical Perspectives” or “Ethical and Historical Reflections”. Candidates should explain in their cover letter how their research connects to these teaching areas. The position includes 60% teaching time (including 5% governance), and 40% research time. The candidate’s responsibilities will include: conducting high-quality research in economics or a closely related field; teaching undergraduate and graduate courses within U.S.E.; contributing to courses at U.S.E. in which economics is reflected upon (e.g. history of economic thought, philosophy of economics, economic methodology, or related themes) but also teach at the Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) programme to which U.S.E. contributes; engaging in interdisciplinary collaboration within Utrecht University, for example with the for the History and Philosophy of the Sciences and the Humanities, a university-wide center that promotes critical reflection on academic disciplines, methods, and the role of knowledge in society. The successful candidate is expected to: hold a PhD, or be close to finishing their degree, in economics or another field related to the position; have a potential for excellence in research, targeting publications in top international peer-reviewed journals; be able to inspire students from undergraduate to graduate levels, and prior teaching experience is a plus; have excellent communication and management skills; have an excellent command of spoken and written English. Please find more info here . Application Deadline: 15 November 2026

articles.title: Vienna University of Economics and Business, Austria
articles.body_html:
Post-doctoral researcher: climate and nature finance for development

The Institute for Ecological Economics is looking for a post-doctoral researcher in climate and nature finance, with a focus and interest on their international development aspects. The position is based at the Institute for Ecological Economics, within the Vienna University of Economics and Business, under the supervision of Irene Monasterolo. You will work with the experts of the Task Force on Climate, Development and the International Financial Architecture led by Boston University in collaboration with the G24 and V20 on reshaping international climate finance for development, in dialogue with multinational development banks and financial institutions.

Within the project, you will contribute to inform how different financial arrangements and instruments could contribute to build resilience to climate and nature risks, in an inclusive and financial stability-aware way. You will explore the conditions for climate development finance to act a global shock absorber in the context of climate and nature risks. In particular, you will provide new conceptual and quantitative insights on debt, financial instruments and measures (e.g. Resilience and Sustainability Facility, Recovery and Resilience Facility, Capital Flow Management Measures, Regional Financing Arrangements, equity), including a global insurance scheme, for emerging markets and low-income economies (EMDEs). This is a crucial topic for the future of international development: growing socio-economic losses from climate change and ecosystem depletion, and geopolitical instability, contribute to decrease countries’ fiscal space and to increase the cost of investing in resilience. In this context, EMDEs face a future of sluggish development, insufficient resilience and sustainability, and new debt crises, with cascading effects on the economy of Global North countries. You will work in close contact with a team of experts in climate finance for development with long experience in development finance institutions. You will have the opportunity to attend international research and policy workshops, conferences, and have policy impact, shaping the discussion about the international climate finance agenda.

Key responsibilities:

  • Developing quantitative tools (in particular Stock-Flow Consistent behavioral model and stress test models) for macro-financial risk assessment of climate and nature risks, and financial instruments.
  • Collaborating with top scholars from leading institutions and think tanks (e.g., Boston University, Utrecht University, University of Venice, Bruegel) and engaging with the Task Force team.
  • Driving impact by informing the design of financial instruments and financial policy in EMDEs.
  • Contributing to academic output through publishing high-quality research in peer reviewed high ranked journals.
  • Support the project dissemination activities by participating in relevant conferences, workshops, and seminars.

Job profile:

  • PhD in Economics, Finance, Statistics, Physics, or a related field.
  • Proven experience with macro-financial and financial risk modeling, using either Stock-Flow Consistent models, or Agent-Based models, or network models.
  • Expertise and interest with climate and nature finance, and development finance.
  • Strong coding skills in Matlab and Python.
  • Fluency in English both spoken and written (other languages are a plus) and willingness to travel international for conferences and meetings.
  • Ability to deliver quality and relevant work, meet deadlines, manage tasks independently, work in team.
  • Ability to write and present research for academic and policy audiences independently.

Location: Vienna, one of the cities with the highest quality of life in Europe, with access to facilities and a dynamic international research environment.

Starting date: January 2027 (negotiable)

Duration: 14 months (potential extension based on performance)

Remuneration: in accordance with the applicable collective labour agreement, including social security coverage and paid annual leave.

To apply, please send your curriculum vitae, including a letter of motivation and at least two published or unpublished papers, and two references. A first round of online interviews will take place in November. Expected starting date of the position is January 2027.

For more information about this position, please contact Prof. Dr. Irene Monasterolo or click here.

Application Deadline: 28 October 2026

articles.title: Call for Nominations: 2027 Alice Amsden Book Award
articles.body_html:
The Society for the Advancement of Socio-Economics (SASE) invites nominations for its 2027 Alice Amsden Book Award for an outstanding scholarly book that breaks new ground in the study of socio-economics. Eligible books must have a 2025 or 2026 first edition publication date and cannot be edited volumes. The deadline for nominations is 1 February 2027.

Only current SASE members are invited to nominate a book for the prize, and authors are welcome to nominate their own work .

To nominate a book, authors must send an electronic copy that can be shared with all committee members to sasebookaward@sase.org. In addition to the required electronic copy, committee members would appreciate it if the publisher could send a hard copy to each member, if possible. Both the hard copies and the electronic copy must be received by the 1 February deadline. You must include a brief nomination letter that states how the book contributes to SASE’s intellectual mission.

Please note: All books/submissions must be in English, and have a first edition publication date of 2025 or 2026. Also note that achieving diversity and inclusion is a priority for SASE.

For further information please click here.

Submission Deadline: 1 February 2027

articles.title: Winners Announcement: AISPE Award 2026
articles.body_html:
AISPE is pleased to share with our entire community the names of the recipients of AISPE Award 2026.

Best Book:

Antonella Rancan e Francesco Sergi, Modelling Europe. A History of Multi-Country Models at the European Commission (1970-2005), Palgrave, 2024.

Best Article:

David Gindis and Steven Medema, (2025). "One Man a Committee Does not Make: Henry Manne, the AEA-AALS Joint Committee", History of Political Economy, 57(3): 405-443.

Best Ph.D. dissertation:

Mirek Hosman, The World Bank, Economic Expertise, and the Reinvention of Global Economic Governance in the 1960s.

articles.title: Capitalism at the Limit: A Political Ecology of a World in Crisis
articles.body_html:
by Ulrich Brand & Markus Wissen | 2025, Polity

Capitalism is hitting the buffers. Unable to handle the various crises that its inherent logic of growth, profit, and competition has produced, it has led the world into a state of emergency - with the authoritarian right on the rise globally and progressive forces unable to realize the transformations needed to secure the future prosperity of people and planet. 'The old is dying and the new cannot be born', Gramsci said. We are caught between forces agitating for fundamental change, Green Capitalist modernizers, and fierce defenders of the status quo. How did this happen, and what is to be done?

In this new book, Ulrich Brand and Markus Wissen, authors of the acclaimed The Imperial Mode of Living, trace how capitalism has reached its very limits. Alongside the mutually reinforcing environmental, geopolitical, and social crises we face, they analyse the struggles that will determine the fate of humanity. Critiquing dominant pathways - from Green Capitalism to authoritarian and anti-ecological policies - that reinforce the Global North's imperial mode of living, the authors offer a fairer alternative based on solidarity and collective self-limitation. Capitalism at the Limit is a clear-sighted look at the dynamics driving the critical conflicts of our time.

Please find a link to the book here.

Capitalism at the Limit is a clear-sighted look at the dynamics driving the critical conflicts of our time. Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: Commodifying Plunder – Unequal Exchange and the Hidden Logic of Imperialism
articles.body_html:
by Crelis Rammelt | 2026, Merlin Press

Is ‘economic co-operation’ between rich and poor countries truly mutually beneficial, or does it mainly widen the inequalities? How does the expansion of global trade and commerce fuel violence, pillage, and deeper exploitation in less wealthy countries?​

Contemporary corporations and their owners - equipped with wealth, influence, and empowered by dominant states and global institutions - embody old-style colonial ruthlessness in new forms. Violence riddles global production, through routinised sweatshop labour, environmental degradation, resource grabs, lost livelihoods - behind a veil of 'development' and 'civilised' progress. ​

Strip away overt violence, and contemporary trade is still plunder, just neatly commodified and concealed – a phenomenon we call ‘unequal exchange’. Lengthy and complex supply chains obscure the conditions in which products are made. Few of us would steal food from a starving three-year-old or abduct a mother to exploit her, and yet our everyday participation in the economy has the same effect. ​

This book explains unequal exchange through basic Marxist concepts and concrete attempts to measure the phenomenon. It seeks to be a resource for scholars and activists - accessible while preserving depth, serious but not opaque. It has a simple message: This system does not end well unless we end it.​

Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: Contradictionary: An Almanac of Resistance
articles.body_html:
edited by Bernd Herzogenrath and Nicol A. Barria-Asenjo | Open Humanities Press, 2026

CONTRADICTionary: An Almanac of Resistance is a collective intervention into the politics of language at a time when words themselves are being policed, erased, and weaponized. Emerging from the suppression of terms like ‘diversity,’ ‘intersectionality,’ and ‘climate crisis,’ the project reclaims and expands this contested vocabulary through contributions from over 100 scholars, artists, and activists worldwide. Each entry interrogates how language shapes what can be known, said, and done, while offering new, situated meanings rooted in lived experience and critical inquiry. Neither dictionary nor manifesto alone, CONTRADICTionaryoperates as a living archive of dissent, embracing contradiction as method and multiplicity as strength. By transforming banned words into sites of analysis, imagination, and action, it challenges regimes of silence and invites readers to actively participate in redefining the terms that govern collective life.

articles.title: Modern Economics and Social Reality
articles.body_html:
edited by Ioana Negru, Stephen Pratten and Yannick Slade-Caffarel | Routledge, 2026

Tony Lawson is among the most influential economists of his generation. He has reclaimed a place for explicit, sustained, ontological analysis in economics demonstrating how its decades-long neglect has hampered the discipline. Regarding social theorising more generally, Lawson has been centrally involved in developing a compelling account of the very nature of social reality (systematised as social positioning theory), showing how it can sponsor powerful new treatments of the nature of money, corporations and gender. He has also engaged in ethical theorising to explore possibilities for emancipatory change. For those seeking a relevant approach to economics specifically, or indeed social theorising in general, his work has been agenda-setting.

The chapters in this volume have been written in Tony Lawson’s honour. Leading heterodox economists, social theorists and legal scholars engage constructively and critically with Lawson’s landmark contributions. The chapters explore cutting-edge developments in social ontology; issues at the interface between ontology, economics and ethics; and topics concerning the state and history of economics. Collectively, the chapters demonstrate that the perspectives Lawson outlines have critical purchase upon an extraordinary range of vital contemporary issues.

This book will interest those searching for new relevant directions in social theory and philosophy and all concerned with the future (and history) of economics.

articles.title: Subordination and Development: Emerging Market Economies of Asia and Latin America
articles.body_html:
by Sunanda Sen | 2026, Tulika Books

Sunanda Sen provides, in the present book, an analysis of subordination faced by the developing countries of the global South, with implications which include their retarded development. Imposed by the advanced industrial countries, subordination of these countries includes an implicit compulsion on their part to follow neoliberal economic policies having broad acceptance from corporate capital as well as the Bretton Woods institutions from the global North.

Compliance with policies as above on the part of the subordinated countries is ensured by the liberalized global market, operating as an agent of corporate capital and the state overseas. Deviations, if any, from the prescribed neoliberal policies in the developing countries often encounter reprisals by the market with reversals of capital flows, mediating signals for the subordinated countries to look for conformity with remedial measures. Subordination as spelt out above is distinct from ‘dependence’ which prevailed in the post-war years till the mid-1970s, when official aid was the major string for overseas governments to exercise direct control over aid-receiving countries.

Moving from dependence, subordination faced by the developing nations came up along with liberalization of capital flows during the 1990s. It achieved for the overseas partners a steady flow of surpluses, while ensuring continuity of the prescribed policies with harmful consequences in the subordinated nations. The book also dwells on the economic dynamics of the structural changes which let finance attain dominance for those economies with deleterious consequences for the real economy.

Analysis in the book includes the conceptual aspects of both mainstream neoliberal policies and their heterodox critiques. The observed links between economic policies and the enabling sociopolitical environment supplement the arguments in the book which hopefully will open up a new dimension for analysing subordination and the lack of development.

articles.title: The Origins and Evolution of Experimental Economics
articles.body_html:
by Charles A. Holt | Edward Elgar Publishing, 2026

In this expansive book, Charles Holt evaluates early findings in the evolution of experimental economics and explores pathways for future discoveries. The book presents a sequence of experiments that fit together, punctuated with descriptions of the people involved and their motivations.

Chapters present a historical perspective on primary areas of experimental economics, illustrated with critical data-based figures. Topics covered include market experiments, asset market bubbles, prospect theory, risk preferences, belief elicitation, behavioral biases, behavioral and stochastic game theory, and trust and incentives. The book also provides practical insights into auction design based on the author''s extensive experience developing instruments including emissions and irrigation permits, combinatorial broadcast licenses and a diverse set of securities.

This book is highly recommended for scholars and students interested in the implications and the history of controlled economic experiments. Those in the field of experimental economics and related social sciences such as political science will benefit from this book’s insights.

Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: Transit Asia Critical Concepts
articles.body_html:
edited by Joyce C. H. Liu and others | 2026, Open Humanities Press

Concepts hold the world together. But what happens when the world fragments, explodes in war, faces the epistemic collapse wrought by AI, or the ravages of climate spun out of control? Concepts also disintegrate, lose their self-positing status. And yet critique does not simply dissolve in conditions of radical uncertainty. There is a hunger to critique. It finds new forms, partial, provisional, forged from within instability rather than above. Transit Asia Critical Concepts emerges from this conceptual turbulence.

The concepts gathered in this book are not designed to map Asia, to fix its contours, or confirm its coherence. They move across Asian environments, through infrastructures of labour and logistics, inside computational architectures and their human remainders, against the unevenly distributed catastrophes of climate and war in ways that exceed the regional frame they inhabit. That excess is not incidental. It is what thinking from Asia produces, a movement beyond the cultural imaginaries, institutional settings, and lived encounters that give Asia its apparent shape.

articles.title: CHOPE Visiting Scholars Program 2027-28
articles.category: Heterodox Graduate Programs, Scholarships and Grants
articles.body_html:
The Center for the History of Political Economy at Duke University is now accepting applications for the 2027-28 Visiting Scholars program.

Academic Visits

The Center for the History of Political Economy sponsors two regular programs the HOPE Workshop and HOPE lunches series. Scholars wishing to present their work in either venue should contact the organizer, Steven Medema.

Self-sponsored shorter term visitors who wish to be affiliated with the Center should contact the Center Director, Steven Medema, to receive an invitation. Academic visitors are welcome at the Center on a space-available basis.

Visitors are encouraged to explore our Visitors Resource Guide for information on hotels, transportation around the University.

The Center for the History of Political Economy also sponsors Visiting Scholars for a semester or an academic year.

For a complete description of the program and how to apply, please visit the Visiting Scholar Page on the Center website.

Submission

Please submit your materials via Strongbox. Label your document packet with your last name and the year (e.g. Smith 2027). After submitting, notify us by emailing chope@econ.duke.edu.

If you do not receive an acknowledgment of your application within one to two days, please email us to confirm that we have received your submission.

The application process is competitive; only a portion of applicants will be selected.

Application Deadline: 4 January 2027

articles.title: EPOG-JM Erasmus Mundus Joint Master
articles.category: Heterodox Graduate Programs, Scholarships and Grants
articles.body_html:
Economic POlicies for the Global bifurcation (EPOG-JM)

Economic POlicies for the Global bifurcation (EPOG-JM) is an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degree in economics, supported by the European Union. It offers a world-class integrated Master's programme on the (digital, socioeconomic, ecological) transition processes with a pluralist approach and interdisciplinary perspectives.

The main objective of the programme is to give birth to a new generation of international experts, able to define and assess economic policies and evolve within different political, social and regional contexts. Towards this objective, the EPOG-JM Master’s programme goes beyond the reach of standard economic theory to include various heterodox/institutionnalist political economy approaches.

The full partners (degree awarding institutions) include a wide set of prestigous institutions:

  • University of technology of Compiègne (UTC),
  • Sorbonne University,
  • University of Turin,
  • Berlin School of Economics and Law,
  • University of Rome 3,
  • University of Geneva
  • University of the Witwatersrand (Wits),
  • Vienna University of Economics and Business,
  • Federal University of Rio de Janeiro,
  • University of Campinas.

It also involves more than 30 (academic and non-academic) associated partners in Europe and the world.

Scholarships

The very best students from all over the world will be eligible for scholarships awarded for 2 years by the European Commission, based on our selection.

The Erasmus Mundus scholarship covers:

  • student participation costs (tuition fees, full health insurance coverage and any other mandatory costs related to student participation in the course),
  • a monthly allowance of € 1400 per month (during both academic years).

More details here.

Application Deadline: 27 January 2027
