articles.title: Frederic S. Lee Heterodox Economics Scholarship - Spring 2027
articles.category: Heterodox Graduate Programs, Scholarships and Grants
articles.body_html:
The application for the Spring 2027 semester is now open.

The Frederic S. Lee Heterodox Economics Scholarship was established by Frederic and Ruth Lee in 2014 to help students to continue their study in heterodox economics. Over the past 13 years, the Scholarship awarded 27 doctoral students from five heterodox economics programs in the United States—that is, American University, Colorado State University, the New School for Social Research, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, and the University of Missouri Kansas City.

To be eligible, the applicant must be enrolled in a doctoral heterodox economics program in the US and demonstrate financial need. This scholarship will not provide scholarship aid for dissertation credit hours or for credit hours that are not directly relevant for the completion of the doctoral program's coursework.

Selection criteria include:

  • Priority will be given to students who have no scholarship support at all and need support to continue in their heterodox doctoral program. Students who have only partial scholarship support and need additional support to continue in their heterodox doctoral program will also be considered.
  • Preference will be given to students who are interested in working in heterodox microeconomics. Applicants from other ﬁelds of study are also encouraged to apply, especially if they are willing to do heterodox economics in an integrative manner (as opposed to adhering to a single heterodox economics tradition).

Read about the heterodox economics of Frederic S. Lee at https://sites.google.com/view/leefs

Scholarships will be awarded prior to the fall and spring semesters. Scholarships are not renewable; however, previous recipients may reapply.

Apply here.

Application Deadline: 15 November 2026

Economic POlicies for new Global cooperation and alliances (GLOBAL COOP) is an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degree in economics, supported by the European Union. It offers a world-class integrated Master’s programme focused on economic policies for navigating a rapidly evolving geopolitical landscape. The programme trains experts to design and implement policies that foster new forms of global cooperation and alliances between countries in the Global North and the Global South. It covers international trade, the international monetary and financial system, and the just socioecological transition, while adopting an interdisciplinary and various heterodox/institutionnalist political economy approaches.

The full partners (degree awarding institutions) include prestigious institutions in Europe and beyond:

  • Sorbonne Nouvelle University (France)
  • Sorbonne University (France)
  • University of technology of Compiègne (France)
  • University of Siena (Italy)
  • National University of San Martín (Argentina)
  • University of Campinas (Brazil)
  • Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
  • National University of Colombia (Colombia)

It also involves more than 30 (academic and non-academic) associated partners in Europe and the world.

It offers a world-class integrated Master’s programme focused on economic policies for navigating a rapidly evolving geopolitical landscape. The programme trains experts to design and implement policies that foster new forms of global cooperation and alliances between countries in the Global North and the Global South. It covers international trade, the international monetary and financial system, and the just socioecological transition, while adopting an interdisciplinary and various heterodox/institutionnalist political economy approaches. The full partners (degree awarding institutions) include prestigious institutions in Europe and beyond: Sorbonne Nouvelle University (France) Sorbonne University (France) University of technology of Compiègne (France) University of Siena (Italy) National University of San Martín (Argentina) University of Campinas (Brazil) Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Brazil) National University of Colombia (Colombia) It also involves more than 30 (academic and non-academic) associated partners in Europe and the world. Scholarships The very best students from all over the world will be eligible for scholarships awarded for 2 years by the European Commission, based on our selection. The Erasmus Mundus scholarship covers: student participation costs (tuition fees, full health insurance coverage and any other mandatory costs related to student participation in the course), a monthly allowance of € 1400 per month (during both academic years). More details here . Application Deadline: 27 January 2027

articles.title: The Wealth Cap Declaration
articles.body_html:
We live in a time of extreme wealth inequality.

Wealth is increasingly accumulating in the hands of a few while most citizens face rising living costs, deteriorating public services, and shrinking opportunities. An ultra-rich minority grows richer every day by exploiting an unjust system, exerting disproportionate influence over institutions, governments, and our economies, with far-reaching consequences for everyone's lives.

No one should be able to undermine democracy, put their personal interests above society's, or dictate the direction our economies should take. As wealth and power become increasingly concentrated, the growing divide not only threatens justice and progress, but also our collective liberty.

It is time to change this!

The signatories, defend a clear solution: a European cap on extreme wealth.

Countries in Europe must implement a standardized limit on the amount of wealth a single person can own to prevent extreme wealth accumulation in the hands of a few. The wealth cap shall spark widespread wealth redistribution in Europe, reviving our public services, funding universal social programs, financing the green transition, and promoting innovation to improve everyone's lives. The time has come to move towards a democratic economic system where everyone takes part in progress. This is the only way to guarantee a better future for everyone, one in which no one is left behind. It is time to act, and it is more necessary than ever before.

For further information or to sign the declaration click here.

articles.title: DIY Macroeconomic Model Simulation: New Chapters and Workshops
articles.body_html:
The open-source website DIY Macroeconomic Model Simulation, an online script for simulating macroeconomic models, was launched three years ago by Karsten Kohler (University of Leeds) and has since been extended. All chapters now come with both R and Python code. Nine further chapters cover stock-flow consistent modelling, conflict inflation, business and housing cycles, neoclassical growth and open-economy macroeconomics (including the Solow model and Dornbusch’s exchange rate overshooting model), and evolutionary game theory. The most recent addition, co-authored with Nitin Nair (University of Leeds), opens a new part on empirical applications. It shows how to calibrate a macroeconomic model to empirical data with the method of simulated moments, and further chapters on empirical applications are planned. All materials are freely available, and feedback is welcome.

Further information can be found here.

The material is also used in workshops. The next one is a NARTI workshop for PhD students in Leeds on 4 December. It is open only to students from universities that are members of the NARTI network. Further information on the workshop can be found here. Institutions interested in hosting a workshop on macroeconomic model simulation, in person or online, can contact k.kohler@leeds.ac.uk.

articles.title: In Memoriam Perry Mehrling: A Statement from the History of Economics Society (HES)
articles.body_html:
The History of Economics Society joins his family and friends in grieving for Perry Mehrling, Professor of International Political Economy at Boston University and, previously, longtime Professor of Economics at Barnard College.

We have learned from a close colleague of his at the INET that Perry died Monday night from injury sustained in a fall several days earlier.

Perry was among the most highly esteemed scholars in our worldwide community of historians of economics for upwards of thirty years. His four sole-authored books, The Money Interest and the Public Interest: American Monetary Thought, 1920-1970 (Harvard, 1997); Fischer Black and the Revolutionary Idea of Finance (Wiley, 2005); The New Lombard Street: How the Fed Became the Dealer of Last Resort (Princeton, 2011); and Money and Empire: Charles P. Kindleberger and the Dollar System (Cambridge, 2022) are indispensable contributions to the histories of monetary economics, financial economics, and international political economy.

His works are also so eminently readable as to be useful in debates about money, finance, and financial power in the present day. What Perry wrote of Kindleberger is equally true of himself. He “was never content just to satisfy his own curiosity. He wanted to tell others so that they could use this new knowledge – indeed, he felt a positive duty to do so” (2022, p. 260).

The many people whose thinking and careers Perry touched will have their own recollections of him. We are eager to hear them. Ours in the HES include the numerous conference sessions in which he presented and participated; his collaboration with several of us on projects ranging from edited volumes to guest lectures and student events; his HES Best Article Prize for “The Monetary Economics of Benjamin Graham: A Bridge Between Goods and Money?” (JHET 33.3, Sept. 2011); and his appreciated efforts, which we promise to carry on, to host next year’s HES conference in Boston.

Nor can we forget his off-conference “Keynes’s Regret” dinners -- the best reminder that, when we convene as scholars, we are (Champagne or no) among friends. We will miss our friend Perry.

Cristina Marcuzzo, HES President

Pedro Garcia Duarte, HES Vice President

Stephen Meardon, HES Secretary

articles.title: In Memoriam: Anwar Shaikh: An Obituary by Nikolaos Chatzarakis (AHE)
articles.body_html:
Nikolaos Chatzarakis’s obituary for Anwar Shaikh was published on the Association for Heterodox Economics website.

…quando coeli movendi sunt et terra

On Tuesday 6th of October, one of the greatest political economists of our time passed away. Anwar Shaikh indeed “moved heavens and earth” by offering an entirely new, highly sophisticated and deeply impacting (both scientifically and politically) vision in the critical economic thought. Being one of the landmark figures in erstwhile heterodox political economy, he brought forth a unique amalgamation of classical thought, inspired by Smith, Ricardo, Marx, Schumpeter and Keynes, and concrete mathematical and statistical foundations. Equipped with an Engineering degree from Princeton University; with deep knowledge of Mathematics and Physics – but also of Philosophy and Political Theory; and with a fervent political and social awareness (having partcipated in the civil rights movement and the anti-war protests of the ‘60s and ‘70s), Shaikh became one of the most fitting persons to continue and expand the tradition of the ‘Surplus Approach’ and turn mainstream economics on their head. His unique approach, deeply rooted in data (but not data-driven) and empirically derived stylised facts (yet never empiricist), and heavily influenced by the unique political and institutional constitution of capitalism (the role of class, race and gender), as well as his methodical questioning of widespread beliefs, has marked many contemporary economists and has entirely reshaped our understanding of what political economy is and what it can accomplish.

His 55-year long career was marked by a huge number of breakthroughs that few other economists (heterodox or otherwise) could claim; the range of topics covered spans from the theory of value to a reconceptualision of finance, and can be compared only with that of the classical worldly philosophers (like Smith, Ricardo and Marx) or with that of the major economic theorists of the 20th century (like Samuelson and Galbraith). His magnum opus, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises, the result of a lifelong research project, is not only the culmination of all these topics, but also a radical and pragmatist perspective on a number of economic matters (from production theory to exchange rate dynamics). And that highlights Shaikh’s highest objective and his greatest offer to modern Economics: his attempt to reconstruct the entire economic theory, founded on the classical and Marxian tradition as well as on solid empirical grounds, and provide the grounds for applications and economic policies beyond the narrow grounds of modern neoclassical perspectives or from their naïve heterodox alternatives.

“I have but to swallow this … and be for the rest of my days, persecuted by a legion of goblins, all of my own creation. Humbug, I tell you— humbug!”

His first breakthrough came at the time he was a PhD student at Columbia University (supervised by Ronald Findlay, himself a student of Robert Solow) between 1968 and 1973. His argument was simple enough: aggregate production functions, like the ones used in many neoclassical models (e.g., the Solow-Swan growth model) are “humbug”. And to prove it, what he did was compare the regressions of output per capita against capital-labour ratios in Solow’s growth accounting to similar regressions of artificially constructed data that spelled the word HUMBUG on a graph. But, this was just the beginning. Shaikh explained that what is actually measured in these regressions is not the generation of output on aggregate (as a production function should do), but its distribution between capital and labour. By doing so, he connected this brilliant result to the ongoing debates about theorising and measuring capital that have been fought between the ‘orthodox’ economists of Cambridge, MA and the ‘heterodox’ of Cambridge, UK. His impact on this field was so big that Joan Robinson (who had herself started that debate more than 20 years ago) wrote to him “It was very useful to me … I knew that it was ‘humbug’ for 20 years, but I could never nail it down”. Anwar’s blow was unfortunately only half-given: his paper on the subject, Laws of Production and Laws of Algebra, was accepted in the Review of Economics and Statistics only as a short note, with Solow having the chance to reply, whereas he hadn’t.

“Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing.”

In 1972, before finishing his PhD, he was already employed in the New School for Social Research, his work having impressed the esteemed economists of the institution, Robert Heilbroner and Adolph Löwe. Shaikh spent his entire career in the New School, teaching, researching and supervising several students. Interestingly, some of the first issues on his research (and on that of his students) were related to the validity of the labour theory of value and its implications. The total contribution took almost twenty years and left an important body of work, that is continued and still inspiring researchers today.

The first part was a paper published in 1977 titled Marx’s Theory of Value and the ‘Transformation’ Problem, where he presented the view that Marx was not incorrect in his attempt to solve the ‘transformation’ from values to prices; he understood his calculations were merely one step in a longer sequence and he bothered not to continue it. By continuing it, Anwar showed that the algorithm Marx seemingly proposed converges to the ‘correct’ prices of production and the ‘correct’ rate of profit (as calculated by Bortkiewicz, and as they would in any Leontief-Sraffa model). This algorithm mimics the price adjustment of actual firms to conform to competitive capital reallocation that would lead to a uniform rate of profit, exactly in the manner Marx presents it in Capital, vol. III. The second part focused on the computation of actual labour values and prices of production, making his first breakthrough in 1984 with The Transformation from Marx to Sraffa (continued in 1998 with The Empirical Strength of the Labour Theory of Value), where he showed that it is possible to compute these categories from input-output data and that the labour values really approximate prices of production well. At a time where neoclassical and neo-Ricardian thought alike were targeting Ricardo’s and Marx’s use of the labour theory of value, Shaikh not only proved its empirical strength, but also the validity of Ricardo’s and Marx’s arguments around the price-value deviations. This work was continued and is still continued today by many scholars around the world. It also led to an entire reconceptualisation of national accounts – a work that Shaikh (and many of his students) undertook over the next years, culminated in one of Shaikh’s and Tonaks’ greatest publications, Measuring the Wealth of Nations, and it is still forming part of the heterodox economics’ landscape.

“The dynamic and brutal war … appears here as a decorous ballet.”

Shaikh’s next big contribution was on the sphere of competition. Unlike many Marxists of the time, Shaikh felt discomfort using the concepts of ‘monopoly’ and ‘monopolistic competition’ to contrast contemporary capitalism with the earlier industrialised capitalism described by Marx; and unlike many Sraffians of the time, he felt discomfort with the idea that the choice of technique is static and does not involve competitive adjustments within and between industries. The source of this discomfort was that both were trapped in a conception of competition advanced by the marginalists, where different firms are presented as passive and price-taking, while the relation between them as a careful choreography. Competition is “war between capitals”, he said, in his 1980 paper Marxian Competition versus Perfect Competition; and the tendencies we observe (towards a uniform price within industries, and towards a uniform rate of profit between industries) are the results of this dynamic and turbulent process. Uniform prices and rates of profit do not really exist, but are the abstractions we make when the results of competition have been fully assumed. Shaikh also proposed the concept of ‘regulating capital’, i.e., the capital representing the typical technique of each industry (whether actually in use or not), on which occur the equalisation of prices within-industry and the equalisation of rate of profit between-industries.

The concept could be easily utilised outside the strict theoretical description of competition. The most obvious and most important application was the application of the law of value in international trade – an idea that, at the time, had already been popularised by Emmanuel and other theorists of unequal exchange. In a two-part paper in 1979 and 1980, titled Foreign Trade and the Law of Value, he explained how this theory of competition extends to the international level and gives an absolute cost-competitive advantage to countries that have higher concentrations of capital and operate closer to the ‘international regulating capital’, thus explaining economic imperialism, uneven development and the international transfers of value in a consistent value-theoretic manner. This proposal (also applied later in the dynamics of exchange rates, in his 1999 paper Real Exchange Rates and the International Mobility of Capital) has been widely popular, with many theorists refining it and applying it even today.

“Profit is the life blood of capitalism”

Shaikh praised Heilbroner’s remark about profit being the raison d’ être of the capitalist system, the manifestation of the self-interest, that all capitalists pursue. This praise though was not a simple theoretical remark, but rather a way to reconceive the way the capitalist system operates and leads itself to growth and prosperity, but also to inequality, inflation, unemployment and crises – the very themes that much of his work and his magnum opus explore. His long trajectory on this issue starts with a revival of Henryk Gorssman’s and Maurice Dobb’s theory of crises in his 1978 papers, Political Economy and Capitalism: Notes on Dobb’s Theory of Crises and An Introduction to the History of Crisis Theories, where he proposed that the decline of the rate of profit is responsible for the historical trajectory of the capitalist system, but also the cause of major crises (e.g., the Great Depression of the ‘30s and the Stagflation of the ‘70s). In his subsequent works, he pointed out that the decline of the rate of profit combined with the stagnation of the mass of profits leads to overaccumulation of capital and to the outburst of a crisis roughly every fifty years, connecting this Marxian explanation to the Kondratieff waves. For Shaikh, the accumulation of capital is driven by the reinvestment of profits and, thus, goes hand-in-hand with the disproportionate expansion of capital stock and deterioration of old techniques and labour practices; this is an inherent death-trap that capitalism has to face periodically and its only way out is a cathartic crisis, that will devaluate capital, push the adoption of new techniques and raise profitability high enough for capitalists to keep investing. This perspective become central to his later economic thought. Most notably, in his 2004 paper, The Power of Profit, he accurately predicted the outburst of the 2007-2008 crisis and the subsequent recession. But, his thought expanded further: in his book, he showed how the failure of capitalist countries to reinvest profits led to de-industrialisation and financialisation in the US, the UK and elsewhere, persistent unemployment, an exponential rise of inflation after the ‘60s and rising inequalities (including the cost-of-living crisis in many countries today).

“Unhappy the land that is in need of heroes.”

It suffices to say that Anwar Shaikh’s contributions go far beyond these few examples. A mere browsing of his latest book, or a simple search of his numberless papers online can show the multitude of themes he (and his students) has worked on. Yet, one remarkable trait is given throughout his whole work: the deep and wholehearted critique of meainstream theories, the employment of the labour theory of value and the theory of real competition, and the centrality of profit in explaining capitalist dynamics seem to cut straight through all of it. His complete reconstruction of national accounts, his reconceptualisation of economic theory from the ground up, his unique vision of capitalism as a self-regulating, yet turbulent and chaotic system that spits out inequality, uneven development and crises – all came from the same root and all pointed to the same telos: real economics to understand the real world.

In a sense, his passing couldn’t be timelier. At a time when academic freedom is constantly threatened, when education and research are pushed to their limits (institutionally, financially and technologically), when scholars are frightened to take a moral stance towards the wide problems of the world, his brightness flashes for one last moment to remind us what scientific and personal integrity mean. Anwar Shaikh illuminated a path for us. How we can turn century-old orthodoxies upside down and build our new visions of the world. How we can use modern tools to falsify and revive old, yet realistic visions. But, also, how we can think on our own about the shape of our world (even our little academic world). As a teacher, he inspired many to study and work for what they believed; and as a researcher, he inspired much more to keep questioning and seek the deeper, harder truths. His torch has not been blown – we must carry it on.

You can find the obituary for Anwar Shaikh by Nikolaos Chatzarakis in its original form here.

On Anwar Shaikh's website Real Economics you can learn more about his life and work, there is also a link to large numbers of his research publications as well as some video lectures held by him.

Being one of the landmark figures in erstwhile heterodox political economy, he brought forth a unique amalgamation of classical thought, inspired by Smith, Ricardo, Marx, Schumpeter and Keynes, and concrete mathematical and statistical foundations. Equipped with an Engineering degree from Princeton University; with deep knowledge of Mathematics and Physics – but also of Philosophy and Political Theory; and with a fervent political and social awareness (having partcipated in the civil rights movement and the anti-war protests of the ‘60s and ‘70s), Shaikh became one of the most fitting persons to continue and expand the tradition of the ‘Surplus Approach’ and turn mainstream economics on their head. His unique approach, deeply rooted in data (but not data-driven) and empirically derived stylised facts (yet never empiricist), and heavily influenced by the unique political and institutional constitution of capitalism (the role of class, race and gender), as well as his methodical questioning of widespread beliefs, has marked many contemporary economists and has entirely reshaped our understanding of what political economy is and what it can accomplish. His 55-year long career was marked by a huge number of breakthroughs that few other economists (heterodox or otherwise) could claim; the range of topics covered spans from the theory of value to a reconceptualision of finance, and can be compared only with that of the classical worldly philosophers (like Smith, Ricardo and Marx) or with that of the major economic theorists of the 20th century (like Samuelson and Galbraith). His magnum opus, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises , the result of a lifelong research project, is not only the culmination of all these topics, but also a radical and pragmatist perspective on a number of economic matters (from production theory to exchange rate dynamics). And that highlights Shaikh’s highest objective and his greatest offer to modern Economics: his attempt to reconstruct the entire economic theory, founded on the classical and Marxian tradition as well as on solid empirical grounds, and provide the grounds for applications and economic policies beyond the narrow grounds of modern neoclassical perspectives or from their naïve heterodox alternatives. “I have but to swallow this … and be for the rest of my days, persecuted by a legion of goblins, all of my own creation. Humbug, I tell you— humbug!” His first breakthrough came at the time he was a PhD student at Columbia University (supervised by Ronald Findlay, himself a student of Robert Solow) between 1968 and 1973. His argument was simple enough: aggregate production functions, like the ones used in many neoclassical models (e.g., the Solow-Swan growth model) are “humbug”. And to prove it, what he did was compare the regressions of output per capita against capital-labour ratios in Solow’s growth accounting to similar regressions of artificially constructed data that spelled the word HUMBUG on a graph. But, this was just the beginning. Shaikh explained that what is actually measured in these regressions is not the generation of output on aggregate (as a production function should do), but its distribution between capital and labour. By doing so, he connected this brilliant result to the ongoing debates about theorising and measuring capital that have been fought between the ‘orthodox’ economists of Cambridge, MA and the ‘heterodox’ of Cambridge, UK. His impact on this field was so big that Joan Robinson (who had herself started that debate more than 20 years ago) wrote to him “It was very useful to me … I knew that it was ‘humbug’ for 20 years, but I could never nail it down”. Anwar’s blow was unfortunately only half-given: his paper on the subject, Laws of Production and Laws of Algebra , was accepted in the Review of Economics and Statistics only as a short note, with Solow having the chance to reply, whereas he hadn’t. “Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing.” In 1972, before finishing his PhD, he was already employed in the New School for Social Research, his work having impressed the esteemed economists of the institution, Robert Heilbroner and Adolph Löwe. Shaikh spent his entire career in the New School, teaching, researching and supervising several students. Interestingly, some of the first issues on his research (and on that of his students) were related to the validity of the labour theory of value and its implications. The total contribution took almost twenty years and left an important body of work, that is continued and still inspiring researchers today. The first part was a paper published in 1977 titled Marx’s Theory of Value and the ‘Transformation’ Problem , where he presented the view that Marx was not incorrect in his attempt to solve the ‘transformation’ from values to prices; he understood his calculations were merely one step in a longer sequence and he bothered not to continue it. By continuing it, Anwar showed that the algorithm Marx seemingly proposed converges to the ‘correct’ prices of production and the ‘correct’ rate of profit (as calculated by Bortkiewicz, and as they would in any Leontief-Sraffa model). This algorithm mimics the price adjustment of actual firms to conform to competitive capital reallocation that would lead to a uniform rate of profit, exactly in the manner Marx presents it in Capital, vol. III. The second part focused on the computation of actual labour values and prices of production, making his first breakthrough in 1984 with The Transformation from Marx to Sraffa (continued in 1998 with The Empirical Strength of the Labour Theory of Value ), where he showed that it is possible to compute these categories from input-output data and that the labour values really approximate prices of production well. At a time where neoclassical and neo-Ricardian thought alike were targeting Ricardo’s and Marx’s use of the labour theory of value, Shaikh not only proved its empirical strength, but also the validity of Ricardo’s and Marx’s arguments around the price-value deviations. This work was continued and is still continued today by many scholars around the world. It also led to an entire reconceptualisation of national accounts – a work that Shaikh (and many of his students) undertook over the next years, culminated in one of Shaikh’s and Tonaks’ greatest publications, Measuring the Wealth of Nations , and it is still forming part of the heterodox economics’ landscape. “The dynamic and brutal war … appears here as a decorous ballet.” Shaikh’s next big contribution was on the sphere of competition. Unlike many Marxists of the time, Shaikh felt discomfort using the concepts of ‘monopoly’ and ‘monopolistic competition’ to contrast contemporary capitalism with the earlier industrialised capitalism described by Marx; and unlike many Sraffians of the time, he felt discomfort with the idea that the choice of technique is static and does not involve competitive adjustments within and between industries. The source of this discomfort was that both were trapped in a conception of competition advanced by the marginalists, where different firms are presented as passive and price-taking, while the relation between them as a careful choreography. Competition is “war between capitals”, he said, in his 1980 paper Marxian Competition versus Perfect Competition ; and the tendencies we observe (towards a uniform price within industries, and towards a uniform rate of profit between industries) are the results of this dynamic and turbulent process. Uniform prices and rates of profit do not really exist, but are the abstractions we make when the results of competition have been fully assumed. Shaikh also proposed the concept of ‘regulating capital’, i.e., the capital representing the typical technique of each industry (whether actually in use or not), on which occur the equalisation of prices within-industry and the equalisation of rate of profit between-industries. The concept could be easily utilised outside the strict theoretical description of competition. The most obvious and most important application was the application of the law of value in international trade – an idea that, at the time, had already been popularised by Emmanuel and other theorists of unequal exchange. In a two-part paper in 1979 and 1980 , titled Foreign Trade and the Law of Value, he explained how this theory of competition extends to the international level and gives an absolute cost-competitive advantage to countries that have higher concentrations of capital and operate closer to the ‘international regulating capital’, thus explaining economic imperialism, uneven development and the international transfers of value in a consistent value-theoretic manner. This proposal (also applied later in the dynamics of exchange rates, in his 1999 paper Real Exchange Rates and the International Mobility of Capital ) has been widely popular, with many theorists refining it and applying it even today. “Profit is the life blood of capitalism” Shaikh praised Heilbroner’s remark about profit being the raison d’ être of the capitalist system, the manifestation of the self-interest, that all capitalists pursue. This praise though was not a simple theoretical remark, but rather a way to reconceive the way the capitalist system operates and leads itself to growth and prosperity, but also to inequality, inflation, unemployment and crises – the very themes that much of his work and his magnum opus explore. His long trajectory on this issue starts with a revival of Henryk Gorssman’s and Maurice Dobb’s theory of crises in his 1978 papers, Political Economy and Capitalism: Notes on Dobb’s Theory of Crises and An Introduction to the History of Crisis Theories , where he proposed that the decline of the rate of profit is responsible for the historical trajectory of the capitalist system, but also the cause of major crises (e.g., the Great Depression of the ‘30s and the Stagflation of the ‘70s). In his subsequent works, he pointed out that the decline of the rate of profit combined with the stagnation of the mass of profits leads to overaccumulation of capital and to the outburst of a crisis roughly every fifty years, connecting this Marxian explanation to the Kondratieff waves. For Shaikh, the accumulation of capital is driven by the reinvestment of profits and, thus, goes hand-in-hand with the disproportionate expansion of capital stock and deterioration of old techniques and labour practices; this is an inherent death-trap that capitalism has to face periodically and its only way out is a cathartic crisis, that will devaluate capital, push the adoption of new techniques and raise profitability high enough for capitalists to keep investing. This perspective become central to his later economic thought. Most notably, in his 2004 paper, The Power of Profit , he accurately predicted the outburst of the 2007-2008 crisis and the subsequent recession. But, his thought expanded further: in his book, he showed how the failure of capitalist countries to reinvest profits led to de-industrialisation and financialisation in the US, the UK and elsewhere, persistent unemployment, an exponential rise of inflation after the ‘60s and rising inequalities (including the cost-of-living crisis in many countries today). “Unhappy the land that is in need of heroes.” It suffices to say that Anwar Shaikh’s contributions go far beyond these few examples. A mere browsing of his latest book, or a simple search of his numberless papers online can show the multitude of themes he (and his students) has worked on. Yet, one remarkable trait is given throughout his whole work: the deep and wholehearted critique of meainstream theories, the employment of the labour theory of value and the theory of real competition, and the centrality of profit in explaining capitalist dynamics seem to cut straight through all of it. His complete reconstruction of national accounts, his reconceptualisation of economic theory from the ground up, his unique vision of capitalism as a self-regulating, yet turbulent and chaotic system that spits out inequality, uneven development and crises – all came from the same root and all pointed to the same telos: real economics to understand the real world. In a sense, his passing couldn’t be timelier. At a time when academic freedom is constantly threatened, when education and research are pushed to their limits (institutionally, financially and technologically), when scholars are frightened to take a moral stance towards the wide problems of the world, his brightness flashes for one last moment to remind us what scientific and personal integrity mean. Anwar Shaikh illuminated a path for us. How we can turn century-old orthodoxies upside down and build our new visions of the world. How we can use modern tools to falsify and revive old, yet realistic visions. But, also, how we can think on our own about the shape of our world (even our little academic world). As a teacher, he inspired many to study and work for what they believed; and as a researcher, he inspired much more to keep questioning and seek the deeper, harder truths. His torch has not been blown – we must carry it on. You can find the obituary for Anwar Shaikh by Nikolaos Chatzarakis in its original form here . On Anwar Shaikh's website Real Economics you can learn more about his life and work, there is also a link to large numbers of his research publications as well as some video lectures held by him.

articles.title: New committee of The History of Economic Thought Society of Australia
articles.body_html:
The History of Economic Thought Society of Australia (HETSA) recently held its Annual General Meeting at the HETSA/JSHET Joint Conference hosted by Doshisha University in Kyoto, Japan.

At that meeting Alex Millmow stood down as President of HETSA after 19 years of service. The membership is very grateful for Alex's significant contribution.

The following leadership roles within HETSA were re-established and the following persons were elected unopposed:

  • President: David Gilchrist (University of Western Australia)
  • Secretary: Mathew Frith (University of New England)
  • Treasurer: Ben Perks (University of Western Australia)

The new committee is looking forward to working with members and the global HET community to advance our important work. Please contact committee members directly if you have any queries.

Additional news includes:

  • A meeting of the Editorial Board of our journal, the (HER), was held at the conference. Rogério Arthmar (Federal University of Espírito Santo) and Riko Stevens (University of Notre Dame Australia) were reappointed as Editors and John Hawkins (University of Canberra) was appointed as the new Book Review Editor.
  • Anthony Endres (University of Auckland) was honoured as a Distinguished Fellow of HETSA.
  • The next HETSA conference will take place on 4-6 July 2027 in Melbourne, the same week as the Australian Conference of Economists which will follow on immediately from HETSA 2027. Alex Millmow will be convening HETSA 2027 and other details including a call for papers will be distributed as soon.

For further information please visit HETSA's recently redeveloped website.

issues.title: Heterodox Economics Newsletter #365
issues.editorial_html:
For more than a decade, I have been writing editorials for the Heterodox Economics Newsletter. Some commented on current events; others reflected on developments in economics, academia, or the wider world. A few dealt with the peculiar pleasures and recurring frustrations involved in doing pluralist research or keeping academic infrastructure alive.

Until now, these texts were dispersed across individual Newsletter issues. This made them part of the record, but not a particularly accessible one: finding an old editorial often required remembering roughly when it was written—or being willing to browse through a considerable number of past issues.

This has now changed. The editorials have found a new, searchable home in the HEN Blog:

https://www.heterodoxnews.com/blog 🦄🎉

Making these texts easier to access has produced an unexpected effect: taken together, they form a small and necessarily subjective archive of heterodox economics over the last decade. They document intellectual debates, changing institutional conditions, political events, organisational experiments, and recurring concerns over pluralism, academic freedom, and the survival of independent scholarly spaces.

Of course, not every editorial has aged equally well. Some diagnoses look overly optimistic in retrospect; others remain uncomfortably familiar. But this is perhaps precisely why such an archive may be useful. It reminds us that heterodox economics is not only a set of theoretical traditions or research programmes. It is also a community that must continually build, maintain, revise, and sometimes defend the institutions that make intellectual exchange possible.

The Newsletter has always depended on collective effort. I am deeply grateful to the many people who have helped sustain it: our volunteer IT support, the colleagues who have offered advice and encouragement, the editorial assistants who have contributed their time and skills, and the many readers, contributors, and IAPHE members who have made the Newsletter possible. So in case you value the Heterodox Economics Newsletter as a key academic infrastructre, please consider supporting IAPHE as a member or volunteer (just send a short email in case you are interested).

In that sense, the HEN Blog is not just a repository of past texts. Independent intellectual communities need more than good ideas. They also need places where those ideas can meet, circulate, and be remembered. It requires some care: attention, cooperation, material support, and people willing to do often invisible work.

All the best,

Jakob

articles.title: 39th Annual SASE Conference: Rebuilding Foundations and Hope: Creative Reconstruction in a Moment of Disruption (Glasgow, June 2027)
articles.body_html:
30 June - 3 July, 2027 | Glasgow, UK

39th Annual SASE Conference: Rebuilding Foundations and Hope: Creative Reconstruction in a Moment of Disruption

The theme of this year’s SASE’s meeting is to highlight this pushing back. The organizers aim to take stock of these experiments and projects of reconstruction and reassembly, consider their ability to promote shared prosperity and democracy, and analyze conditions for realizing these possibilities. For example, how can small business sectors and micro-enterprises leverage their embeddedness in networks, extended family, communities and associations to endure and even sidestep tariffs, price shocks, cost shifting by large firm partners, or immigration raids? What can they achieve by rerouting supply chains and contracts, adopting new technologies or product mixes or organizing mutual aid schemes? What about innovations in anti-trust strategies or labor organizing to address new digital and technology titans? Does it help when transnational activists drag firms to court to hold them responsible for environmental harms? What led trade unions to organize to support migrant workers in workplaces and local communities? What can we make of sometimes grassroots efforts to organizationally diversify capitalism, from sustaining or extending public banking to promoting worker cooperatives, either on their own or in combination with unions or municipal development programs? What do citizen-led innovations to contest AI, address climate change, or repair democracy reveal about their prospects?

This is a critical moment, perhaps a critical juncture, where actions now will have lasting effects. If we can sample from the multitude of ongoing efforts to rebuild key institutional and political foundations, we can facilitate comparison and discovery, surface possibilities, accelerate learning, avoid balkanization, and counter framings of failure or resignation. SASE is fortunate to have a wealth of analytical resources, accumulated knowledge and expertise, and the energy for this task. And where better to sort out new visions or strategies for addressing corporations, conspiracies against the public, moral sentiments, and the foundations for capitalist economies organized for shared prosperity than Glasgow and Scotland, the home of Adam Smith and the Scottish Enlightenment.

Submissions are welcome on the main theme and on other relevant topics across all research networks and mini conferences. The organizers look forward to gathering a diverse and engaged community of scholars in Glasgow.

Mini-Conference Theme: Petro- versus Electrostates? Global and domestic struggles over green energy transitions

We live through a critical moment in green energy transitions globally. In the past years, the adoption of renewables has accelerated, mainly thanks to Chinese industrial policy. Many countries, particularly in Europe, have now entered advanced power sector transitions, generating more than half of their electricity from wind and sun. But challenges to these transitions remain unexpectedly high. Donald Trump aims to entrench the United States as a primary petro-state and has reversed the green push of the Inflation Reduction Act. European leaders have committed to support this project by buying extraordinary volumes of US hydrocarbons, in exchange for favorable trade terms. Chinese renewables buildout and electrification are record-breaking. But the country continues to consume huge volumes of fossil energy – domestic coal as well as oil and gas imported from the very states (U.S., Russia, Saudi Arabia) that spearhead a global anti-decarbonization alliance. European leaders in renewables also face domestic challenges: Soaring energy prices related to oil and gas during the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars; problems of integrating new energy sources with existing grid management; and the strengthening of anti-decarbonization forces on the extreme right. Emerging economies, from Brazilian re-invention of modern renewable energy auctions, Ethiopia’s Grand Renaissance Dam hope to power an entire continental region, or Vietnam’s bold bet on offshore wind energy, constitute political projects to transform economies through energy, generating their own domestic and international struggles.

Energy has always been a critical topic for socio-economics but continues to remain weakly integrated into our understandings of (geo-)political as well as capitalist change. For instance, much of the geopolitics literature is on oil but very little has been written about the geopolitical implications of renewable electrification. Recent literature on domestic energy politics concentrates on conflicts around renewable technologies but little research addresses system-level issues (grids etc.). In the SASE context, these topics sit uncomfortably between several networks and remain underrepresented (also within SER). Aspects are covered in sessions on regulation, comparative capitalism, and in discussions on climate change/policy. But the SASE community has not given sustained attention to the radical transformations of energy systems experienced during our times and the deep international as well as domestic conflicts revolving around them. We see a strong demand for exploring intersections between domestic and global changes in energy and the multi-level conflicts revolving around them. Material interests, but also international networks of expertise, financing regimes, investment protection practices, and ideational change need to be explored as possible factors shaping these transitions and conflicts.

Recently, colleagues have proposed an integrative perspective by juxtaposing petro- against electro-states: the former – the US, Saudi Arabia, Russia - entrenching fossil dependencies, the latter – most notably China – rapidly transitioning to renewables at home while forging trade relations around green tech, in particular with Europe. However, these ideas of international energy realignments remain poorly developed. For instance, the supposed electro-regimes in China and Europe continue to foster fossil relationships while experiencing new challenges for renewables expansion and electrification at home. New resource dependencies emerge over critical minerals. The United States may be pivoting to hydrocarbon exports, but its model of domestic consumption-led growth, let alone its project of reindustrialization, stand in contradiction with these aims (reflected recently in the Iran war-related inflationary surge). These contradictions parallel domestic politics struggles, as exemplified in Canada’s or Brazil’s hydro versus oil wealth regimes. Labor relations and the role of industry conglomerates should feature more prominently in the literature.

The organizers thus think the time is ripe for the SASE community to dedicate a mini-conference to conflicts around rapidly transforming energy systems that can be observed domestically as well as internationally. This mini-conference would help to bring regular SASE scholars from different networks together with researchers who usually present work in other venues. The topic is complementary to, but does not fully overlap with other networks. Cross-listings could be made with networks E, H, L, and S.

Indicative panel themes:

Different transition speeds or true divergence?

A first panel theme revolves around the question of whether the notion of ongoing green transitions with different speeds still holds, or whether we observe a true divergence between accelerated expansion of renewables in some regions and significant slowdown in others, leading to divergent energy systems, political economies, and climate regimes.

Foreign energy interests versus domestic decarbonization

Do countries’ energy interests towards other countries align or conflict with domestic energy and climate policy interests? Mechanisms of convergence exist, e.g. when export-oriented green tech sector lobby for domestic renewables deployment and electrification. However, we can also see divergent pathways, e.g. when countries join green value chains without incentives for domestic decarbonization.

Grid integration conflicts

In the process of expanding renewables, many countries and regions plan to build larger and often cross-national grids in order to deal with intermittency and to increase energy security. Examples of this are the European common market project, China’s Global Energy Interconnection, North American grid integration, and the unfinished project of a Central American grid. However, these projects raise conflicts over infrastructure costs, the effects on energy prices, and over different ideologies, pitting local self-sufficiency/autonomy against international cooperation.

States or markets in coordinating system overhaul

The early phases of renewables expansions in Europe and the US have been shaped by a combination of liberalization plus technology support policies; the respective countries now face an abundance of project- and decades-long interconnection queues. When centralized planning has occurred, they have remained private or outside the scope of public scrutiny. By contrast, Chinese renewables buildout has been state-driven, though coordination between various provinces and state-owned companies has remained complex. In advanced transitions, system overhaul becomes increasingly pressing. An increasingly relevant meta-conflict concerns the role of the state or markets in accomplishing such high-level coordination.

Industrial reorganization struggles around power

Geographical size of the optimal power grids matters in shaping energy-manufacturing co-location, the resilience and complexity of grid management, and the extent of necessary system overhaul. Questions of “engineering” design converge with industrial policy and the organization of the electric power sector. Examples include China’s “zero-carbon industrial-park” initiative, Pakistan’s rapid expansion of rooftop solar, and the deployment of renewable-powered data-centers. These developments reduce sub-national dependencies on traditional utilities and reshape domestic energy politics and “geographical” politics by shifting decision-making authority toward regional or corporate owners of microgrid infrastructure.

Mini-Conference Theme: The New Politics of Derisking: Reconstruction, Resilience, and Hope

16-18 June, 2027 | Online

By placing derisking at the centre of analysis, the mini-conference addresses both the possibilities and the limits of contemporary reconstruction efforts. It considers how current and historically comparable practices of risk allocation may stabilise investment while entrenching unequal distributions of power and exposure. It also engages with emerging attempts to reconfigure risk sharing through institutional innovation at multiple scales, including municipal initiatives, public financial institutions and transnational forms of coordination.

Finally, it considers how derisking reshapes global production networks, strategic industries, and cross-border investment, creating opportunities for some regions and dependencies for others. In doing so, this mini-conference introduces a perspective that remains relatively underrepresented within SASE, namely a systematic focus on derisking as a governing logic of contemporary and long-run capitalism and as a terrain of political contestation in processes of reconstruction. This builds on the successful mini-conference on derisking held at SASE 2026. The current proposal reframes derisking as a contested instrument of creative reconstruction and institutional rebuilding in a moment of disruption, while the 2026 version presented derisking as a political project reshaping state-market relations and global hierarchies.

Key questions

  • How is derisking being mobilised in efforts to reconstruct economic institutions, productive capacity, and public infrastructure?
  • What institutional and financial architectures underpin derisking, what liabilities do they create, and how are these funded?
  • How does derisking reshape global production, strategic industries, foreign investment, and economic dependencies across states and regions?
  • How are risks, returns, costs, and governing authority distributed across states, firms, workers, communities, and territories in either the current or comparative historical context?
  • How do labour, civil society, municipalities, and local communities contest or develop alternatives to dominant derisking arrangements?

Proposed themes

  • Institutional architectures and productive reconstruction. Examines how derisking is embedded in efforts to rebuild state capacity, public infrastructures, strategic industries, and productive capabilities. Contributions may analyse public financial institutions, guarantees, revenue commitments, industrial policy instruments, and other arrangements through which investment is enabled and governed.
  • Geopolitics, economic security, and uneven development. Analyses how derisking shapes responses to geopolitical fragmentation, trade conflict, supply chain disruption, and economic security concerns. It considers regionalisation, friend-shoring, global production networks, and the uneven distribution of productive capacities and dependencies across regions and between the Global North and South.
  • Finance, distribution, and democratic accountability. Investigates how derisking redistributes risks and returns, creates public and private liabilities, and allocates costs across states, firms, organised labour, and communities. This theme includes work on financialisation, corporate concentration, public guarantees, labour, social protection, and the democratic governance of long-term financial commitments.
  • Contestation and alternative forms of risk-sharing. Explores how labour organisations, civil society, municipalities, and local communities contest or rework dominant derisking arrangements. It also examines alternatives such as public banking, cooperative ownership, municipal industrial strategies, mutualised finance, and other institutional arrangements intended to embed investment within more accountable and socially oriented forms of governance.

Mini-Conference Theme: Who builds the Transition? Trade Unions, Worker Power, and Ecological Reconstruction

The ecological transition is unfolding amid profound disruptions to both work and the institutions through which workers have historically exercised collective power. Climate impacts are intensifying as resurgent reactionary right-wing and ethno-nationalist leaders and their movements, increasing militarization, much of which is funded and enabled by new technologies of machine production and surveillance (Henaway 2023). Each of these trends, in ways both great and small, worsens both local and global environmental conditions. Meanwhile, many of the institutions and policies that were expected to underpin a transition toward low-carbon economies, including green industrial policy, public investment, and international climate cooperation are contested, weakened, or redirected. Yet, moments like these can create openings for rebuilding institutions, solidarities, and relations of production. With that backdrop, labour environmentalism must not only consider how workers and trade unions respond to ecological transition but what role they can play in reconstructing its alternatives.

Take for instance the notion of “just transition”. The original notion of a just transition, advanced by Tony Mazzochi, was that just like an environmental superfund, so too should there be one for workers (Leopold 2007). Mazzochi’s vision, however, was arguably much broader and ambitious in scope than much of how “just transition” is often invoked by both scholars and policy makers today. The emphasis on the simple one-to-one replacement of carbon-intensive jobs with new ones, often of marginal quality, winnows down the political horizon of labour environmentalism. Of course, the notion of a just transition is not the only idea advanced by labour environmentalists. New strategies for collective bargaining, public ownership proposals, worker cooperatives, sectoral planning, industrial policy, community-labour coalitions, migrant worker organizations, reforms to the working day, and other eco-social political economic arrangements for alternative forms of living also feature. All the while, each political potential must grapple with the tension of who is or is not recognized as a “worker” in the pursuit of these policies (Barca 2024; Akbulut, 2024). And, relatedly, how can solidarities and resonances between workers be appreciated with both breadth and depth? Finally, do these alternatives help build power to make change possible?

This also requires critical attention to who constitutes the worker within broader socio-ecological transition politics. Labor movements themselves are internally differentiated by migration status, race, gender, citizenship, occupation, geography, and uneven access to collective representation. Michael Denning’s concept of “wageless life” offers a productive intervention to re-imagining labor struggles within socio-ecological transitions. Denning argues that analyses of capitalism should not begin with the employment contract, but with the dispossession that produces the imperative to earn a living in the first place. The proletarian, in this account, is not just the wage laborer but the person made radically dependent upon the market for subsistence. Employment is therefore not universal, nor secure. Workers continually confront the possibility that capital will have no use for their labor. This perspective complicates familiar narratives of Just Transition. If ecological reconstruction is imagined primarily through the creation of “green jobs,” what happens to those whose labor is informal, unwaged, reproductive, intermittently employed, or rendered surplus through economic and technological restructuring?

For SASE 2027, submissions are encouraged that engage labor environmentalism and the question of: how can workers rebuild the foundations of socio-economic systems so that the majority of people’s’ ability to live is decoupled from capital’s mute compulsion (see Mau 2023)? Organized by the Trade Unions and Labour Environmentalism (TULE), a cross-national and interdisciplinary network foregrounding the role and function of labour in socio-ecological transitions. Prospective papers are invited that engage with the themes and/or questions outlined below, with an emphasis on direct engagement with the workplace (broadly construed), communities, and/or sectoral case studies.

  • Is employment creation an adequate horizon for Just Transition, and what would ecological reconstruction beyond the wage look like?
  • How does the enclosure, dispossession and wagelessness underlying capitalist labour markets shape workers’ capacity to contest environmentally destructive industries?
  • How might Just Transition and/or other frameworks commit to socio-ecological transitions account for the unemployed, informal, migrant, seasonal, precarious, and reproductive and subsistence workers? And what forms of solidarity can connect them to organized labour?
  • What labour-led alternatives and experiments can advance social and ecological well-being? (e.g., bargaining for the common good, community-labour coalitions etc.,)
  • What are the implications of ecological restructuring for transnational and emerging “green sector” labour forces, and what does worker power look like when stable employment is no longer its presumed foundation?
  • What does a labour led eco-social politics look like and how might it be scaled?
  • Reflections on “doing” labour environmentalism including participatory, worker-led comparative, historical, and other methodological approaches.

These questions speak directly to SASE 2027’s call to examine efforts to “rebuild key institutional and political formations” amid disruption and to learn from experiments capable of promoting shared prosperity and democracy. They also build upon TULE’s ongoing commitment to foregrounding trade unions and organized labour within environmental labour studies while remaining critically attentive to the contradictions and limitations of organized labour itself, including its own historically uneven engagement with gender and social reproduction. By bringing together research across sectors, countries, and disciplinary transitions, this mini conference asks what labour environmentalism can contribute not merely towards managing ecological transition, but to reconstructing economies around different relations between work, nature, democracy, and collective life. At a moment when existing institutions are being dismantled and ecological crises deepen; the challenge is not to defend what remains but to build in its place

Mini-Confernce Theme: Financial subordination and alternative pathways: limits of reform, possibilities for transformation

Recent decades have witnessed the deepening integration of economies into a global financial system characterised by persistent asymmetries of power, uneven access to credit and liquidity, hierarchical monetary arrangements, and unequal patterns of development. The concept of international financial subordination has emerged as a valuable framework for understanding how these asymmetries shape the developmental trajectories of countries, regions, firms, and social groups. By highlighting the structural constraints imposed by the international monetary and financial system, financial subordination sheds light on the ways in which financial hierarchies reproduce economic dependency, vulnerability to crises, and unequal opportunities for growth and social transformation.

At the same time, the contemporary global economy is experiencing profound disruptions. Escalating geopolitical tensions, climate change, technological transformations, recurrent financial crises, and the reconfiguration of global value chains have intensified debates about the future of globalisation and the institutional foundations of economic development. In this context, established assumptions regarding financial governance, development strategies, and international economic cooperation are being challenged. New initiatives, institutions, and policy experiments have emerged, while calls for economic sovereignty, development alternatives, and more democratic forms of economic coordination have gained renewed prominence.

This mini-conference seeks to explore the analytical and political implications of financial subordination in this changing context. In particular, it aims to address a central question: does recognising financial subordination point towards pragmatic reconstruction within existing capitalist institutions, or does it reveal the limits of reform and the need for more radical forms of economic and social transformation?

The mini-conference invites contributions that engage with financial subordination as a framework for understanding contemporary capitalism and for identifying alternative pathways for development. It is particularly interested in dialogue across heterodox traditions, including post-Keynesian, Marxian, dependency, structuralist, institutionalist, feminist, ecological, and decolonial approaches. In line with SASE's commitment to pluralism and its interest in underrepresented perspectives, the mini-conference also encourages contributions from and about the Global South, as well as work addressing race, ethnicity, migration, and other dimensions of uneven development.

Possible themes include, but are not limited to:

  • Financial subordination, dependency, and uneven development;
  • Monetary hierarchies, currency internationalisation, and global liquidity;
  • The political economy of economic sovereignty and policy space;
  • Financialisation and the reproduction of inequalities across countries and regions;
  • Financial subordination and the production of inequalities across class, gender, race, and space;
  • Climate change, green transitions, and sustainable development under conditions of financial subordination;
  • Technological change, digital finance, and new forms of dependency and exclusion;South-South cooperation and alternative financial architectures;
  • Geopolitical realignments, multipolarity, and the future of the international monetary system;
  • The role of development banks, industrial policy, and public investment in overcoming financial constraints;
  • Feminist, decolonial, and anti-racist perspectives on financial hierarchies and development;Historical and contemporary experiences of resistance, reform, and transformation.

By bringing together scholars from diverse disciplinary and theoretical backgrounds, the mini- conference aims to advance debates on the causes, consequences, and future of financial subordination. Beyond diagnosing contemporary challenges, it seeks to examine how alternative institutions, development strategies, and collective political projects might contribute to rebuilding the economic foundations necessary for more equitable, sustainable, and hopeful futures. In doing so, the mini-conference directly engages with the broader conference theme by asking how societies can move beyond entrenched forms of dependency and inequality and create new possibilities for development in a moment of global disruption.

Network Q Theme: Remaking Asian Capitalisms – New Paths of Development in Times of Disruption

Please find the general SASE 2027 entry here.

Network Q promotes theory and research on the diversity of socio-economic systems and capitalist development in Asia as well as its global implications. The network welcomes a wide range of theoretical perspectives (e.g. comparative and international political economy, economic sociology, management studies, industrial sociology, innovation studies, political science and international relations, geography, development studies, anthropology).

Across Asia, governments, firms, workers and communities are seeking to explore new paths of development amid geopolitical tension, technological change and climate disruption. Debates over industrial policy, energy transitions, labour rights and social protection ask not only how economies can adapt, but who directs reconstruction, who bears its costs and whether it can support more secure livelihoods.

Development is increasingly an intra-Asian process. Investment, supply chains, technology, energy and labour migration connect Asian economies, but not on equal terms. As production and strategic industries are reorganised, established centres may gain new forms of influence, while emerging manufacturing and resource-producing economies may gain opportunities without gaining equivalent control over technology, finance or value. These shifts may reproduce, unsettle or create new centre–periphery relationships within Asia.

While China remains a magnet for debates on Asian Capitalisms, to reflect on these dynamics, we particularly welcome work on and from South and Southeast Asia. We also seek to expand the presentation of work on Japan and South Korea.

Network Q also seeks to bring detailed knowledge of Asian economies and regions into dialogue with broader debates in political economy. The network welcomes contributions that use area expertise to develop, challenge or refine theories of capitalism, development, institutional change and global political economy.

The network welcomes papers and panels addressing, inter alia:

  • Industrial policy and the building and rebuilding of productive capacity.
  • Changing relationships among states, firms, workers and communities within structural change.
  • Intra-Asian investment, trade, finance and production networks.
  • Shifting centres and peripheries within Asia: who controls technology, captures value and carries risk?
  • The prospects and limits of economic self-reliance, strategic autonomy and regional cooperation.
  • The political economy energy security, climate adaptation, and green transitions.
  • Digital infrastructure, platforms, AI and semiconductor policy.
  • Labour migration, workers’ organising, wages, and skills in transnational Asian capitalism.
  • Urban and rural development, including uneven access to infrastructure and investment.
  • Contestation and resistance across Asian capitalisms.

For the 2027 conference, Network Q invites individual paper submissions, submissions for thematic panels, and SASE Book Salon panels on recently published books. Abstracts should be no longer than 1,000 words (plus references).

Thematic panels can address any themes and issues related to the aims and scope of the network and should be based on paper drafts with a structured discussion including a discussant. Book Salon panels consist of a book author, a chair/moderator, and a maximum of four discussants with relevant expertise on a recently published book speaking to Network Q themes. Note that SASE seeks to promote gender equality. We thus strongly encourage you to take gender balance into account in panel proposals.

Submissions should be done through the SASE website.

Please send your abstracts by 1st November 2026 (approx. 1,000 words)

As part of the mini-conference, the organizers will host one virtual session during the virtual conference days (16th-18th June 2027). There will be no hybrid sessions during the on-site conference.

Submissions should be done through the SASE website.
