How are risks, returns, costs, and governing authority distributed across states, firms, workers, communities, and territories in either the current or comparative historical context? How do labour, civil society, municipalities, and local communities contest or develop alternatives to dominant derisking arrangements? Proposed themes Institutional architectures and productive reconstruction. Examines how derisking is embedded in efforts to rebuild state capacity, public infrastructures, strategic industries, and productive capabilities. Contributions may analyse public financial institutions, guarantees, revenue commitments, industrial policy instruments, and other arrangements through which investment is enabled and governed. Geopolitics, economic security, and uneven development. Analyses how derisking shapes responses to geopolitical fragmentation, trade conflict, supply chain disruption, and economic security concerns. It considers regionalisation, friend-shoring, global production networks, and the uneven distribution of productive capacities and dependencies across regions and between the Global North and South. Finance, distribution, and democratic accountability. Investigates how derisking redistributes risks and returns, creates public and private liabilities, and allocates costs across states, firms, organised labour, and communities. This theme includes work on financialisation, corporate concentration, public guarantees, labour, social protection, and the democratic governance of long-term financial commitments. Contestation and alternative forms of risk-sharing. Explores how labour organisations, civil society, municipalities, and local communities contest or rework dominant derisking arrangements. It also examines alternatives such as public banking, cooperative ownership, municipal industrial strategies, mutualised finance, and other institutional arrangements intended to embed investment within more accountable and socially oriented forms of governance. Mini-Conference Theme: Who builds the Transition? Trade Unions, Worker Power, and Ecological Reconstruction The ecological transition is unfolding amid profound disruptions to both work and the institutions through which workers have historically exercised collective power. Climate impacts are intensifying as resurgent reactionary right-wing and ethno-nationalist leaders and their movements, increasing militarization, much of which is funded and enabled by new technologies of machine production and surveillance (Henaway 2023). Each of these trends, in ways both great and small, worsens both local and global environmental conditions. Meanwhile, many of the institutions and policies that were expected to underpin a transition toward low-carbon economies, including green industrial policy, public investment, and international climate cooperation are contested, weakened, or redirected. Yet, moments like these can create openings for rebuilding institutions, solidarities, and relations of production. With that backdrop, labour environmentalism must not only consider how workers and trade unions respond to ecological transition but what role they can play in reconstructing its alternatives . Take for instance the notion of “just transition”. The original notion of a just transition, advanced by Tony Mazzochi, was that just like an environmental superfund, so too should there be one for workers (Leopold 2007). Mazzochi’s vision, however, was arguably much broader and ambitious in scope than much of how “just transition” is often invoked by both scholars and policy makers today. The emphasis on the simple one-to-one replacement of carbon-intensive jobs with new ones, often of marginal quality, winnows down the political horizon of labour environmentalism. Of course, the notion of a just transition is not the only idea advanced by labour environmentalists. New strategies for collective bargaining, public ownership proposals, worker cooperatives, sectoral planning, industrial policy, community-labour coalitions, migrant worker organizations, reforms to the working day, and other eco-social political economic arrangements for alternative forms of living also feature. All the while, each political potential must grapple with the tension of who is or is not recognized as a “worker” in the pursuit of these policies (Barca 2024; Akbulut, 2024). And, relatedly, how can solidarities and resonances between workers be appreciated with both breadth and depth? Finally, do these alternatives help build power to make change possible? This also requires critical attention to who constitutes the worker within broader socio-ecological transition politics. Labor movements themselves are internally differentiated by migration status, race, gender, citizenship, occupation, geography, and uneven access to collective representation. Michael Denning’s concept of “wageless life” offers a productive intervention to re-imagining labor struggles within socio-ecological transitions. Denning argues that analyses of capitalism should not begin with the employment contract, but with the dispossession that produces the imperative to earn a living in the first place. The proletarian, in this account, is not just the wage laborer but the person made radically dependent upon the market for subsistence. Employment is therefore not universal, nor secure. Workers continually confront the possibility that capital will have no use for their labor. This perspective complicates familiar narratives of Just Transition. If ecological reconstruction is imagined primarily through the creation of “green jobs,” what happens to those whose labor is informal, unwaged, reproductive, intermittently employed, or rendered surplus through economic and technological restructuring? For SASE 2027, submissions are encouraged that engage labor environmentalism and the question of: how can workers rebuild the foundations of socio-economic systems so that the majority of people’s’ ability to live is decoupled from capital’s mute compulsion (see Mau 2023)? Organized by the Trade Unions and Labour Environmentalism (TULE), a cross-national and interdisciplinary network foregrounding the role and function of labour in socio-ecological transitions. Prospective papers are invited that engage with the themes and/or questions outlined below, with an emphasis on direct engagement with the workplace (broadly construed), communities, and/or sectoral case studies. Is employment creation an adequate horizon for Just Transition, and what would ecological reconstruction beyond the wage look like? How does the enclosure, dispossession and wagelessness underlying capitalist labour markets shape workers’ capacity to contest environmentally destructive industries? How might Just Transition and/or other frameworks commit to socio-ecological transitions account for the unemployed, informal, migrant, seasonal, precarious, and reproductive and subsistence workers? And what forms of solidarity can connect them to organized labour? What labour-led alternatives and experiments can advance social and ecological well-being? (e.g., bargaining for the common good, community-labour coalitions etc.,) What are the implications of ecological restructuring for transnational and emerging “green sector” labour forces, and what does worker power look like when stable employment is no longer its presumed foundation? What does a labour led eco-social politics look like and how might it be scaled? Reflections on “doing” labour environmentalism including participatory, worker-led comparative, historical, and other methodological approaches. These questions speak directly to SASE 2027’s call to examine efforts to “rebuild key institutional and political formations” amid disruption and to learn from experiments capable of promoting shared prosperity and democracy. They also build upon TULE’s ongoing commitment to foregrounding trade unions and organized labour within environmental labour studies while remaining critically attentive to the contradictions and limitations of organized labour itself, including its own historically uneven engagement with gender and social reproduction. By bringing together research across sectors, countries, and disciplinary transitions, this mini conference asks what labour environmentalism can contribute not merely towards managing ecological transition, but to reconstructing economies around different relations between work, nature, democracy, and collective life. At a moment when existing institutions are being dismantled and ecological crises deepen; the challenge is not to defend what remains but to build in its place Mini-Confernce Theme: Financial subordination and alternative pathways: limits of reform, possibilities for transformation Recent decades have witnessed the deepening integration of economies into a global financial system characterised by persistent asymmetries of power, uneven access to credit and liquidity, hierarchical monetary arrangements, and unequal patterns of development. The concept of international financial subordination has emerged as a valuable framework for understanding how these asymmetries shape the developmental trajectories of countries, regions, firms, and social groups. By highlighting the structural constraints imposed by the international monetary and financial system, financial subordination sheds light on the ways in which financial hierarchies reproduce economic dependency, vulnerability to crises, and unequal opportunities for growth and social transformation. At the same time, the contemporary global economy is experiencing profound disruptions. Escalating geopolitical tensions, climate change, technological transformations, recurrent financial crises, and the reconfiguration of global value chains have intensified debates about the future of globalisation and the institutional foundations of economic development. In this context, established assumptions regarding financial governance, development strategies, and international economic cooperation are being challenged. New initiatives, institutions, and policy experiments have emerged, while calls for economic sovereignty, development alternatives, and more democratic forms of economic coordination have gained renewed prominence. This mini-conference seeks to explore the analytical and political implications of financial subordination in this changing context. In particular, it aims to address a central question: does recognising financial subordination point towards pragmatic reconstruction within existing capitalist institutions, or does it reveal the limits of reform and the need for more radical forms of economic and social transformation? The mini-conference invites contributions that engage with financial subordination as a framework for understanding contemporary capitalism and for identifying alternative pathways for development. It is particularly interested in dialogue across heterodox traditions, including post-Keynesian, Marxian, dependency, structuralist, institutionalist, feminist, ecological, and decolonial approaches. In line with SASE's commitment to pluralism and its interest in underrepresented perspectives, the mini-conference also encourages contributions from and about the Global South, as well as work addressing race, ethnicity, migration, and other dimensions of uneven development. Possible themes include, but are not limited to: Financial subordination, dependency, and uneven development; Monetary hierarchies, currency internationalisation, and global liquidity; The political economy of economic sovereignty and policy space; Financialisation and the reproduction of inequalities across countries and regions; Financial subordination and the production of inequalities across class, gender, race, and space; Climate change, green transitions, and sustainable development under conditions of financial subordination; Technological change, digital finance, and new forms of dependency and exclusion;South-South cooperation and alternative financial architectures; Geopolitical realignments, multipolarity, and the future of the international monetary system; The role of development banks, industrial policy, and public investment in overcoming financial constraints; Feminist, decolonial, and anti-racist perspectives on financial hierarchies and development;Historical and contemporary experiences of resistance, reform, and transformation. By bringing together scholars from diverse disciplinary and theoretical backgrounds, the mini- conference aims to advance debates on the causes, consequences, and future of financial subordination. Beyond diagnosing contemporary challenges, it seeks to examine how alternative institutions, development strategies, and collective political projects might contribute to rebuilding the economic foundations necessary for more equitable, sustainable, and hopeful futures. In doing so, the mini-conference directly engages with the broader conference theme by asking how societies can move beyond entrenched forms of dependency and inequality and create new possibilities for development in a moment of global disruption. Network Q Theme: Remaking Asian Capitalisms – New Paths of Development in Times of Disruption Please find the general SASE 2027 entry here . Network Q promotes theory and research on the diversity of socio-economic systems and capitalist development in Asia as well as its global implications. The network welcomes a wide range of theoretical perspectives (e.g. comparative and international political economy, economic sociology, management studies, industrial sociology, innovation studies, political science and international relations, geography, development studies, anthropology). Across Asia, governments, firms, workers and communities are seeking to explore new paths of development amid geopolitical tension, technological change and climate disruption. Debates over industrial policy, energy transitions, labour rights and social protection ask not only how economies can adapt, but who directs reconstruction, who bears its costs and whether it can support more secure livelihoods. Development is increasingly an intra-Asian process. Investment, supply chains, technology, energy and labour migration connect Asian economies, but not on equal terms. As production and strategic industries are reorganised, established centres may gain new forms of influence, while emerging manufacturing and resource-producing economies may gain opportunities without gaining equivalent control over technology, finance or value. These shifts may reproduce, unsettle or create new centre–periphery relationships within Asia. While China remains a magnet for debates on Asian Capitalisms, to reflect on these dynamics, we particularly welcome work on and from South and Southeast Asia. We also seek to expand the presentation of work on Japan and South Korea. Network Q also seeks to bring detailed knowledge of Asian economies and regions into dialogue with broader debates in political economy. The network welcomes contributions that use area expertise to develop, challenge or refine theories of capitalism, development, institutional change and global political economy. The network welcomes papers and panels addressing, inter alia: Industrial policy and the building and rebuilding of productive capacity. Changing relationships among states, firms, workers and communities within structural change. Intra-Asian investment, trade, finance and production networks. Shifting centres and peripheries within Asia: who controls technology, captures value and carries risk? The prospects and limits of economic self-reliance, strategic autonomy and regional cooperation. The political economy energy security, climate adaptation, and green transitions. Digital infrastructure, platforms, AI and semiconductor policy. Labour migration, workers’ organising, wages, and skills in transnational Asian capitalism. Urban and rural development, including uneven access to infrastructure and investment. Contestation and resistance across Asian capitalisms. For the 2027 conference, Network Q invites individual paper submissions, submissions for thematic panels, and SASE Book Salon panels on recently published books. Abstracts should be no longer than 1,000 words (plus references). Thematic panels can address any themes and issues related to the aims and scope of the network and should be based on paper drafts with a structured discussion including a discussant. Book Salon panels consist of a book author, a chair/moderator, and a maximum of four discussants with relevant expertise on a recently published book speaking to Network Q themes. Note that SASE seeks to promote gender equality. We thus strongly encourage you to take gender balance into account in panel proposals. Submissions should be done through the SASE website . Please send your abstracts by 1st November 2026 (approx. 1,000 words) As part of the mini-conference, the organizers will host one virtual session during the virtual conference days (16th-18th June 2027). There will be no hybrid sessions during the on-site conference. Submissions should be done through the SASE website . Submissions to networks (papers and panels): 16 December 2026 Submission Deadline Mini-Conferences: 1 November 2026

articles.title: A World of a Thousand Cuts: Forests, Wood, and Industrialisation across the Globe in the 19th and 20th Centuries (Turin, July 2027)
articles.body_html:
6-8 July 2027 | Turin, Italy

The mainstream historiographies of industrialisation habitually emphasise the novel energy sources and materials that powered this transformative era, such as coal, steel, steam and electricity, implicitly assuming that wood, an important pre-industrial resource, was destined for an inevitable decline. Histories of industrialisation also disproportionately focus on Europe and North America. Stemming from the research vectors of the ERC Starting Grant “Industrial Wood: European Industrialisation as Seen from the Forests (1870-1914)”, this conference aims to rethink the relevance of wood in an unevenly industrialising world throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. It follows more recent interpretative paths, which draw attention to the material diversity of industrial metabolism, in order to achieve a more complex understanding of the social, economic and environmental histories of industrialisation. The conference also seeks to geographically decentre the research perspective and discover the links between forests and industrialisation in the global context.

Industrialisation, understood as a systemic social and economic transformation underpinned by technological innovations and leading to changes in production regimes, was an uneven and chronologically mis-aligned process within Europe and globally, stretching from the late 18th century far into the 20th century. Consequently, the relationship between industrialisation and forest exploitation varied depending on the national and international politics, markets, law regulations, access to technology, environmental movements, property and labour regimes, imperial dynamics and colonial power. Attentive to these complexities, the organisers have approached industrialisation as an a-synchronous, multi-focal and globally encompassing social and economic process, activated by a confluence of economic impetus and political agenda.

Even if in the course of industrialisation wood has been marginalised as a combustible, it maintained its significance in industrial economies as a construction material. Moreover, innovations in technology and transportation – both the drivers and the outcomes of industrialisation – made forests increasingly accessible for large-scale extraction, thus bringing industrial logging into the furthest reaches of the woods and fundamentally reshaping them economically, socially and ecologically. Recent historical, anthropological and archeological studies, focusing mostly on North America and Europe, show that extractivism, (im)migration and environmental degradation were a part of this process. They also reveal that industrialisation of timber production did not mean a complete break with rural economies, and that the demand for wood as fuel or production material (for paper or packaging, for example) changes depending on the historical moment. Through this conference, we aim to broaden the conversation geographically to include global histories of industrialisation and to answer these questions: how did industrialisation change the world’s forests? What kinds of new relationships, dependencies and hierarchies did the arrival of industrialisation within the forest context instigate with regards to natural environments and the working lives linked to their transformation? How does our understanding of industrialisation change when we cease to read it as a sequence of substitutions and instead view it as a process of persistence, accumulation and re-articulation, wherein old material and energy flows are not erased by new ones but are intricately woven into them, undergoing profound transformation? Ultimately, what does the industrialisation of forests mean? And how do we adjust our research methodologies to answer these questions?

The conference seeks to explore cases, with a double focus on forests and industrialisation, in various political contexts and across different geographies throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. The papers should relate to but do not have to be limited to the following themes:

  • industrialisation and wood consumption
  • labour, migration, gender and ethnicity
  • empires, colonialism and decolonisation
  • industrial wood uses, wood-based businesses and geographies of timber flow
  • networks, circulation of ideas and technology
  • industrial timberscapes (timber production complexes, workers settlements, infrastructure)
  • deindustrialisation and its impact on livelihoods
  • environmental effects of industrialisation in forests

Scholars in humanities and social sciences, interested in these topics, are welcome to apply. Ultimately, the conference aims to foster an interdisciplinary confluence between environmental history, social history, economic history, environmental anthropology and related sub-disciplines. We invite contributions from doctoral students, post-doctoral researchers and senior scholars.

Abstract Submission Deadline: 30 November 206

Full Paper Submission Deadline: 15 June 2027

articles.title: Global South–Europe Conference on Economy, Justice and Marginalized Communities 2026 (Online, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
9-10 November, 2026 | Online

The Global South–Europe Conference on Economy, Justice and Marginalized Communities 2026 is an international online conference bringing together researchers from the Global South, Europe and beyond to discuss contemporary economic and social challenges. The conference creates a space for dialogue across regions and disciplines, with particular attention to the links between economic transformation, inequality, justice, vulnerability and community resilience. Participation is free, and both presenters and attendees who wish to join the discussions without presenting a paper are warmly welcome.

The programme covers two complementary areas. The first focuses on the Global South, justice and marginalized communities, including conflict and reconstruction, trade disruptions and sanctions, economic vulnerability, food security, health inequality, climate justice, gender, social exclusion and Global South–Europe relations. The second welcomes a broad range of economic research, including labour markets, poverty and inequality, education and human capital, health economics, finance and financial inclusion, public economics, regional development, the digital economy and AI, international trade and macroeconomic change. The conference welcomes theoretical, empirical, applied, qualitative, quantitative, interdisciplinary and policy-oriented research.

Authors are invited to submit complete manuscripts rather than abstracts. Submitted papers will be evaluated by the Scientific Committee, and selected authors will be invited to present their research in thematic online sessions. All presenters will receive a Certificate of Participation in recognition of their contribution to the conference. Selected papers may also be recommended for submission to the peer-reviewed journals Positive Science – Economics and the Journal of Marginalized Communities and Social Justice (JMCSJ); all recommended papers remain subject to the journals’ independent editorial assessment and peer-review procedures.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 7 November 2026

articles.title: Interdisciplinary conference on "Democracy Under Pressure: Conditions of the Authoritarian Turn Yesterday and Today" (Vienna, May 2027)
articles.body_html:
24-26 May 2027 | WU Vienna, Austria

From Trump in the US to the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, authoritarian candidates and parties win elections around the world. To understand this current rise in authoritarian tendencies, the conference Democracy Under Pressure: Conditions of the Authoritarian Turn Yesterday and Today brings law and socioeconomics into an interdisciplinary conversation.The conference "Democracy Under Pressure: Conditions of the Authoritarian Turn Yesterday and Today" (WU Vienna, 24–26 May 2027) brings law and socioeconomics into an interdisciplinary conversation to examine the current rise of authoritarian tendencies around the world. It explores key threats to democratic governance and analyzes which socioeconomic, legal and institutional responses could strengthen democratic resilience. The conference addresses these issues in dialogue with four pivotal thinkers – Friedrich Hayek, Karl Polanyi, Hans Kelsen, and Carl Schmitt – whose influential yet antagonistic accounts of the proper economic and constitutional order still provide a highly relevant analytical framework for today’s challenges.

Abstracts and complete panel proposals from scholars in law, socioeconomics, political economy, constitutional theory, political science, economic sociology, history and related research fields are welcomed — at all career stages, and from all regions, including the Global South.

Abstract Dubmission Deadline: 15 October 2026

articles.title: International Critical Management Studies (ICMS) Conference 2027 (Lancaster, June 2027)
articles.body_html:
30 June - 2 July, 2027 | Lancaster, UK

Conference theme: Critical Management Studies beyond the Academy?

It seems that the legitimation crises of the University and the Academy are a recurrent feature of modernity (or late- or post- modernity). Today, this question presses with a particular urgency. The university has come to appear simultaneously as an institution estranged from a unifying sense of public purpose, organised under increasingly vacant terms of legitimation and accountability – “excellence”, “student experience”, “research impact”, “knowledge exchange”, “graduate employability/outcomes”. It has become subjected to the remorseless disciplines of managerial neoliberalisation, marketisation, and hierarchical bureaucratic authority; and to ‘competition’ by commercialised forms of dissemination and algorithmically-legitimated simulacra of epistemic claims. These present crises, then, appear to ostensibly concern precisely the foreclosure of this question: as the university’s purposes are increasingly homogenised by the vacuous language of managerialism, its constitutive relation to the wider social worlds beyond its institutional boundaries becomes more pressing than ever. This is despite long-standing critical work showing that the Academy and academic work and labour more broadly, is always implicated in the institutions, communities, struggles, and material conditions it helps to shape (see, for example Boussebaa, 2020; Cunliffe and Pavlovich, 2022; Goddard et al., 2016; Goddard and Vallance, 2013; Parker, 2023; Smith, 2008; Zanoni et al., 2025).

Building on these tensions as points of consolidation and departure, the organizers seek to stimulate and explore how the ideas and concepts pursued within Critical Management Studies (CMS) and allied disciplines are experienced and played out in the communities, workplaces and social spaces beyond the ‘standard’ sites of academic practice (Butler et al., 2018; Fleming and Banerjee, 2016; King and Land, 2018; Spicer et al., 2009). The organizers also seek to enquire into what other modes of epistemic production may be caring, or generative for practice, research and/or theory (Antoni and Beer, 2024; Bartunek and Lei, 2026), as well as critiquing the reproduction of the ‘Academy’ and the politics of particular forms of epistemic production and dissemination (Boussebaa, 2020; Muzanenhamo and Chowdhury, 2023; Parker, 2023; Prasad and Śliwa, 2024; Santos, 2012).

The organizers welcome submissions for streams, sessions, workshops, panels, ideas, proposals, epistemic forays and other fora or activities which address or problematise the primary question of “What relations are there (or should there be?) between the forms of organising that are conceptualised, critiqued and encouraged in academic writing and research and the world beyond the Academy?” For example, are these forms of organising imaginable, possible, infectious, realisable, resonant, transmissible, reworked, discordant, resisted, liveable, mimetic, translatable, rendered untenable and/or generative beyond the Academy?. In posing this primary question, we encourage critical scrutiny of potential assumptions and biases inherent within it – whether prefiguring beyond as refusal, reworking, a mode of surpassing, co-witnessing or co-production. Secondarily, we also seek critical engagements with the constriction, assault upon, precariatisation and restructuring of the Academy in many parts of the world, and the institutionalised and commercialised processes of academic publication and dissemination. Likewise, we also encourage creative excursions in critical management studies and allied disciplines, for example, in terms of different modes of epistemic engagement, co-production or reception.

The organizers also encourage streams that reflect and inquire into the following, including but not limited to:

  • The broad range of critical management studies topics – for example, labour process theory; labour regime theory, critical global value chain research; critical accounting studies; critical finance studies; critical entrepreneurship studies; critical leadership studies; critical marketing studies; heterodox and ecological economics; critical management education and pedagogical studies; critical studies of innovation; critical diversity studies;
  • Crossovers and conversations with other allied disciplines and topic areas where the phenomenon of management entails critical questioning – for example, critical political ecology; sociology and cultural studies; public and social policy and administration; discard/waste studies; gender studies; decolonial/postcolonial studies; media and communication studies; critical legal studies; critical governance studies; science and technology studies; critical discourse studies; critical psychological and/or psychodynamic studies;
  • The temporal, geographic, and cultural diversity of forms of managing and organising, and how they are conceptualised or constructed, for example, studies from within or about Latin America, Africa, South-East Asia, Oceania, amongst other regions of the world, and indeed, outer space;
  • Types of interventionist research, engagement or pedagogy with a critical or emancipatory intent – for example, critical action research, activity theory, co-design research, the pedagogy of the oppressed.

Submissions are now open for streams, sessions, workshops, panels, ideas and proposals which could include (but are not limited to):

  • Paper presentations
  • Critical Development Workshops (including research community, paper development, or professional development)
  • Activist Workshops
  • Public Engagement Workshops, Lectures, or Panels
  • Exhibitions, Installations, Creative Sessions, Events or other interventions (e.g. music, poetry, storytelling, nature-based rambles, guided discussions or social gatherings, participatory practices etc)
  • Other proposals beyond the above

This should not be considered as a comprehensive or restrictive list, and the organizers would welcome all submissions that creatively embody critical management studies and/or practices in form and/or content.

Please find more info here.

It seems that the legitimation crises of the University and the Academy are a recurrent feature of modernity (or late- or post- modernity). Today, this question presses with a particular urgency. The university has come to appear simultaneously as an institution estranged from a unifying sense of public purpose, organised under increasingly vacant terms of legitimation and accountability – “excellence”, “student experience”, “research impact”, “knowledge exchange”, “graduate employability/outcomes”. articles.title: WINIR 2027 Conference on "Institutions for Innovation, Breakthrough Technologies and Global Challenges" (São Paulo, June 2027)
articles.body_html:
1 - 3 June | São Paulo, Brasil

Innovation and technological change are central to economic development, but their benefits are neither automatic nor evenly distributed. New technologies can transform production, raise productivity, and create opportunities for growth, yet their effects depend fundamentally on the institutions within which they emerge, spread, and are used. These questions are particularly important in theGlobal South, where investment in innovation does not always translate into productivity growth, structural transformation, or inclusive development.

Recent technological breakthroughs make these questions increasingly pressing. Artificial intelligence, digital platforms, and other emerging technologies are reshaping markets, firms, states, and societies, while geopolitical realignment and climate change place new demands on existing institutional arrangements. These developments raise important questions about which institutions encourage innovation, facilitate the productive use of new technologies, and enable societies to respond effectively to global challenges.

Returning to Brazil, this Twelfth WINIR Conference will take place in collaboration with the São Paulo School of Business Administration at Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV-EAESP). As Brazil’s industrial, financial, and innovation centre, São Paulo provides a fitting setting to reflect on these questions, paying particular attention to the experiences, opportunities, and challenges within the Global South.

The conference will open in the afternoon of Tuesday 1 June and end with a dinner on Thursday 3 June during which the 2027 Elinor Ostrom Prize and the JOIEReviewer of the Year Award will be announced. There will be an optional tour on Friday 4 July.

The conference will be preceded by a WINIR Young Scholars Workshop on Monday 31 May. A separate call for this event will be circulated shortly.

We invite submissions of individual papers and 3- or 4-paper sessions proposals related to the conference theme or any aspect of institutional research, in line with WINIR’s aims and research priorities. All submissions are evaluated by the WINIR Scientific Quality Committee.

Submission Deadline: 20 December 2026

For further information please click here.

articles.title: Workshop: From the Origin to the Future of Money (Linz, March 2027)
articles.body_html:
31 March - 2 April, 2027 | Linz, Austria

Workshop theme: From the Origin to the Future of Money

Institute of Philosophy and Scientific Method (JKU Linz, Austria)

Political and scientific debates about the future of money are often underpinned by diverging accounts of money’s origin. This pattern appears to be relatively stable in the history of monetary theory. Carl Menger put forward an explanation of the spontaneous emergence of money as a market phenomenon which is invoked by later members of the Austrian School in their argumentation against state intervention in the monetary system. Georg Friedrich Knapp described money as a “creature of the legal order”; Alfred Mitchell-Innes understood money as credit. Both inspired post-Keynesians and proponents of MMT to advocate for the active construction and management of monetary systems. Karl Marx based his rejection of monetary reform on his view of money as a necessary feature of capitalism which, if abolished, would spontaneously re-originate.

How to best make sense of the connection between descriptive accounts of the origin of money and normative proposals for the future of money? Do investigations into money’s origin allow insights about its “essential nature” which, in turn, has normative implications? Are positions regarding the origin, nature, and politics of money as well as the proper method of investigation embedded in distinct worldviews? Or is the supposed connection merely a result of naturalist fallacies and strategic attempts at persuasion?

Addressing these interdisciplinary questions requires joint efforts by philosophers, economists, and historians. This workshop aims to facilitate such fruitful interaction and cooperation. Topics for submission include but are not limited to:

  • Development of different schools of monetary theory and their interaction
  • Comparing and evaluating theories of the origin of money
  • “What is money”: essentialism vs. nominalism
  • Descriptive and normative aspects of monetary theory
  • Discretionary vs. rule-based monetary policy
  • Contemporary proposals for the future of money (cryptocurrencies, CBDC, MMT, etc.)
  • Methodological individualism and its discontents
  • Methodological problems of different price indices (CPI, OOHPI, …)
  • Worldviews and adversarial collaboration

Abstracts should be 300-400 words (including references, if needed) and be submitted via e-mail to Jakob Gschwandtner, in an editable format (DOCX, ODT, etc.). All presentations are in person in Linz.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 10 December 2026

articles.title: 23rd Historical Materialism Conference (London, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
5-8 November, 2026 | London, UK

Conference theme: Planetary Warscapes Ablaze: Imperial Mutations in Infernal Times

Since October 2023, genocide has unfolded in Gaza, executed by Israel but underwritten by the US, Britain, and the EU. This colonial violence has expanded across Palestine into Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Iran. The US and Israeli war against Iran is already engulfing the entire region in a wider war, disrupting energy and trade flows and putting significant pressure on the economies of the other major western capitalist states. In Ukraine, the war persists, fuelled by inter-imperialist competition between NATO and Russia. Trump’s threats to seize Greenland from Denmark, including tariffs and refusal to rule out military force, have fractured the Western bloc in ways unseen since 1945. Meanwhile, Washington escalates confrontation with China through trade wars, technology blockades, and military encirclement in the Pacific. In Latin America, the US intensifies sanctions and hybrid warfare against Venezuela and Cuba.

These are not signs of imperial confidence but markers of desperation. US hegemony fragments, as the MAGA vision of the ‘West’ does not include the same commitments to allies as the previous arrangements, while the US economy has failed for a long time to be the ‘growth engine’ of the global economy. China’s rise, despite the contradictions of this form of state-led capitalism, appears impossible to arrest. Regional powers manoeuvre between blocs, seeking room for autonomous accumulation. Dollar-denominated debt and investment structures face important challenges. The liberal order that claimed to transcend naked imperial rivalry has given way to increasingly brutal assertions of power.

The decline of US hegemony and the collapse of the ideological projection of a ‘unipolar world’ that was the cornerstone of post-1989 imperial euphoria have not produced a more peaceful multipolar order but have rather intensified competition between rival imperial centres.

This imperial competition unfolds on the background of faltering dynamics of capitalist accumulation. The 2007-2008 crisis was not followed by robust growth and the exit from the pandemic recession led to stagflation rather than an increase in productive investment. Financial speculation reaches ever more parasitic heights, while debt crises persist in the Global South. AI and platform capitalism reshape the labour process and generate new forms of surveillance and control, but not the envisaged leaps in productivity. Forms reminiscent of primitive accumulation return: land grabs for carbon-offset schemes, resource extraction in the lithium triangle, biopiracy dressed as green transition. Climate breakdown accelerates, as decarbonisation policies are abandoned, overshoot becomes the norm, and climate agreements and targets become a dead letter.

Imperial decline is combined with an authoritarian turn within capitalist states themselves. Far-right forces gain ground across Europe and the Americas. Attacks on migrants, reproductive rights, trans rights, and basic democratic freedoms intensify. Racism and white supremacy and islamophobia accompany the new idealisation of the ‘West’.

How should Marxists analyse this conjuncture? How can we combine the analysis of the contradictions of capitalist accumulation and the new dynamics of crisis with the new forms of imperial aggression and rivalry? What explains the brutality of Western imperialism as exemplified in the complicity to the genocide in Palestine or the war against Iran at this historical moment? Is US decline producing a genuine multipolar world or new hierarchies under different management? How do we understand China’s challenge to US hegemony without either adopting Washington’s Cold War framing or romanticising emerging power configurations?

How do these experiences inform debates about socialist strategy? How is the return of inter-imperialist competition reshaping global labour regimes and processes of accumulation? How do struggles against genocide, ecological catastrophe, and authoritarian reaction connect to the fundamental antagonism between capital and labour? What strategic orientations can overcome the fragmentation of left forces, caught between reformist accommodation and sectarian isolation? These questions demand rigorous historical-materialist analyses.

Please find registration details here.

articles.title: Age of Planning Conference (Berlin, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
15-16 October, 2026 | Berlin, Germany

In the wake of the Global Financial Crisis, the Covid-19 pandemic and the accelerating climate crisis, the failure of markets to address urgent collective problems has pushed the question of economic planning back onto the academic and political agenda. While much of the debate remains focused on models of post-capitalist planning, the “Age of Planning?” returns to the departure point of the new planning debate, that is, the observation that planning is already endemic in capitalism. Empirical work that engages with the concept of planning remains fragmented across three largely separate literatures: one tracing how corporations increasingly coordinate production, supply chains and investment outside of price signals ("corporate planning"); one tracing how states are returning to industrial policy, state ownership and green economic planning amid a new wave of state capitalism ("state planning"); and one tracing how the conscious decisions of central banks and institutional investors increasingly divorce investment decisions and funds available for them from previous market competition ("financial planning").

"Age of Planning" brings these three strands into direct conversation for the first time. The guiding questions:

  • How do we define planning in our different fields?
  • Is planning making a comeback across such different fields and if yes why? How can we measure an increase or decrease of planning?
  • What connects corporate, state and financial planning conceptually and empirically?
  • How can we theorize these transformations in a way that also speaks to a normatively grounded, democratic perspective on planning?

The conference opens on the morning of 15 October with "Rethinking Macroeconomic Planning in Europe" (MacroHub), a public policy workshop organised by the Netzwerk Plurale Ökonomik in cooperation with the research project "Heterodox Planning" (Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin / Einstein Foundation). From 9:00–12:00, Ilias Alami (Cambridge University), Jacob Hasselbalch (Copenhagen Business School) and Hannah Bensussan (LADYSS Paris) will discuss how strategic public coordination can help navigate Europe's fiscal rules and steer the green transition, moderated by Maxine Fowé.

The academic conference continues through the afternoon of 15 October and all of 16 October, with panels on financial planning, digital platforms, supply chain planning, decarbonization, social reproduction, municipal planning, state planning capacity and legitimacy, and the broader politicization of the economy.

Please find more info here.

If you’d like to attend the conference please register here.

articles.title: CRILS Workshop: Corporate Concentration in the Meat Industry (Online, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
8 October, 2026 | Online

Workshop theme: Corporate Concentration in the Meat Industry: Market Power and Competition Policy

Speakers: Margot Gibbs (Lighthouse Reports), Kagiso Zwane (Localisation Support Fund)

Corporate Concentration in the Meat Industry: Market Power and Competition Policy workshop will discuss the growing scale of monopolisation in the meat industry and its implications for farmers globally. Through Margot Gibb’s work, we will discuss the consolidation of France’s meat sector and how limited access to slaughterhouses increases farmers’ dependency on dominant meat processors. Kagiso Zwane’s presentation will draw from his extensive work at The Competition Commission South Africa on the Poultry Market Inquiry, which identifies barriers to entry for smallholder farmers.

Margot Gibbs is an investigative journalist at nonprofit newsroom Lighthouse Reports. She has led investigations into the hedge funds driving the cost-of-living crisis through food speculation, the US government's funding of attacks on pesticide scientists, and most recently the impact of monopolies on sustainable livestock farming. Before joining Lighthouse she was a Senior Reporter for the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and Finance Uncovered, where she reported on money flows underpinning corruption, labour and environmental abuses.

Kagiso Zwane is a development economist working in competition and industrial policy. His work spans several sectors, including agri-food industries. articles.title: CRILS Workshop: Floating Factories (Online, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
2 November, 2026 | Online

Workshop theme: Floating Factories: Corporate Power, Communities, and Aquatic Food Systems

This workshop will examine the expansion of industrial sea bass and sea bream farming and its impact on local communities, ecologies and global food systems, particularly in Turkey and in West African countries like Guinea-Bissau and Mauritania. Participants will critically discuss aquaculture as a new commodity frontier, extracting fish from the shores of the Global South for incorporation into the fishmeal and fish oil industries, to highlight the contested livelihoods and ecological damage. Exploring production processes that evade traceability and accountability, the workshop will highlight the importance of alternative ecological frameworks such as Blue Justice to foreground the importance of local ecologies, diets, and labour conditions.

The workshop will bring together Dr. Pınar Ertör Akyazı, Dr. Irmak Ertör, and Davide Mancini. Pınar Ertör Akyazı is an ecological economist and Associate Professor at Boğaziçi University, whose work focuses on fisheries, food sovereignty, biodiversity, political ecology, and agroecology. Irmak Ertör is a political ecologist and Associate Professor at Boğaziçi University, specialising in fisheries, aquaculture, food systems, environmental justice, and socio-environmental conflicts. Davide Mancini is a freelance environmental journalist specialising in Southern Europe and the Mediterranean, with experience reporting on issues including wildfires, water pollution, illegal fishing, and marine ecosystems through cross-border investigative journalism. The workshop will be chaired by Dr Mehroosh Tak, a Reader/Associate Professor of Economics at SOAS University of London and the PI for CRILS.

Please register here.

articles.title: El Cambalache Workshop on "Collectively Situated Knowledge: A decolonial research method for constructing collective auto-narratives and positionalities" (Online, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
20 October - 11 November, 2026 | Online

Workshop title: Collectively Situated Knowledge: A decolonial research method for constructing collective auto-narratives and positionalities

El Cambalache's workshop focuses on the practice of decolonial / anti-colonial research and is for researchers, activists, and community practitioners who already sense that the tools they were given are not adequate for the world they are trying to build and who are ready to develop new ones, together.

Over 8 sessions, participants will:

  • Move beyond extractive academic research toward relational, community-based methodologies.
  • Explore auto-ethnography and collective auto-narrative as rigorous research methods, with guided writing practice.
  • Incorporate the community assembly as a structure for collective knowledge production and decision-making.
  • Develop collective positionalities that reflect the shared nature of the knowledge we produce.
  • Rethink value, exchange, and labor in research from a non-capitalist framework.
  • Build a research ethics grounded in communality, persistence, and resistance to epistemicide.

The workshop is facilitated by:

Dr. Erin Araujo — Economic geographer with a focus on decolonial feminist economic systems, co-founder of El Cambalache. Based in San Cristóbal de las Casas since 2007, she has spent nearly two decades studying and practicing moneyless economies in the majority world Americas.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: Until all spaces are filled.

articles.title: Monetary Diversity Gathering II (Brussels, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
23-25 October, 2026 | Brussels, Belgium

The conversation returns and Monetary Diversity (MoDi) is proud to announce a brand new European Monetary Diversity Gathering, taking place in Brussels from 23–25 October 2026. This three-day professional gathering will bring together municipal and regional representatives, institutional actors, digital infrastructure providers, researchers and monetary innovators from across Europe to explore one central question:

How can new monetary infrastructures strengthen territorial resilience and public innovation?

This gathering is for you if

  • You work in public finance, monetary policy or territorial development and are looking for concrete tools beyond the standard toolbox.
  • You lead or support complementary currency initiatives and want to connect with the institutions that can take your work further.
  • You research monetary systems and want your work to meet the people implementing it.
  • You represent a municipality, region or public body interested in reclaiming monetary leverage at the local level.
  • You build financial technology and believe it should serve communities, not extract from them.

Please find more info here.

articles.title: Utopias of Work: Historical Perspectives (Groningen, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
22-23 October, 2026 | Groningen, Netherlands

Recent changes in the world of work – changes such as growing precarity in people’s access to the goods of work, the rise of platform work, the resurgent popularity of the ideal of productive self-sufficiency, and the unequal impact of automation and AI – have renewed interest in how work might be valued, compensated, and organized differently. The moral issues raised by these changes are not new, however, and we would benefit from revisiting the long history of thinking about ideals of work and its place in the good life.

This conference turns to the history of philosophy and political economy for utopian and radical perspectives on work. Participants will explore how philosophers and political economists from Plato to Gandhi saw the rational or democratic organization of firms, unions, and labor markets as means of advancing justice, freedom, and virtue at work. In particular, the organizers are interested in insights from these figures that might help to address today’s injustices surrounding work. The conference will conclude with a panel on the overall relevance of returning to utopian and revolutionary thinkers from our past. What (if anything) can we learn from them for the 21st century?

This event is part of the Ammodo project "The political philosophy of work - expanding our vision" and is organized by Lisa M. Herzog and Tyler C. Re at the University of Groningen, Faculty of Philosophy. For more information about the project, please visit https://www.rug.nl/staff/l.m.herzog/project-description.pdf.

Conference Organizers

  • Lisa M. Herzog
  • Tyler C. Re

Please find more info here.

articles.title: YSI Workshop at ICAPE 2027 Annual Conference (Washington, D.C., January, 2027)
articles.body_html:
6 January, 2027 | Washingten, D.C., USA

Workshop theme: Inequality from global south: intersectional frameworks to understand and study current crisis

Across the Global South, inequality is shaped by colonial legacies, uneven integration into global capitalism, financial dependency, extractivism, environmental degradation, and persistent intersections of class, gender, race, ethnicity, territory, and migration. These dynamics produce forms of exclusion and dispossession that challenge conventional approaches centered solely on income distribution or social mobility.

This panel invites contributions that place the Global South at the center of debates on inequality, exploring how structural asymmetries are reproduced and contested across different scales. We welcome theoretical, empirical, and methodological papers.

Possible topics include, but are not limited to:

  • Inequality, dependency, and global value chains.
  • Financialization, indebtedness, and social reproduction.
  • Feminist, decolonial, and intersectional perspectives on inequality.
  • Labor market transformations, informality, and precarious work.
  • Extractivism, ecological conflicts, and environmental justice.
  • Poverty dynamics and multidimensional inequalities.
  • Public policies, welfare regimes, and redistribution.
  • Territorial, urban, and rural inequalities.
  • Indigenous, Afro-descendant, and marginalized communities.
  • Migration, mobility, and transnational inequalities.
  • Alternative development strategies and South-South perspectives.

The panel seeks to foster dialogue among young scholars who critically examine the production, persistence, and transformation of inequalities from the experiences, epistemologies, and realities of the Global South, contributing to more plural and context-sensitive understandings of contemporary development.

The motivation is to develop further these problematics and invite more young scholars to explore the intersecctions of inequality, as well as invite to connect with senior scholar during two conferences: the ICAPE Conference and ASSA Conference.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 5 October 2026

articles.title: Bucknell University, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Assistant Professor of Economics

Bucknell University’s Department of Economics invites applications for a tenure-track assistant professor position beginning August 1, 2027, specializing in current heterodox approaches. The position is open to candidates in any research field, with particular interest in scholars working in emerging areas that would expand the department’s curriculum, including the economics of artificial intelligence and digital transformation, ecological economics, complexity economics, and macroeconomics.

Candidates should have a Ph.D. in economics by the start of the appointment. Candidates in the final stages of completing their Ph.D. will be considered. Applicants should demonstrate expertise in heterodox economics, excellence in undergraduate teaching, and the potential for a strong program of scholarship.

The successful candidate will teach five courses per year, including intermediate macroeconomics and electives from a heterodox perspective, and will advise students as well as participate in departmental, university, or professional service. Additional teaching may include introductory economics, and courses in the college core curriculum, including interdisciplinary courses.

The department is committed to pluralism in economics. It values teaching and scholarship that expose students to multiple intellectual, methodological, social, and global perspectives. The department welcomes candidates who demonstrate excellence in student-centered teaching, support students from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences, and value collaboration and interdisciplinarity.

To apply, visit careers.bucknell.edu. The application should include:

  • A cover letter
  • A curriculum vita
  • A teaching portfolio (including a statement of teaching philosophy, course evaluations and syllabi if available, and descriptions of efforts to support students from a wide variety of backgrounds in an inclusive manner.
  • A research statement and research sample
  • Official graduate school transcripts
  • Three letters of recommendation are required and must be submitted separately to the website.
  • Please combine all items into a single PDF file before submitting.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 15 November 2026

articles.title: Franklin & Marshall College, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Tenure Track position in the Department of Economics

Franklin & Marshall College invites applications for a tenure-track position in the Department of Economics beginning August 2027. The appointment is for nine months per year (August - May). The rank will be Assistant Professor or Instructor depending on qualifications. Applicants should possess or be close to completing a doctoral degree. We are interested in candidates who can teach ECO 103 Intro to Economics Perspectives and ECO 203 Value and Distribution. These courses require training in heterodox economics and political economy approaches. We are also interested in a candidate who can teach elective courses on global economic issues, such as postcolonial perspectives on economic development and the ongoing impact of colonial legacies in the global South. In addition, the candidate would offer courses that build on the Department’s offerings along with contributions in the College’s general education program, Connections. Faculty maintain active research programs and contribute to the College’s shared governance.

The college provides immigration sponsorship for specific roles that meet our sponsorship criteria. The criteria do not permit sponsorship for H-1B cases that require payment of the $100,000 proclamation fee.

Candidates must submit the following items electronically via Interfolio:

  • a cover letter;
  • curriculum vitae;
  • graduate transcript(s) (unofficial copies are fine);
  • a holistic statement on your approach to inclusive excellence in teaching and student success; a research statement;
  • teaching evaluations and/or observations (if available);
  • and one list of three reference names (Note: letters of reference will be solicited at a later stage, and once they are solicited referees will need to supply them within two weeks).

For full consideration, applications should be received by October 30, 2026.

The department and Franklin & Marshall College are committed to teaching and mentoring individuals with varied backgrounds and perspectives. In your cover letter, please describe how you could work with the department to create a more inclusive and equitable educational community where diverse cultures, viewpoints, and experiences are valued.

Individuals who need accommodation due to a disability in order to submit an application or to otherwise participate in the employment process should contact the lead academic coordinator, Shari Vegso.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 30 October 2026

articles.title: HEC Montréal, Canada
articles.body_html:
Job title: Faculty Position in International Affairs

The Department of International Business at HEC Montréal is seeking to recruit one or more professors in international business, depending on the department's needs, with expertise and interest in major global issues and the transformations of economic, social, and institutional dynamics. The committee is particularly interested in candidates whose research addresses, among other topics, international trade, global governance, the management and strategy of multinational enterprises, innovation and globalization, local/regional and national economic development, as well as new themes related to sustainable and inclusive economic development in diverse national and international contexts.

Department of International Business: The Department of International Business at HEC Montréal is composed of 15 full-time faculty members from diverse disciplines. Faculty members have published their research in leading academic journals, including Technological Forecasting and Social Change, Journal of International Business Studies, Research Policy, Strategic Management Journal, Journal of Business Ethics, Journal of Management Studies, Management Science, World Development, Journal of Development Economics, Regional Studies, Journal of Economic Geography, among others.

The Department seeks primarily to recruit at the rank of Assistant Professor, ideally a recent PhD graduate or a candidate close to completing a doctorate in international business or a related field (e.g., economics, geography, political science) Responsibilities of the selected candidate include teaching at the undergraduate and graduate levels, as well as advancing a research program in international business.

Requirements:

  • A completed PhD (or near completion) in international business or a related field. Priority will be given to recent PhD graduates intending to begin their careers at the rank of Assistant Professor, although exceptional candidates at higher ranks will also be considered.
  • A demonstrated record of, or strong potential for, scholarly research achievement.
  • A passion for teaching and for engaging with students at different levels.
  • Have an aptitude for teaching qualitative research methods.
  • The main language of instruction at HEC Montréal is French, and some courses and programs are offered in English. Proficiency in English is required to teach courses in this language, to communicate with non-French-speaking students, and to carry out certain research activities. The person must be able to teach and work in French after 2 years in the position. Substantial support will be provided by HEC Montréal to help achieve this objective, in an environment conducive to improving French language skills. It is strongly recommended to mention any prior knowledge of French in your application file.

Application procedure:

Interested candidates should submit as a single PDF document, before November 1, 2026, including: curriculum vitae, a cover letter, teaching evaluations, a sample of recent publications. In their cover letter, candidates must describe their academic background and state their experience in research and teaching. They are also encouraged to describe their past contributions or future aspirations to internal and external community service.

Three letters of recommendation must be submitted by the referee via this form.

Applicants with disabilities who might need accommodations at any stage of the application process may communicate in a confidential manner dap@hec.ca.

Application Deadline: 1 November 2026

Faculty members have published their research in leading academic journals, including Technological Forecasting and Social Change, Journal of International Business Studies, Research Policy, Strategic Management Journal, Journal of Business Ethics, Journal of Management Studies, Management Science, World Development, Journal of Development Economics, Regional Studies, Journal of Economic Geography, among others. The Department seeks primarily to recruit at the rank of Assistant Professor, ideally a recent PhD graduate or a candidate close to completing a doctorate in international business or a related field (e.g., economics, geography, political science) Responsibilities of the selected candidate include teaching at the undergraduate and graduate levels, as well as advancing a research program in international business. Requirements: A completed PhD (or near completion) in international business or a related field. Priority will be given to recent PhD graduates intending to begin their careers at the rank of Assistant Professor, although exceptional candidates at higher ranks will also be considered. A demonstrated record of, or strong potential for, scholarly research achievement. A passion for teaching and for engaging with students at different levels. Have an aptitude for teaching qualitative research methods. The main language of instruction at HEC Montréal is French, and some courses and programs are offered in English. Proficiency in English is required to teach courses in this language, to communicate with non-French-speaking students, and to carry out certain research activities. The person must be able to teach and work in French after 2 years in the position. Substantial support will be provided by HEC Montréal to help achieve this objective, in an environment conducive to improving French language skills. It is strongly recommended to mention any prior knowledge of French in your application file. Application procedure: Interested candidates should submit as a single PDF document, before November 1, 2026, including: curriculum vitae, a cover letter, teaching evaluations, a sample of recent publications. In their cover letter, candidates must describe their academic background and state their experience in research and teaching. They are also encouraged to describe their past contributions or future aspirations to internal and external community service. Three letters of recommendation must be submitted by the referee via this form . Applicants with disabilities who might need accommodations at any stage of the application process may communicate in a confidential manner dap@hec.ca . Application Deadline: 1 November 2026

articles.title: John Jay College, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Assistant Professor – Department of Economics

Position overview:

The Economics Department of John Jay College invites applications for a tenure-track faculty position in any field at the Assistant Professor level to begin Fall 2027. The department is dedicated to pluralism and diversity; applicants with a background in heterodox economics are strongly encouraged to apply. The successful applicant will teach at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, mentor undergraduate and graduate students, develop curricula, serve as course coordinator, and interact effectively with colleagues to support and enhance department culture. The hiring committee is especially interested in applicants who contribute to the goals of the college through their leadership, community service, research, and/or lived experiences.

Candidates are expected to bring enthusiasm and demonstrated commitment to teaching and to develop and maintain an active research and publication agenda. Individuals from demographic groups underrepresented in the economics profession are particularly encouraged to apply. The successful candidate should be enthusiastic and well-prepared to work with students from a wide range of backgrounds and demonstrate a commitment to fostering an inclusive and supportive learning environment. Consistent with John Jay College’s Seven Principles for a Culturally Responsive, Inclusive, and Anti-Racist Curriculum ( https://www.jjay.cuny.edu/john-jays-seven-principles ), the College seeks faculty who thrive in a multicultural, collaborative academic environment and are committed to both access and excellence in higher education.

Qualifications:

Ph.D. degree in Economics or equivalent. Also required are the ability to teach successfully, the potential for scholarly productivity, willingness to participate in course and program development, and the ability to work with others for the good of institution. Candidates are expected to bring enthusiasm and a commitment to teaching, service and scholarship.

Comopensation:

Salary commensurate with academic accomplishments and experience within the range of $73,294 - $102,460.

CUNY offers faculty a competitive compensation and benefits package covering health insurance, pension and retirement benefits, paid parental leave, and savings programs. We also provide mentoring and support for research, scholarship, and publication as part of our commitment to ongoing faculty professional development.

How to apply:

  • Go to www.cuny.edu/employment
  • Click "Search job postings.”
  • Click the link for “Faculty” and browse to job Opening ID number 32642
  • Click on the "Apply Now" button and follow the instructions.

Once registered or logged in, candidates should submit the following: an application letter to include how they would contribute to the goals of the College, C.V., research statement, job market paper, and a statement of teaching philosophy, including a discussion of how to create an equitable and accessible learning environment for our students. All items to be uploaded must be combined in a single document preferably in PDF format.

In addition, please have three reference letters sent to EconomicsPosition@jjay.cuny.edu. Here candidates can also submit any supplemental materials, not submitted over CUNYFirst.

For further information please click here.

Application Deadline: October 15, 2026 (Starting of Review process)

articles.title: Peter J Tobin College of Business, US
articles.body_html:
Job title: Assistant Professor, Economics

The Department of Economics and Finance in the Tobin College of Business at St. John’s University is seeking applicants for a full-time tenure track faculty position in Economics at the rank of assistant professor, to begin in fall 2027. Approximately 3,000 students are enrolled in the Tobin College of Business. Together they represent 36 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, American Samoa and 75 foreign countries. The Tobin College of Business has AACSB accreditation.

The Department offers BS/BA in economics in both the Tobin College of Business and St. John’s College of Arts and Sciences. It also supports the undergraduate business core, graduate business programs and undergraduate and graduate programs in various liberal arts disciplines.

Job Responsibilities

Responsibilities include maintaining an active research profile, teaching both undergraduate and graduate courses, and contributing to the university through service. These activities are all essential for tenure and promotion at the Tobin College of Business. The faculty engage in professional and program development, assessment, and service to the university and the broader community.

Competencies, Education, Experience

A Ph.D. in Economics is required for tenure track position. The department seeks colleagues whose research and teaching will strengthen the undergraduate and graduate programs and contribute to the intellectual life of the Department, College and University.

The department is particularly interested in the following fields:

  • Business Economics/Industrial Organization/Competition Policy
  • Environment Economics
  • Health Economics
  • Sustainable Development
  • Ability to teach a diverse student body is essential.

Applications will be accepted until the position is filled. Please submit a letter of application, CV, statement of research interests and teaching philosophy, and contact information for three professional references.

Please find more info here.

Questions should be sent to Charles M. A. Clark.

Application Deadline: 15 October 2026

articles.title: RMIT University, Australia / BITS Pilani, India
articles.body_html:
Job title: PhD Opportunity in Energy and Disaster Risk Management

Project description:

There is growing demand to explore the potential linkage between SDG-7 (which emphasises energy) and SDG-13 (which emphasises climate actions). In this context, the primary goal is to develop a conceptual link between access to energy and climate adaptation. Researchers have claimed that access to energy is a critical enabler for development. It is also important to see the relationship between access to energy and development practices. Researchers claimed that appropriate integration of energy works as a catalyst for rural development activities (Gevelt et al., 2018). But it is not clear how energy influences climate adaptation capacities and development outcomes. The role of the modern energy system has been given emphasis for post-disaster recovery and reconstruction globally. The access to energy becomes crucial for increasing climate threats on vulnerable communities in the world. It is also established that development planning and practices are influenced by the positive outcome of access to energy and climate adaptation efforts. Electricity supply is very essential in disaster affected areas to fulfil the services during an emergency. Studies have found that coastal regions are highly prone to saline water flooding and cyclones due to climate change (Hoque et al.,2019). The hydro-climatic natural hazards often affect the electric supply and therefore, disaster mitigation measures are affected. Solar power is one of the most reliable sources of energy when traditional power grids are susceptible to damage during disasters. Solar energy infrastructures operate individually and generate power when the main grid fails and provide a stable supply of energy. Solar power becomes an ideal off-grid solution in disaster affected areas having limited sources of conventional energy. Solar power becomes essential for emergency shelters, providing emergency health and communication services. As per Scott et al., (2017) solar energy based power supply increase the three core resilience capacities namely anticipatory, adaptive and absorptive capacities of vulnerabilities people in rural areas. Therefore, the present mixed methdological research will explore how solar energy contribute to the lives and livelihood of people living with disasters. The study will analyse how the solar energy resource contribute coping mechanism of households after disaster.

This work offers:

  • A joint PhD award from BITS Pilani, India and RMIT University, Australia
  • Full tuition scholarships from RMIT and highly subsidised fees at BITS
  • A stipend, health cover, and return airfare while based in Melbourne
  • Co-supervision from faculty at both institutions and access to their world-class research infrastructure
  • A global academic experience, starting at BITS and extending with up to a year in Australia
  • A clear four-year progression, including structured coursework, confirmation milestones, and thesis completion
  • Research opportunities aligned with RMIT’s impact-driven platforms, spanning both STEM and non-STEM domains

For further information please click here.

Application Deadline: October 10, 2026

articles.title: University of Chemnitz, Germany
articles.body_html:
Job title: Full-time position (fixed term until 06/2029, TzBfG) on modeling labor market dynamics at Chemnitz University of Technology

The research group Microeconomics at Chemnitz University of Technology is looking to fill a full-time position (fixed term until 06/2029, TzBfG). The position is part of the project "MARS – Modellierung der Arbeitsmarktverschiebungen in Südwestfalen" (Modeling Labor Market Shifts in South Westphalia).

Tasks and responsibilities:

  • Data, development, and programming work for the preparation, development, and implementation of the scientific model
  • Development of publications and media to ensure the long-term availability of results
  • Liaison with project partners and third parties (stakeholders, the scientific community, regional institutions, data providers)
  • Preparation, organization, execution, and follow-up of workshops and outreach events

The ideal candidate should have the following qualifications:

  • A completed university degree (Diplom, Master’s, or equivalent) in Economics, Business Mathematics, Business Informatics, Socio-economics, Business Administration/Finance, Business Administration/Data Science, or comparable disciplines, qualifying the holder for the corresponding level of professional qualification.
  • Good to very good written and spoken German and English skills
  • Knowledge of and interest in the following areas are an advantage: dynamics of complex systems, microeconomics, heterodox approaches in economics, labor market dynamics, working with microdata in economics, and/or computational economics.

For further information please click here.

Application deadline: October 7, 2026
