articles.title: Queering Economics: Reimagining the Dismal Science
articles.body_html:
by Michael E. Martell , Leanne Roncolato | 2026, University of California Press

How queering economics will better serve society.

Despite its tremendous influence, economics is one of the least diverse and most exclusionary social science disciplines. In this book, Michael E. Martell and Leanne Roncolato reveal how economics has created a dangerous hierarchy that deters dissent and marginalizes underrepresented voices. They argue that diversification can benefit the field. By highlighting the voices of LGBTQ+ economists and utilizing qualitative and quantitative data, the authors accompany their call to action with a step-by-step plan for queering economics.

Drawing on critical race, feminist, and queer perspectives and movements, Queering Economics shows how making economics inclusive has multiple tangible benefits. Not only will the field benefit from attracting the best and most diverse talent, but the discipline will better represent the contrasting ways we experience the economy while promoting prosperity and inclusion for all, especially the most vulnerable.

Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: Routledge Handbook of the Economic History of Colonialism
articles.body_html:
edited by Ewout Frankema and Tirthankar Roy | 2026, Routledge

European colonial rule in Asia, Africa, and the Americas was a world-changing force and left a variety of legacies – demographic, economic, environmental, technological, and cultural. The economic history of colonialism has seen an outburst of research in the last 20-odd years; but, with many significant new works appearing in specialist journals, students and teachers of the field may still find it challenging to explain what this scholarship adds up to, its most significant claims and breakthroughs and how it relates to older versions of the economic history of colonialism.

This handbook gathers a set of specially commissioned essays written by leading contributors to the field which focus on the two principal waves of European colonialism since the 15th century: the first in which Europeans converged mainly on the Americas (c. 1490s–1820s) and the second in which attention was focused on acquiring control over large swathes of Asia and Africa (c. 1850s–1970s). It shows students of economic history the key facts that need to be explained about the imperial powers, the colonial experience, and why the European empires outside Europe are significant for the economic history of the world. The handbook also includes studies of the Japanese and American Empires in Asia, as these were provoked by and in nature quite comparable to the formation of European empires thus providing worthwhile and meaningful comparisons.

This handbook will serve as a vital resource for research, teaching, and reference, offering readers insights into economic history, colonialism, globalisation, and the forces that have shaped the modern world economy.

Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: The Common Good Economy: How to Make Capitalism Work for Us All
articles.body_html:
by Mariana Mazzucato | 2026, Hachette Book Group

Whether it’s the water crisis, widespread poverty, or the next global pandemic, the problems that threaten humanity require collective action. But policymakers are confronting these problems armed with economic models that are missing one crucial element: They do not treat the common good as an objective worth achieving.

In this ambitious and timely book, economist Mariana Mazzucato issues a corrective to prevailing economic thinking by defining a new theory of economics with the common good at its center. She shows how to go beyond fixing markets around the edges and instead reshape them to embody principles of reciprocity rather than extraction, and collectivism rather than individualism. It is not enough, she argues, to talk about “public goods” and the “commons”; we must truly achieve the “common good.”

Drawing on wide-ranging philosophical traditions and global examples where seeds of the common good are found, Mazzucato reveals how common-good economics can help systematically transform how we build community and an economy that serves all.

The Common Good Economy is a stirring call for governments, the private sector, and everyday people to act boldly to achieve the greater good.

articles.title: GDAE Climate 2026 Updates: African “Green Revolution” Failures
articles.body_html:
2026 Climate Policy Brief

2026 was a critical year for climate science and policy. A new climate policy brief by Jonathan Harris and Grant Moore sums up recent developments and examines the prospects for the next global climate conference, COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, in November 2026. Climate scientists have recently revised projections, with both good news and bad: the worst-case and best-case scenarios have both been discarded, still leaving a projected future with a wide range of climate outcomes. There is also both good and bad news on climate policy, with significant progress especially on renewable energy but continued inadequate policy and financing commitments. See all climate policy briefs.

New Working Paper on “African Green Revolution”

As the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA) reaches its 20th anniversary, GDAE Senior Research Fellow Timothy A. Wise finds little to celebrate. In a new Working Paper, Wise shows that heavy promotion of chemical-intensive farming has generated anemic productivity growth, displaced climate-resilient African staples, and contributed to an alarming increase in the number of hungry people. As Wise has argued in an earlier article, agroecological systems provide a better model for Africa and the world.

New Policy Brief on One Health Circular Bioeconomy

A new Policy Brief from the Boston University Economics in Context Initiative (ECI) discusses the case for composting and policies for a dietary protein transition. Eric Christine finds that “To resolve the mounting climate and health externalities of the US food system, policymakers must pair expanded composting infrastructure with economic incentives that simultaneously drive waste reduction and dietary shifts.”

This is the second in a series of Policy Briefs from the ECI project “Toward a Circular Economy: A Mapping Review of State Compost, Soil and Health Policy.”

GDAE Researcher Presents on Wetlands Conservation

GDAE Senior Researcher Gillian Davies was a panelist on an August 12, 2026 webinar organized by the IUCN, titled “Freshwater Wetland Ecosystems: Global Conservation and Assessment.” A distinguished panel of international experts discussed advances and challenges in freshwater wetland conservation, assessment methodologies, emerging technologies, and the critical role of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in wetland stewardship.

Free Teaching Modules on Social and Environmental Issues in Economics

ECI’s teaching modules on social and environmental issues in economics are designed for use as stand-alone supplements in undergraduate or graduate-level courses, and are publicly available as PDFs. The modules range from 25-70 pages, and most include discussion questions, glossary, references, and exercises. Topics include:

  • The Economics of Global Climate Change
  • Energy Economics and Policy
  • Trade and the Environment
  • Water: Economics and Policy
  • Population and the Environment
  • Alternatives to Growth-Centric Development
  • The Economics of Renewable Energy
  • Environmental Justice: Income, Race and Health

Green Economics

GDAE’s program in Green Economics, led by Senior Researcher Jonathan Harris, seeks to develop economic and social analyses of the issues involved in a transition to a fully sustainable economy with renewable energy, regenerative agriculture, clean and efficient industry, and stable population. Recent work includes a book chapter on the Green New Dealand a survey of books on Ecological Economics.

New Edition of Environmental Text

The sixth edition of the text Environmental and Natural Resource Economics: A Contemporary Approach is now available! The sixth edition includes enhanced and updated material on energy, climate change, population, agriculture, forests, water, and other topics. As in previous editions, the text balances the analytical techniques of environmental economics with a pluralistic perspective from ecological economics, emphasizing practical policy solutions to modern environmental challenges.

articles.title: Call for Applications: Editor-in-Chief or Co-Editors for Review of Social Economy
articles.body_html:
The Association for Social Economics (ASE) invites applications and nominations for the position of Editor-in-Chief or Co-Editors of the Review of Social Economy (RoSE). The current aims and scope of RoSE, for reference, are available here.

The incoming Editor-in-Chief or Co-Editors will have an important opportunity to shape the next phase of the journal’s development. Working with ASE, the successful candidate(s) will lead efforts to strengthen editorial processes, broaden international reach, and expand the geographical, intellectual, methodological, and institutional range of scholarship.

Editorial Responsibilities

The Editor-in-Chief or Co-Editors will provide overall intellectual and administrative leadership for RoSE. The Editor-in-Chief or Co-Editors will be supported by Associate Editors, an editorial board, Taylor & Francis staff, and the ASE Publications Committee.

Responsibilities of the Editor-in-Chief or Co-Editors include:

  • articulating and advancing the journal’s intellectual vision in a manner consistent with its commitment to interdisciplinary and pluralistic scholarship while positioning RoSE as a complement to the Association’s other journal Forum for Social Economics;
  • developing clear and consistent editorial policies and workflows;
  • recruiting associate editors, an advisory board, authors, and reviewers while ensuring and expanding the diversity of subject areas and methodological approaches;
  • overseeing the receipt, assignment, and disposition of submitted manuscripts and making final editorial decisions that are timely, fair, transparent, and supported by rigorous peer review;
  • monitoring submission patterns, review times, acceptance rates, publication pipelines, and other indicators of journal performance;
  • encouraging submissions from geographical regions, institutions, scholarly traditions, and communities that have historically been underrepresented in economics publishing;
  • identifying opportunities for special issues, symposia, invited contributions, review essays, or other initiatives that advance the journal’s mission;
  • promoting RoSE and its published scholarship through conferences, professional networks, digital outreach, and other venues;
  • serving as RoSE’s representative on ASE’s Executive Council and completing other duties as prescribed in the ASE’s By-Laws (e.g., chairing one of the Association’s award committees and selecting and presenting award recipients);
  • hosting regular editorial board meetings and maintaining regular communication with the ASE Publications Committee; and
  • preparing and presenting annual reports on the journal’s activities, performance, challenges, finances, and strategic priorities.

Qualifications and Priorities

Applicants should have a strong record of scholarship in social economics or in fields closely connected to the journal’s aims and scope. Candidates should demonstrate the scholarly standing, professional judgment, organizational capacity, and collaborative leadership necessary to manage an international peer-reviewed journal.

Prior experience as an editor, co-editor, associate editor or editorial board member, is strongly preferred. ASE will also consider applicants whose broader scholarly leadership experience provides evidence of their readiness to assume the position.

The successful candidate or editorial team should demonstrate:

  • a compelling vision for the future of RoSE;
  • an ability to evaluate and oversee scholarship in social economics across different theoretical traditions, methodological approaches, and geographical contexts;
  • the organizational and communication skills to manage manuscript flows and an editorial team with commitment to publication ethics and research quality and integrity;
  • ideas for strengthening the journal’s reputation, authorship, readership, submissions, influence, and international reach.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 1 October 2026

articles.title: Call for Proposals: Networking Meeting on Pluralist Economic Journalism (Germany)
articles.body_html:
Netzwerk Plurale Ökonomik e.V. is looking for an individual or a team to design, organise and run a new annual networking meeting for journalists working on economic, financial and social affairs in Germany.

Economic journalists play a central role in translating economic concepts for a wider public and thus shape how economic policy is perceived. Yet there is currently no regular, low-threshold forum in which journalists from different outlets and formats can exchange experiences, share sources and expert networks, and develop reporting approaches beyond the economic mainstream. The planned meeting aims to close this gap. It is conceived as a half-day event with a deliberately participatory character — short impulses, barcamp-style sessions proposed and moderated by participants, and ample room for informal exchange rather than panel presentations. The first edition is intended to serve as a blueprint for subsequent years.

The call covers the full responsibility for the event: programme design, participant management, facilitation and follow-up. A total budget of €5,000 is available (€3,000 fee, €2,000 for venue, catering and technology). Applications should include a short profile of the person or team, a concept sketch of no more than two pages, a proposed venue and time frame, and a cost estimate.

The event will be held in German. Applications and enquiries: dana.morisse@plurale-oekonomik.de

Application Deadline: 20 October 2026

issues.title: Heterodox Economics Newsletter #363
issues.editorial_html:
A newsletter collects news, no matter whether they cause joy or sadness. In the past weeks we have been saddened to learn that Robert Blecker (1956-2026) has passed away. Robert was a leading heterodox economist, widely known for his applications of post-Keynesian ideas to questions on international trade and finance, many of which turned into archetypical contributions that helped guide the further development of the field. Just recently, this Newsletter featured a Special Issue in the Review of Keynesian Economics dedicated to illuminating and expanding Robert Blecker's work on international economics. His major textbook on Heterodox Macroeconomics – authored jointly with Mark Setterfield – can and should be seen as a lasting contribution that illustrates and underscores Robert's masterful scholarship.

On top of all that, Robert was also a community guy – he regularly sent updates and comments to the Newsletter and was one of the first international readers to join the International Association for Political Economy and Heterodox Economics (IAPHE) we created last year to provide institutional and foundational support to the Heterodox Economics Newsletter. Tellingly, Robert insisted on becoming an “active” rather than merely a “supporting” member – a small gesture that speaks to the passionate, all-in attitude that inspired and motivated me. I suspect many younger researchers had similar experiences with Robert, who was not only an archetypical scholar but also a generous and inspiring colleague.

If you want to read up a little on Robert's work, I can – in addition to what is mentioned above – recommend his highly cited classic on the interplay of international competition, distribution and growth, his take on the profit-led vs. wage-led debate or one of his more specialized papers on development economics. Two key candidates in the latter category are his work on the interaction of gender equality and export success (with Stephanie Seguino) as well as his insightful analysis of fallacies of compositions in trade policy (with Arslan Razmi), which asks what happens if all countries try to expand manufacturing at the same time.

It goes without saying that Robert will be dearly missed – as an impressive scholar, a generous colleague and an inspiring teacher.

All the best,

Jakob

articles.title: "Challenges to Monetary Policy" – Joint University of Leeds & Bank of England Workshop (Leeds, February 2027)
articles.body_html:
17-18 February, 2027 | Leeds, UK

Conference Theme: Challenges to Monetary Policy

The Department of Economics at the University of Leeds, in partnership with the Bank of England, is organising an in-person joint workshop on "Challenges to Monetary Policy". The event will take place in person in Leeds, UK, on 17th–18th February 2027.

The workshop features a confirmed keynote speech fromHuw Pill(Chief Economist, Bank of England). The organizers are inviting research addressing contemporary and future challenges across core themes:

  • Central bank autonomy: Navigating modern systemic risks.
  • Central bank communication: Strategies and public efficacy.
  • CBDCs: Global development and macro challenges.
  • Dual-pillar frameworks: Design and operational insights.
  • Inflation targeting: The structural future and historical lessons.
  • Geopolitical risks: Implications for absolute price stability.
  • Inflation dynamics: Assessing multi-order core shocks.
  • Policy transmission: Dynamics in hyper-dynamic environments.
  • Labor markets: Intersections with monetary frameworks.
  • Trade disruptions: Supply shocks and trade wars.
  • Biophysical neutrality: Ecological limits of central banking.
  • Fiscal interactions: Ensuring fiscal and monetary stability.
  • Regional disparities: Distributional impacts of policies.
  • Global spillovers: International spillovers and spillbacks.

The organizers would be deeply grateful if you could also share this call for papers with colleagues or any networks you think might be interested in submitting.

Please email your paper or abstract directly to Muhammad Ali Nasir.

Key Workshop Details:

  • Submission Deadline: 10th December 2026
  • Acceptance Notification: 20th December 2026
  • Logistics: There is no attendance fee. The event is in-person only, and participants are responsible for arranging and funding their own travel and accommodation.

Submission Deadline: 10 December, 2026

articles.title: 4th International Workshop on Empirical Stock-Flow Consistent Modelling (Paris, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
26-27 November, 2026 | Paris, France

The aim of this workshop is to bring together empirical SFC practitioners to take stock of current practices across these interconnected fronts and build a common understanding on emerging best practices. Specifically, the workshop seeks to map the approaches currently in use, to identify methodological and infrastructural gaps and identify a set of priorities that could guide the empirical SFC research programme in the coming years, potentially reported in a community white paper.

Workshop shedule

  • Session 1: Methods for the Estimation of Parameters in Stock-Flow Consistent Models
  • Session 2: Identification Strategies and Model Validation
  • Session 3: Sensitivity Analysis: Methods in Use and Parameter Uncertainty
  • Session 4: Moving Beyond Pure Demand-led Models: Modelling the Supply Side and the Respective Constraints
  • Session 5: Integration of Dynamic Input-Output Structures in SFC Models
  • Session 6: Engaging with the Broader Modelling Community

Please find more info here.

Extended Submission Deadline: 31 August 2026

articles.title: Call for Proposals for Special Issues in the Socio-Economic Review
articles.body_html:
Socio-Economic Review (SER) is pleased to invite proposals for Special Issues to be published in 2027 or 2028.

A Special Issue is a peer reviewed collection of articles on a specific theme. The theme should normally focus on a new or distinctive area of inquiry insufficiently explored in socio-economic literature, has a broad relevance, and falls within the aims and scope of the journal. Thereby, a special issue provides an opportunity to collectively explore a new topic, develop insightful new lines of research and exchange in dialogue across disciplines such as sociology, political science, economics, business, law, or history.

The proposal should contain the following information:

  1. The names, contact details, and positions of the proposed Guest Editors together with brief biographical details.
  2. The title of the proposed special issue.
  3. A one-page Call for Papers indicating the main theme, key topics, and methodological foci for submissions to the Special Issue.
  4. A list containing titles and short abstracts of any potential contributions, information about the authors and indication of their commitment. Guest editors are not permitted to submit regular peer review papers for the special issue but are encouraged to write a substantive introductory article developing the state of the art around the topic.
  5. A description of the behind the proposal, its planned scope, innovative nature in relation to existing published work, and likely relevance for readers of Socio-Economic Review. Please read the Editorial Policy Statement of SER via the following webpage:
  6. An envisioned timetable including a deadline for the first submission, a period for review and resubmission, and deadline for final print-ready papers.

The team of Guest Editors for the Special Issue will handle all manuscripts from their initial submission; they assign reviewers, and they make decisions (reject, revise, conditionally accept) and communicate those decisions to the authors. While Special Issues are always accompanied by an Open Call for Papers, Guest Editors are also encouraged to reach out to potential contributors to solicit quality submissions. All manuscripts for the Special Issue must undergo double-blind peer review and revisions according to normal SER review process and in accordance with SER’s editorial policy and formal guidelines. Final acceptance of papers is done in consultation with the Chief Editors of SER.

A special issue typically has 6-10 regular length papers plus editors’ introduction. SER manuscripts are generally no longer than 10,000 words in length (inclusive of references, but excluding tables, figures, appendices and online appendices). Manuscripts should follow a clear line of argument and be written in a concise style without sacrificing meaningful content.

Proposals and queries may be sent to chief editors Akos Rona-Tas and Alya Guseva.

Application Deadline: 30 September 2026

articles.title: Call for sessions: World Economic History Congress 2028 (Montevideo, July 2028)
articles.body_html:
24-28 July, 2028 | Montevideo, Uruguay

Conference theme: World Powers and Conflicts

The 21st World Economic History Congress will convene from 24 to 28 July 2028 in Montevideo, Uruguay. The IEHA has a particular interest in strengthening the scientific approach to the historical and social sciences and in promoting exchange, cooperation, and understanding among all people.

The theme of the Congress is World Powers and Conflicts, which highlights central issues facing humanity today and connects to a broad and diverse range of historical problems, particularly those concerned with resources, inequality, and sustainability, central topics of the last two congresses (Paris and Lund).

Sessions may be proposed by any member of the international economic history community, whatever their institutional affiliation or status, as well as by scholars in related disciplines. The organizers strongly encourage proposals from early-career researchers. Sessions can also be proposed by non-national IEHA member organizations.

Submissions are welcome on the economic and social histories of all places and periods, and the organizers especially encourage proposals from the global South. Given the diversity of the membership, the organizers will consider any submission that advances the study, teaching, and public presentation of economic history. The organizers welcome panel proposals that highlight emerging scholarship from different fields of economic history, as well as contributions on innovative methodological and theoretical approaches.

The 5-day Montevideo Congress will feature approximately 180 sessions, with each day divided into 90-minute blocks (two before and two after lunch). It will be possible to combine two sessions into larger, coherent units. The proposals must make clear whether they apply to one or two blocks.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 14 September 2026

articles.title: International Karl Polanyi Society (IKPS): Interdisciplinary Conference 2027 (Vienna, May 2027)
articles.body_html:
24-26 May, 2027 | Vienna, Austria

Conference theme: Democracy Under Pressure: Conditions of the Authoritarian Turn Yesterday and Today

The conference brings together scholars from law and socioeconomics to examine the current rise of authoritarian tendencies around the world and to explore which socioeconomic, legal, and institutional responses could strengthen democratic resilience. The conference addresses these challenges in dialogue with four pivotal thinkers – Friedrich Hayek, Karl Polanyi, Hans Kelsen, and Carl Schmitt – whose influential yet antagonistic accounts of the proper economic and constitutional order remain highly relevant for contemporary debate. Confirmed keynote speakers are Katharina Pistor (Columbia University) and Quinn Slobodian (Boston University).

The organizers welcome the submission of individual abstracts as well as proposals for complete panels from scholars in law, socioeconomics, political economy, constitutional theory, political science, economic sociology, history and related research fields — at all career stages, and from all regions, including the Global South.

Please find the full call for papers here.

Submission Deadline: 15 October 2026

articles.title: Joint CEPR-UCD-Central Bank of Ireland workshop (Dublin, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
13 November, 2026 | Dublin, Ireland

Workshop theme: The Return of Industrial Policy: Historical Lessons and Contemporary Challenges

Industrial policy has returned to the centre stage of economic policymaking. Across the EU, the US, and East Asia, governments are increasingly intervening to support strategic sectors, strengthen supply chains, accelerate the green transition, and secure technological leadership. Initiatives such as the EU Green Deal Industrial Plan, the Net-Zero Industry Act, and the European and US Chips Acts reflect a broader shift toward active state involvement in industrial transformation and economic security. After decades in which industrial policy played a more limited role in advanced economies, geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruptions, and decarbonisation have renewed interest in state-led economic coordination. Consequently, questions surrounding subsidies, strategic protection, industrial targeting, innovation policy, and economic resilience have returned to the forefront of academic research and policymaking.

While of contemporary relevance, government efforts to shape industrial development have a long history. States have long sought to influence the direction and location of economic activity. This historical record provides a valuable laboratory for understanding past successes and failures and informing future policy.

The organizers invite completed papers or extended abstracts by Friday 28 August 2026, with preference given to completed papers. Applications are welcome from researchers at all career stages. Submissions will be selected on originality, analytical rigor, and policy relevance.

The workshop will feature a keynote lecture by Prof. Claudia Steinwender (LMU Munich & CEPR) and a panel discussion on the future of industrial policy in Ireland.

Please email your paper or extended abstract (PDF) to info.indpolhistory@gmail.com.

Submission Deadline: 28 August 2026

articles.title: Journal of Institutional Economics: Symposium on "The Institutional Foundations of Stakeholder Theory. Insights from Original and Non-Mainstream Institutional Economics"
articles.body_html:
Stakeholder theory is often presented as an ethical correction to shareholder primacy. That framing captures an important normative disagreement, but it leaves the theory’s institutional content underdeveloped. Firms and corporations are not neutral containers within which managers decide whose interests to consider. They are institutional arrangements constituted by formal and informal rules that allocate authority, voice, property claims, responsibilities, exposure to risk, and access to remedies.

The stakeholder question is therefore not only whether managers should care about non-shareholding groups. It is how institutions define relevant participants, organise their interdependence, structure conflicts, distribute decision rights, and adapt when existing rules cease to support viable cooperation.

The symposium’s organising question

How do institutions constitute stakeholder relationships, distribute authority and vulnerability among stakeholder groups, and evolve in response to conflict, uncertainty, power, and changing social and ecological conditions?

Original institutional economics offers powerful resources for this task. Veblen directs attention to evolving habits, technologies, power structures, and ceremonial valuations. Commons treats institutions as collective action that controls, liberates, and expands individual action, and analyses transactions as legally and socially constituted relations involving conflict, dependence, bargaining, and working rules. Later institutionalist work extends these insights through social provisioning, cumulative causation, institutional change, and the legal-economic nexus.

The symposium also welcomes contributions drawing on post-Keynesian, feminist, ecological, behavioural, humanistic, evolutionary, social, legal, comparative, polycentric, and organisational approaches. These traditions are relevant when they illuminate the design, operation, persistence, change, or comparative effects of identifiable institutions. The collection will not be a loose set of critiques of mainstream economics; it will be a focused institutional analysis of stakeholder governance.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 31 January 2027

articles.title: MARXISM21: Special Issue on "Marxian Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence"
articles.body_html:
MARXISM21, founded in 2004, is a bi-lingual (Korean and English), quarterly academic journal specialized in Marxist studies. The editors are planning the special issue on ‘Marxian Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence’ for the Autumn 2027 (to be published on August 20, 2027).

The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence and large-scale machine learning systems across economy and everyday life demands engagement from the Marxist tradition. AI raises questions about the core categories Marxism uses to analyze capitalism such as labor, value, class, and ownership of the means of production, etc. Marx's own writing on machinery and the general intellect in Grundrisse, along with later Marxist work on automation and technological unemployment, provides a foundation on which this discussion builds. This special issue invites theoretical, empirical, and historical contributions that interrogate AI through Marxian theory.

  • Topics of interest include, but are not limited to:
  • The relevance of labor theory of value in a AI-driven economy
  • How do AI and automation affect technological progress and the tendency of the rate of profit to fall
  • Are data new factor of production?
  • AI-driven labor process transformations and the real subsumption of labor
  • Technofeudalism-related topics, etc.

Those interested in contributing to this special issue are kindly requested to send a tentative title and a short abstract to Dong-Min Rieu by December 31, 2026. The deadline for submitting final manuscripts (max. 12,000 words length) is May 31, 2027.

Submission Deadline: 31 December 2026

articles.title: CSE North Inaugural Workshop (York, September 2026)

The workshop will bring together colleagues from across the North of England and Scotland working on the materialist critique of capitalism to discuss their ideas with like-minded folk and to build solidarities. Throughout the afternoon we will have contributions from those behind other iterations of the CSE, past and present, discussion of the recent Capital and Class special issue on convergences and divergences between Political and Open Marxism, as well as an opportunity to plan future events within the group.

You can find a provisional programme here.

articles.body_html:
October 15, 2026, 09:00 – 12:00 CET | Auditorium at the Jacob-und-Wilhelm-Grimm-Zentrum, Geschwister-Scholl-Straße 1–3, 10117 Berlin (Raum E’701)

Organized by the Network for Pluralist Economics in cooperation with the research project “Heterodox Planning” (Humboldt University/Einstein Foundation)

Europe stands at a critical macroeconomic crossroads. As the continent grapples with the compounding pressures of structural economic crisis, geopolitical fragmentation, and the urgent need for unprecedented socio-ecological investment, conventional market-driven paradigms are failing to provide viable answers.

As highlighted in the recent landscape report by Partners for a New Economy (P4NE), “Fertile Ground: Exploring Europe’s New Economy Ecosystem”, if we are to successfully navigate this era of interlocking crises, the field must elevate macroeconomic planning. No longer dismissed as a relic of the past, strategic public coordination and structural steering are re-emerging as essential tools to reshape the future of European capital, navigate fiscal rules, and steer the green transition. This event brings together leading voices in political economy to dissect how democratic, structural economic planning can be effectively revived and translated to viable policy solutions.

The Panel

Ilias Alami (Assistant Professor at the University of Cambridge, Member of the Green Planning Comission) – will illustrate how the global rise of state-owned enterprises and sovereign wealth funds expands the scope for progressive economic intervention, while questioning how we can push past these frameworks toward deeper systemic transformation.

Jacob Hasselbalch (Associate Professor at Copenhagen Business School) will compare historical and contemporary planning models—spanning France, Denmark, South Korea, and China—to show how states can deploy long-term macroeconomic steering, indicative planning, and strategic investment budgets to manage the green transition.

Hannah Bensussan (Political Economist and EU Economic Policy Expert; Advanced background in institutional economics) will analyze the current French institutional landscape, critique the successes and failures of its planning ministry, and explore how the macroeconomic proposals of La France Insoumise can be expanded for broader European policy.

Moderated by Maxine Fowé (Political Economist and journalist)

Agenda

  • 09:00 – Welcome & Opening Remarks by the Network for Pluralist Economics
  • 09:15 – Flash Talks on Macroeconomic Planning
  • 10:15 – Open Q&A Session
  • 11:30 – Networking & Refreshments (until 12:30)

After the MacroHub workshop: Age of Planning Conference

The exploration of macroeconomic planning continues in the rest of the day and on October 16 with the academic conference “Age of Planning”, which brings together empirical research on corporate and state planning in practice. More information will be sent after registration for the MacroHub.

Register for the MacroHub here.

articles.title: Weekend Seminars: The Future of Pension Policy in Germany (October - November 2026)
articles.body_html:
FiscalFuture, a Berlin-based NGO for financial policy education, in cooperation with the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung NRW, invites participants to two weekend seminars on the future of pension policy in Germany. In a time of intensifying public debate on retirement age, intergenerational equity, and the role of capital-funded elements in the pension system, the seminars offer a space for in-depth political-economic analysis and discussion. Participants will: gain a solid understanding of the mechanics and financing logic of the German pension system (GRV) examine key distributional questions, including gender pension gaps and the situation of low-wage workers engage critically with current reform proposals, from contribution adjustments to capital market-based supplements explore heterodox and institutional perspectives on pension policy beyond mainstream framing develop their own analytical positions through group work and structured discussion.

The seminars are aimed at students, early-career researchers, and practitioners with an interest in social policy and political economy. No prior specialist knowledge required. Reduced participation fees available upon application to the FES.

Note: These seminars are held in german.

1st Opportunity

8 & 11 November, 2026 | Online & Düsseldorf, Germany

Please find more info here.

Registration Deadline: 31 August 2026

2nd Opportunity

5-8 November, 2026 | Dortmund, Germany

Please find more info here.

Registration Deadline: 25 September 2026

articles.title: ASE Member Spotlight: Jon Wisman
articles.body_html:
In this interview, Professor Jon Wisman discusses his book, Why We Must Work: Economic Freedom, Fulfilling Work, and Workplace Democracy. Wisman outlines the central premise of his work: human beings evolved to find work naturally fulfilling, pleasurable, and integrated with leisure, community, and social respect. However, the rise of elite-controlled states roughly 5,500 years ago debased work into an unpleasant means of survival under external command—a view perpetuated by mainstream economics, which treats work as “disutility”.

Wisman argues that despite reaching material abundance in rich nations, modern society faces widespread insecurity, stress, and dissatisfaction because it prioritizes consumption over fulfilling work. To restore work to a source of human thriving, he proposes two major structural reforms within a market framework: guaranteed employment (a job guarantee) and workplace democracy (worker ownership and democratic control). He emphasizes that an interdisciplinary approach—incorporating anthropology, history, and psychology—is essential to understanding these economic dynamics. Ultimately, he frames workplace democracy and reduced inequality not only as economic improvements, but as urgent political necessities to preserve democracy and avoid global ecological collapse.

Please find a link to the interview here.

articles.title: ASE Member Spotlight: Muzna Alvi
articles.body_html:
In this interview, Salewa Olewoye spoke with Dr. Muzna Alvi, a Research Fellow at the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and the winner of the prestigious ASE Helen Potter Award. The conversation centers on Dr. Alvi’s award-winning research examining the complex dynamics of gender, caste, religion, and female labor force participation in India.

Key Takeaways from the Discussion

  • India’s Unique Paradox: Unlike typical economic development trends, India experienced a multi-decade decline in female labor force participation. Dr. Alvi breaks down the factors behind this shift, including changing cultural norms, structural shifts in a services-led economy, longer schooling for young women, and data measurement biases.
  • The Intersection of Religion and Caste: The interview explores why communities with similar economic deprivations exhibit vastly different labor outcomes. Dr. Alvi addresses why Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST) women display high rates of labor participation while Muslim women face significantly lower rates, attributing much of this disparity to economic “ghettoization” and local job availability rather than purely cultural factors.
  • Policy Approaches & Solutions: Dr. Alvi highlights practical pathways forward, emphasizing the role of India’s self-help group movement, national workfare programs, and the vital necessity of supporting smallholder agriculture where most rural women are employed.

Please find a link to the interview here.

articles.title: Leuphana University, Germany
articles.body_html:
Full professorship „Economics and Security“ (W3)

The Leuphana Centre for Cooperative Security (LCCS) is seeking a distinguished researcher to join. The professorship represents the area Economics and Security in research and teaching. The professorship is based at the Institute of Economics and contributes to the establishment and leadership of the LCCS.

The Leuphana Centre for Cooperative Security (LCCS) is an interdisciplinary center for research on security that combines the subjects of law, economics, political science, and psychology. Premised on a broad conception of security that goes beyond the traditional focus on the military security of states, it conducts basic research on the conditions under which cooperation may enhance or undermine security in three principal areas: international security, internal security and economic security. The LCCS also develops recommendations for action in politics, business, and society, focusing on cooperative solutions to the consequences of diverse security threats for Germany in the European context. As a space for research and debate on the pressing security issues of the 21st century, the LCCS connects researchers from Leuphana, Germany, and around the world with expert representatives from the field. The position strengthens the Institute of Economics and the School of Public Affairs by advancing their shared focus on “evidence-based policy” and “resilient society” within the University‘s “Embracing Transformation” framework.

For this position, the LCCS is seeking an outstanding researcher with an international profile to contribute to research on economic security, with a focus on macroeconomics at the intersection of international economic relations and defense economics generating a lasting impact in their field as well as for society. The research areas include topics such as (de-)globalization and international economic (dis)integration, economic dependencies and the resilience of international trade relations and supply chains. Further relevant topics are international financial integration, public finance, as well as the protection of key economic sectors and geoeconomic analyses related to international trade policy, multinational investment, and economic sanctions.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 9 September 2026

articles.title: Winner Announcement: Elinor Ostrom Prize 2026
articles.body_html:
The award for the Elinor Ostrom Prize 2026 was made at WINIR 2026 in Rome, Italy. This year the prize was made jointly to:

Palina Kolvani & Marina Nistotskaya (2025) “On Mechanisms of Meritocratic Recruitment: Competence and Impartiality” JOIE 21(e12)

and

Enrico Petracca & Shaun Gallagher (2025) “Norms are Relational: Cognitive Institutions, Practices, and the ‘Where’ Question” JOIE 21(e39)

Congratulations on this outstanding achievement!

articles.title: A Brief History of the Economy
articles.body_html:
by Daniel Cohen | 2026, Polity Press

Economic growth is the religion of the modern world. It promises a solution to the most basic drama of our human existence: wanting what we don't have. But we live in a time when the frenzied pursuit of economic growth is jeopardizing the planet's viability and our very survival as a species. How did we get to this point in human history? How did we allow the pursuit of growth to become the apotheosis of human development?

To answer these questions, the distinguished economist Daniel Cohen takes us on a journey to understand human desire and the different registers on which it has expressed itself throughout history. He brings his panoramic grasp of the subject to bear on the key stages of social and economic development, from the Neolithic revolution to the digital age. The ideas of the great economists - from Adam Smith and Karl Marx to Joseph Schumpeter and John Maynard Keynes - are situated in their historical contexts and explained clearly and concisely. The result is a triumph of ambition and brevity: a history of the economy in 100 pages.

This book - the final work written by Daniel Cohen - will appeal to anyone interested in the economy and in the tension between a limited world and unlimited desires that lies at the heart of the great challenges we face today.

articles.title: A Research Agenda for Evolutionary Economics
articles.body_html:
edited by Kurt Dopfer | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

Elgar Research Agendas outline the future of research in a given area. Leading scholars are given the space to explore their subject in provocative ways, and map out the potential directions of travel. They are relevant but also visionary.

This Research Agenda combines the work of leading scholars and pioneers in evolutionary economics to plot a clear and compelling overview of the field. It explores core paradigms, highlights major theoretical contributions and examines critical challenges posed by global ecological and digital transformations.

Designed to provide both depth and accessibility, the book outlines the fundamental nature of the subject. Expert authors examine critical issues to emphasise the relevance of evolutionary economics for contemporary societal and economic challenges. Presenting a systematic investigation of the field’s foundations and key conceptual advancements, the Research Agenda looks ahead to illuminate potential avenues for future research.

Essential reading for scholars and students of evolutionary economics, the book is also useful for economists, social scientists and natural scientists interested in the dynamic forces shaping economic and societal change.

articles.title: Designing the Just Transition: Design-Politics, Labor, and the Battle for Post-Carbon Futures
articles.body_html:
by Damian White and Nicholas Pavzner | 2026, Bloomsbury

Environmental politics is clearly at an impasse, increasingly foreclosed by a fragmenting elite consensus on climate change, an escalating populist backlash on the right, and a pervasive sense of climate doom on the left. This book considers what new openings might be offered by a labor-centered transition focused on our creative agency and our collective capacities to design new worlds.

Whilst political mobilizations and smart policy are vital for making progress on decarbonization, Designing the Just Transition suggests that a more environmentally and socially just future will also have to be materialized and built, coded and created, imagined, desired, and enacted by many hands, many skills and many forms of visible and invisible design labor. The mainstream design industry is not to be trusted. Nevertheless, this book brings political ecology and environmental-labor studies into dialogue with critical design praxis, activism, and scholarship. It critically appraises traditions of worker-centered design, ecological and regional planning, sustainable and climate-smart architecture, and 'design when everyone designs.'

Rather than embracing a scolding green politics of limits or techno-utopian propaganda, Designing the Just Transition points to a wealth of resources for thinking about how we still might engage in democratic world-making on a warmer, more restless, and more turbulent planet.

articles.title: Elgar Companion on Inequality and Natural Resources
articles.body_html:
edited by Graham A. Davis | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This timely Companion explores the dynamic relationship between inequality and the use and management of natural resources, highlighting the positive and negative interactions between the two. Within the Companion experts from economics and political science present new data, methodologies and narrative contributions that examine how inequality and inequity are fuelled by how we exploit and manage natural resources in the world economy.

Analysing inequality both within a country and at an international level, the Companion explores topics such as tropical land use change, affordable access to safe drinking water, mining governance, oil cartels, fiscal policy and unequal resource distribution. Contributors demonstrate that institutional quality is a prerequisite for the equitable use of natural resources, both domestically and internationally. The Companion advances our limited understanding of inequality and its relationship with the natural environment, including understudied areas such as gender and ethnicity.

The Elgar Companion on Inequality and Natural Resources is a crucial resource for scholars and students of the natural environment, international development, geography, politics and public policy and sociology. It will also benefit managers and actors responsible for managing and taxing natural resources and multilateral agencies who assist governments in managing their natural resource wealth.

articles.title: Elgar Encyclopedia of International Trade
articles.body_html:
edited by Priyaranjan Jha and Devashish Mitra | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This Encyclopedia provides a comprehensive overview of theories, empirical research and policy in international trade. Eminent scholars examine the economic, political, geographic dimensions of globalization.

Explaining classical frameworks alongside modern developments in theory, authors explore the Heckscher-Ohlin and Eaton-Kortum models, amongst others. The Encyclopedia presents the developments, trends, and impacts of key international trade topics and concepts in entries that are engaging and accessible. Entries outline key topics, including the political economy of policy, foreign direct investment and migration within the context of trade.

This is an invaluable resource for students and scholars of international trade, economics and finance, business and management as well as politics and public policy. Its practical insights are also greatly beneficial for policymakers in international trade.

articles.title: Elgar Modern Guides: A Modern Guide to Urban Poverty
articles.body_html:
edited by Enrica Morlicchio and others | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This Modern Guide provides a new conceptual framework and vocabulary for understanding and addressing urban poverty in contemporary societies. Contributing authors examine detailed case studies from cities in the Global North and South, adopting a range of approaches from quantitative analyses to in-depth ethnographies.

Chapters highlight how large groups of newly urbanized populations develop informal strategies to cope with extreme living conditions in poor neighborhoods or shantytowns. They illustrate how, amid violence and conflict, these populations create networks of solidarity, forms of resilience and political collectives that demand better living conditions and the right to the city. The book also assesses the ambivalent role of public policies in mitigating or exacerbating urban poverty and explores the emerging realities and trajectories of urban poverty.

A Modern Guide to Urban Poverty is a crucial resource for scholars and students of sociology, urban planning, human geography and anthropology. Its insights on the complex interplay of the social, economic and political processes that generate urban poverty are also highly relevant to policymakers and researchers in international NGOs.

articles.title: Gender and Intersectional Inequalities in the Platform Economy
articles.body_html:
edited by Paula Rodríguez-Modroño, Annarosa Pesole and Ivana País | 2026, Routledge

This timely book examines different key aspects around new forms of work and gender and intersectional inequalities in platforms, how the platform economy intervenes, changes and reconfigures the organization of work, and the challenges faced by policymakers and workers’ organizations regarding formalization, professionalization, remuneration, quality of work or social protection of platform work. Including case studies from different countries from the Global North and the Global South, it contributes to a better understanding of how digital platforms are inserting themselves into neoliberal transformations in labour markets, taking advantage of digitization, the commodification of reproductive labour and migrant labour regimes to quickly access a precaritized female migrant workforce with low bargaining power. It will be of interest to all scholars and students of gender studies, social care, labor economics, and sociology more broadly.

articles.title: Handbook of Climate Change and Financial Markets
articles.body_html:
edited by Guglielmo Maria Caporale | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This comprehensive Handbook analyses the effects of climate change on financial markets, examining the policy measures required to mitigate its negative impact on market efficiency and various asset classes such as stocks, bonds, currencies and other financial hedges.

The chapters review the existing literature in the field, carrying out advanced econometric investigations to shed light on the implications of physical climate change and provide relevant policy advice. The contributors focus on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, providing detailed insight into green finance, sustainable investment and increasingly necessary ESG (environmental, social and governance) measures. They explore a range of key topics including the role of monetary and macroprudential policies, carbon taxes and allowances and improvements in national governance systems. They also compare strategies across global, local, public and corporate levels, identifying the most efficient methods of financing a sustainable green transition.

The Handbook of Climate Change and Financial Markets is a valuable resource for scholars and students of financial, macro, monetary, environmental and energy economics. It is also beneficial for investors requiring appropriate portfolio and risk management strategies, as well as authorities tasked with climate change policies.

articles.body_html:
edited by Uwe Cantner and others | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This informative Handbook explores key advancements in evolutionary economics, introducing a unique collection of innovative approaches to analyzing contemporary economic systems and their dynamics.

Chapters cover an extensive set of themes, connecting emerging challenges such as digital transformations and sustainability to established theories and methods rooted in evolutionary economics and Schumpeterian principles. The Handbook features research using diverse methodologies including econometrics, agent-based modeling and data science, as well as practical case studies for analyzing real-world economic phenomena, from emerging market niches to regional cluster dynamics. Organized across nano, micro, meso and macro levels of analysis, it integrates technological, industrial and policy dimensions, providing a multiscale view on industrial and evolutionary economic dynamics.

The Handbook of Research Methods and Applications in Industrial Dynamics and Evolutionary Economics is a necessary resource for scholars and students of economics, innovation studies, management and industrial dynamics. Policy analysts looking to create informed, context-sensitive policies will also benefit from this Handbook’s insights.

articles.title: Heterodox Economics and Social Policy
articles.body_html:
edited by Camilo Andrés Guevara Castañeda | 2026, Routledge

This book critically examines the theoretical and practical foundations of contemporary social policy through the lens of heterodox economic thought.

Despite decades of academic debate and institutional reform, contemporary social policy remains largely anchored in the liberal tradition of equality of opportunity. While this paradigm has advanced important conversations about fairness and justice, it has also become a conceptual boundary that limits more radical critiques of inequality and structural exclusion and exploitation. By rethinking the pervasive focus on equality of opportunity, this volume invites a transition toward the less explored but arguably more transformative principle of equality of place. In contrast to the dominant framework that emphasizes individual access and meritocratic mobility within existing structures, the chapters collected here explore the institutional, spatial, and collective transformations necessary for genuine social justice. Drawing from a wide array of heterodox traditions, including post-Keynesian, stratification economics, structuralist, feminist, ecological, and the common’s perspectives, the volume is organized into two main sections: theoretical debates and applied issues. Together, these contributions interrogate the foundations of mainstream policy frameworks and propose alternative paradigms rooted in redistribution, decommodification, and the commons.

The book will be of great interest to readers in heterodox economics, political economy, social policy, and public policy more broadly.

articles.title: Industrial Relations for a Just Transition: Labour Trajectories in the Energy Sector in Europe
articles.body_html:
edited by Serena Rugiero | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

In this incisive book, leading experts investigate how innovative industrial relations practices can support a just energy transition. Employing empirical case studies, they identify key patterns, challenges and enabling factors that inform policy design and contribute to embedding social justice within Europe’s green transition.

With perspectives from across EU Member States, the book evaluates initiatives implemented at company, sectoral and institutional levels. Chapters examine the energy transition as a systemic transformation affecting employment, skills, work organisation, regional development and socio-environmental sustainability. The authors emphasise that industrial relations and a structured social dialogue are crucial determinants of both the legitimacy and the societal acceptance of ecological transformation processes.

This book will be of great value to scholars of industrial relations and labour studies, sustainability transitions and environmental governance. Policy makers will also benefit from its actionable recommendations for supporting the design of effective just transition strategies.

articles.title: Just Transitions: Advancing Environmental and Social Justice
articles.body_html:
by Éloi Laurent | 2024, Edward Elgar Publishing

This innovative book promotes a holistic, pragmatic and proactive approach to just transitions. Arguing that justice is both a goal and condition of transitions it rearticulates environmental and social challenges and rethinks the policies designed to overcome them.

Éloi Laurent succinctly explores the concepts, frameworks, policy designs, and emerging institutions of just transitions and maps its progress from philosophical streams, to academic fields, to public policies embedded in institutions. Chapters explore a broad spectrum of transition policies, including those aimed at mitigating environmental inequality caused by air pollution and heatwaves, and proactive social-ecological policies such as fair carbon taxation and just mobility regulations. He discusses key examples from across the globe, spanning from food security in France, to water justice in South Africa, to disaster risk reduction in South Asia.

Just Transitions is an essential resource for academics and students specialising in environmental sociology, sociology, social justice, social policy and ecology. Its pairing of theoretical insight and practical examples will also benefit policymakers and stakeholders working in environmental sustainability, climate change and public policy more broadly.

articles.title: Marxism in Music: Constructing a Communist Contra-Culture with The Redskins, Rock'n'roll and Revolution
articles.body_html:
by Gregor Gall | 2026, Bloomsbury Academic

In Marxism in Music: Constructing a Communist Contra-Culture with The Redskins, Rock'n'roll and Revolution, Gregor Gall examines how The Redskins, so-called for their skinhead aesthetics and commitment to a socialist ideal, were a deliberately political band and built a counter-hegemony through their music and activism.
At the height of Thatcherism in Britain, The Redskins were aligned with the politics of the Socialist Workers Party, though the party did not accept their idea of that a working-class culture could exist. Despite resistance and contradiction, The Redskins created stirring and danceable music that introduced young people to socialist politics, playing over 250 gigs between 1982 and 1986, of which one quarter were benefit gigs for, as an example, striking miners.

Featuring a foreword by Redskins bass player Martin Hewes this book analyses the band's political intentions, interpersonal and inter-party tensions and the outcomes of their ideological, political and creative choices by drawing upon interviews with Hewes, other musicians like Billy Bragg, and the band's followers.

The book uses as a comparison another left-wing band of the same period, Easterhouse, to tease out how and why The Redskins were and are influential amongst a certain milieux and how going against the grain, even among comrades, made for the group's particular contribution to music culture and politics.

articles.title: Research Companion to the Construction Industry in Developing Countries
articles.body_html:
edited by George Ofori | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This Research Companion explores the evolution, current state and future of the body of knowledge on the construction industry in developing countries, offering comprehensive coverage of the subject along with the complementary Research Companion to Advances in the Construction Industry in the Global South. It draws on novel analytical approaches to highlight the crucial role of construction in economic growth and national development and reiterate the need to develop the industry.

Fresh perspectives are presented on both foundational and emerging scholarship evaluating the interactions and synergies between established and new components of construction in developing country contexts. Chapters trace the root causes of factors hindering project performance and propose potential solutions and effective strategies for industry improvements. Grounded in a wide variety of case studies, this Research Companion outlines valuable lessons for bolstering economic development now and in the future.

Scholars and students of construction management and economics will benefit from this Research Companion’s insights and proposed research directions. Its relevant policy options also make it an essential resource for administrators and policymakers in the construction industry.

articles.title: Research Handbook of Macroprudential Policy
articles.body_html:
edited by David Aikman and Prasanna Gai | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This forward-looking Research Handbook provides a definitive overview of macroprudential policymaking. It sheds light on the analytical tools and conceptual frameworks that support contemporary financial stability regimes and examines how leading central banks deploy measures from bank capital requirements and housing-credit limits to stress testing.

Leading experts draw on lessons learnt from major financial crises including the 2007-2009 Global Financial Crisis, the 2020 Covid-19 ‘dash for cash’, and the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank crisis, to assess how, and under what conditions, macroprudential instruments succeed and fail. The Research Handbook explores the dynamic interactions between these tools and monetary policy, housing markets, credit cycles and emerging threats such as non-bank finance, crypto, cross-border capital flows and climate risk. Organised into seven thematic sections, the Research Handbook distils international cutting-edge research into practical insights and identifies priorities for further inquiry into how to avert, or better manage, future financial crises.

The Research Handbook of Macroprudential Policy is an excellent resource for scholars and researchers in banking regulation, economics and finance, business and management and public policy. It is also an accessible guide for practitioners, policymakers and regulators looking to make informed decisions on safeguarding financial systemic resilience.

Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: Rethinking Neighborhoods: Connections and Cohesion
articles.body_html:
by William A.V. Clark | 2025, Edward Elgar Publishing

Although neighborhoods are sometimes perceived as just a backdrop to our lives, there is considerable evidence that they are central to our sense of wellbeing, and in the functioning of the city. Rethinking Neighborhoods is about these areas of geography: what we know about how neighborhoods function, why they matter and how we chose where to live.

Emphasizing the importance of place, of connections, cohesion, and local attachment, William A.V. Clark argues that the relevance of the local is increasing, rather than decreasing, and examines how this informs our choices and their outcomes. Situating neighborhoods and their evolution in historical and societal context, he uses a range of international case studies to assess key issues such as residential and neighborhood search, the segregation inequality debate, the connections between neighborhoods and health, the role of planning in the localized city and the 20 minute community.

Written by one of the leading researchers in the field, this book offers a thought-provoking read to those researching and studying society at the neighborhood scale in disciplines including city and regional planning and human geography as well as demography, sociology and public policy.

Clark | 2025, Edward Elgar Publishing Although neighborhoods are sometimes perceived as just a backdrop to our lives, there is considerable evidence that they are central to our sense of wellbeing, and in the functioning of the city. Rethinking Neighborhoods is about these areas of geography: what we know about how neighborhoods function, why they matter and how we chose where to live. Emphasizing the importance of place, of connections, cohesion, and local attachment, William A.V. Clark argues that the relevance of the local is increasing, rather than decreasing, and examines how this informs our choices and their outcomes. Situating neighborhoods and their evolution in historical and societal context, he uses a range of international case studies to assess key issues such as residential and neighborhood search, the segregation inequality debate, the connections between neighborhoods and health, the role of planning in the localized city and the 20 minute community. Written by one of the leading researchers in the field, this book offers a thought-provoking read to those researching and studying society at the neighborhood scale in disciplines including city and regional planning and human geography as well as demography, sociology and public policy. articles.title: Surplus lives under racial capitalism
articles.body_html:
by Barbora Cernusáková | 2026, Manchaster University Press

Surplus lives under racial capitalism theorises the link between political economy, anti-Roma racism and modern forms of white supremacy in East Central Europe. The book shows how the introduction of capitalism in the 1990s overlapped with the rise of racialised disposability of Roma workers. Since then, their surplusing recurrently comes into sharp relief during the time of crisis. Surplus lives under racial capitalism is built on an investigation of how race and class structure the Czech labour regime and how they form a single site of struggle. One which binds workers across racialised divisions as surplusing continuously expands.

articles.title: The Assetocracy: Wealth, Power and Elitism in the House of Lords
articles.body_html:
by Huw Macartney | 2026, Edinburgh University Press

Shows how the power of money has replaced the aristocracy in the House of Lords

  • Draws on the largest repository of the financial and political activities of the House of Lords ever compiled
  • Reveals the eyewatering amount of wealth and remuneration of the Lords
  • Highlights the troubling correlation between immense wealth and political absenteeism

Parliament’s second chamber may no longer be home to hereditary peers, but elitism has far from been eradicated with their departure. In this detailed analysis of the financial and political activity of the members of the House of Lords, Huw Macartney exposes the extent of the wealth elite’s grip on power at the heart of British government.

The introduction of life peerages in the 1950s, the reforms by the Blair government and the removal of the remaining hereditary peers in 2026 were all intended to make the House a more diverse, representative and meritocratic chamber. Macartney’s investigation into the shareholdings, company directorships, landholdings, rental properties, education, attendance, speeches and voting records of the Lords demonstrates how the political apparatus at the heart of Westminster promotes economic structures that protect wealth and ensure that the only route out of poverty for the marginalised is via work and individual effort. Far from reflecting the society they govern, the Lords continue to operate at a remove from the everyday experiences of the British public and increasingly appear to be a club for the assetocratic class.

Please find a link to the book here.

articles.title: The Consumption Function in Economics: History, Method and Policy Implications
articles.body_html:
by Stavros A. Drakopoulos | 2026 Springer Nature

This book examines the historical and methodological development of the consumption function in economics. It provides a discussion of the key stages in the theoretical evolution of the concept, from the beginning of the 20th century through to the modern day. Particular attention is given to the ways in which Thorstein Veblen, John Maynard Keynes, James Duesenberry, Franco Modigliani, Richard Brumberg, and Milton Friedman conceptualized consumption. Further, it examines the latest theoretical and methodological developments within the neoclassical, as well as the heterodox economics traditions. By connecting the history of consumption function to the methodological frameworks in which consumption theories were devised, the work also brings into the fore the important economic policy implications associated to various consumption formulations.

This book offers insight into how different schools of economic thought have defined consumption and how these ideas inform modern economic theories and political discussions. It will be of interest to students and researchers working on macroeconomic policy, economic theory, and the history of economic thought.

articles.title: The Role of Politics in the Combat Against Climate Change
articles.body_html:
by Dag Harald Claes | 2026, Edward Elgar Publishing

This book demonstrates the importance and relevance of politics in overcoming the challenges related to climate change and global warming. Dag Harald Claes advocates for an interdisciplinary approach to the green energy transition and for politics and political science to play an essential role in this.

Chapters cover ten core aspects of politics and political science which are discussed in relation to the climate challenge. Claes highlights how climate policy is centred around energy and the need to substitute the reliance on fossil fuels with non-emitting energy sources, but affirms that politics cannot itself accomplish this transition. The book argues that energy transition requires insight from many scientific disciplines, advances in engineering, technical inventions, and innovations and social adaption. Claes suggests the role of politics is vital, not only by reducing greenhouse gases by itself, but to make others do things that do so.

The Role of Politics in the Combat Against Climate Change is an essential guide for students and academics in politics and public policy, environmental governance and politics, international relations and climate change. It will also be of use to policymakers and industry professionals in these fields working to combat climate change.

articles.title: 2027 William Waters Grant
articles.category: Heterodox Graduate Programs, Scholarships and Grants
articles.body_html:
The William R. Waters Research Grant was established in 1999 in honor of William R. Waters, editor of the Review of Social Economy for many years and President of ASE in 1987. The purpose of the William R. Waters Research Grant Program is to inspire scholars to organize their research in social economics and social economy along the lines suggested by William Waters in his 1988 presidential address to the Association for Social Economics:

“The major concern of social economics is explaining the economy in its broadest aspects; that is, showing how human beings deal with the ordinary business of using human and physical resources to achieve a level of material comfort. Explanation includes cultural, political, and ethical details as they are needed for a full understanding. As in any economics, there are three parts to social economics. First is the philosophical base of the social economist, which may or may not be a reflection of the philosophical base or ethos of the society he/she is studying. Social economics (or any economics) builds upon it. It is the hard core as in the recent popular literature of the philosophy of science. The second part of the discipline is a description of the significant characteristics of the economy. The economist must observe the multiplicity of economic reality and abstract those characteristics that are substantive. The two together, the philosophical premises and the empirical observations, will determine the third part of the discipline, social economic policy. Policy formulation is thus a mix of the first two.”
William R. Waters, presidential address, “Social Economics: A Solidarist Perspective,” Review of Social Economy, 1988, p. 113 ff.

The research grant is for promising graduate students in Ph.D. programs who have not yet completed their dissertation, those holding post-doctoral positions, and for new faculty members who have not yet been granted tenure or who are tenured but have not yet achieved the rank of Associate Professor (or its equivalent outside the US). The current amount of the annual grant is up to $5000.

To apply for the current round of grant funding, the following materials listed below need to be submitted by 5pm Eastern Standard Time on Friday, October 30th, 2026.Unfortunately because of time constraints, extensions cannot be allowed and ALL materials must be in by the deadline.

  1. A completed .
  2. A 4 to 5 page narrative (in 12 pt Times New Roman font single-spaced) explaining the following:
  3. The purpose of the project: What will be learned from the research to be undertaken, and what will be its contribution to knowledge? What are the expected outputs from the work?
  4. A description of the research project to be undertaken, including the issues to be examined, the research methods to be employed (this needs to be sufficiently detailed), and why this constitutes innovative work in comparison to the available evidence in the field.
  5. The relationship of the project to social economics: What conceptual frameworks, topical concerns, and/or empirical methodologies drawn from social economics will be used in the present project? How is the project expected to contribute to social economics?
  6. The plan of work: Include a timetable for the project, resources to be used, travel plans, etc.
  7. The estimated budget: Indicate all costs that would be covered by the grant (e.g., travel expenses, research costs, summer stipend, etc.)
  8. An up-to-date curriculum vitae.
  9. Two letters of recommendation: For students, one letter should be from their dissertation advisor.

The winner of the Waters grant will be announced at the ASE Presidential Breakfast at the ASSA Meetings in January 2027.

For further information please click here.

Application Deadline: 30 October 2026

articles.title: Fully funded PhD scholarships at University of Greenwich
articles.category: Heterodox Graduate Programs, Scholarships and Grants
articles.body_html:
The University of Greenwich/Public Services International Research Unit (PSIRU) is inviting applications for two exciting new co-funded PhD scholarships:

1 (Em)Powering Regional Prosperity: Renewable Energy, Local Value Creation and Economic Resilience in Europe

The purpose of this PhD is to investigate how renewable energy expansion can contribute to regional value creation, economic resilience and inclusive development across Europe.

Please find more info here.

2 Can Public Services Rebuild Democracy? Public Ownership, Social Trust and the Rise of Authoritarian Structures

The PhD project will investigate the relationship between public service accessibility, ownership structures, social trust and support for far right politics. Particular attention will be paid to differences between publicly owned, outsourced and privatised models of service provision, as well as territorial inequalities in access to public services. The study will also examine the role of trade unions as democratic institutions that mediate relationships between citizens, workers and the state.

Please find more info here.

The supervisory teams are led by Vera Weghman. The scholarships are co-funded by Austrian union Younion, Die Daseinsgewerkschaft, and the European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU) in cooperation with Arbeiterkammer Wien (AK Wien), respectively. Successful applicants will join PSIRU's vibrant and supportive PhD community. With these appointments, our PhD community will grow to seven PhD researchers from October 2026 onwards. The scholarship includes a full stipend and a tuition fee waiver at the UK (Home) fee rate. The supervisory team warmly welcomes applications from international candidates; however, please note that international students are required to cover the difference between the UK (Home) and international tuition fees. In addition to a full PhD scholarship, there may also be opportunities to work as a paid PSIRU Research Assistant (1–2 days per week) alongside the PhD. This offers valuable experience working on international research projects with European trade unions and policy institutions, providing excellent networking opportunities and strong foundations for careers in policy-oriented academic research.

For any questions, please reach out to Vera Weghman or Ines Heck.

Application Deadline: 23 August 2026
