articles.title: Launch of the Future Histories LAB
articles.body_html:
After seven years, the Future Histories podcast can look back on a wide range of inspiring collaborations. These experiences gave rise to the idea of creating a space in which the ideas and questions explored through the podcast could be pursued further in new ways and through new forms of collaboration. This vision led to the founding of the Future Histories LAB.

The Future Histories LAB expands upon the work and the many ideas developed over the years, creating an experimental and transdisciplinary space at the intersection of research, art, and social practice.

Through the Future Histories LAB, research projects, publications, workshops, and artistic formats will be developed to explore alternative futures and possibilities for postcapitalist construction.

Please find the lately launched website here.

articles.title: TV Series on Economics: J K Galbraith's Age of Uncertainty
articles.body_html:
The Age of Uncertainty is a 13-part TV Series about economics written and presented by John Kenneth Galbraith. It was three-years in the making and was made in collaboration with the BBC, CBC and other broadcasters. Nearly 50-years on from when it first screened, it remains a unique and valuable resource in introducing economics to a general audience. For many years, it was difficult to find good quality recordings of the series online, but recently this has changed with remarkably high-resolution recordings now available on YouTube (and perhaps also via the BBC iplayer – for those in the UK).

This TV Series is an enormously valuable resource that is recommended viewing regardless of your level of economic knowledge. It is everything you would expect from J K Galbraith: wise, informative, and of course, regularly laugh out loud funny.

Please find the link to the playlist for the entire series here.

articles.title: Contributions to Moneyless Economy (Eranism)
articles.body_html:
This site contains the design of Eranism, an economy that would allow for more prudent use of natural resources, a wasteless and mostly fair distribution of goods, more cooperation than in the present competitive economy, and the reduction of work for which there is no physical necessity. The economy is decentralized in the sense that people themselves report how many goods they want or need and how long they have to work, but it usually does not pay to misreport in order to manipulate the outcome. The economy is directly based on physical and social reality (it is said to be transparant) and therefore does without money. To complete the design, a few questions remain to be answered.

The author Arnold Bomans is asking for assistance with arranging a judgement (in particular by mathematical economists), implementation in a database, development of a user-interface, test, documentation, a (commercial) organization, and ... money.

articles.title: 2027 ASE World Congress and Summer School: Coordinator Search (June 2027)
articles.body_html:
The Association for Social Economics is preparing to hold its combined World Congress and Summer School, a two-day event, in June of 2027.

The World Congress is the largest ASE-sponsored conference, held once every 3 years and preceded by a one-day workshop titled Summer School for graduate students, junior academics, and practitioners in social economics.

The ASE is looking for coordinator(s) to host the event at their institutions or other institutions where they have contacts. Once this is finalized with the ASE leadership,the role of the coordinators will consist of:

  • Being the primary point of contact for all communications with the hosting institution's admins.
  • Arranging on-site locations for conferences and workshops. The conference usually features 3-4 concurrent sessions (with around 20 attendees) and lasts one day. The Summer School is held the day before the conference, which is held in a 30-seat lecture/seminar hall.
  • Finding on-site housing options, such as dormitories, to keep lodging expenses manageable for attendees.
  • Arranging suitable vendors for on-site lunch and coffee service.
  • Suggesting venues for evening social events (could be off-site).
  • Possibly securing in-kind or financial sponsorship from the hosting institution and local organizations to partially offset the event's cost. (This is not a deal-breaker but a welcome perk.)
  • Incorporating the city/location into the program in various ways.

The coordinator will have the ASE leadership’s support and guidance throughout the process, and funding will be available to hire assistants who are students and/or others both before and during the event.

If you are interested in hosting or organizing this high-profile and collegial event, please contact the Association Director, Rojhat Avsar, at rbavsar@gmail.com.

Arranging on-site locations for conferences and workshops. The conference usually features 3-4 concurrent sessions (with around 20 attendees) and lasts one day. articles.title: Call for Editors: Work, Employment and Society
articles.body_html:
The British Sociological Association (BSA) and WES invite applications to join the journal as Associate Editors. Work, Employment and Society is a highly respected journal with an international profile. It is strongly centred in the sociological tradition, drawing upon adjacent disciplines to make an original contribution to debates in the sociology of work and employment. It receives over 1000 submissions a year, has an Impact Factor of 3.8 and is ranked 4 in the Chartered Association of Business Schools Academic Journal Guide. WES is a journal of the British Sociological Association and the current publishing partner is Sage.

The appointed editors will join the current team in editing papers and developing the intellectual agenda and international reach of the journal. In recent years there have been significant, community-led changes with in the journal: editorial and Board structure changes; and the introduction of new initiatives – like the incredibly popular PhD Showcase. Editors, working closely with the Editorial Board, initiate and support such changes during their terms of office.

Editorial responsibilities include the following:

  • Making editorial decisions on submissions, selecting peer reviewers and overseeing the peer review process
  • Working collectively as a team to develop the content of the journal
  • Reporting to/attending the biannual Editorial Board meetings
  • Contributing to the journal’s international and strategic objectives
  • Working with the BSA and SAGE to publicise journal content and activities
  • Understanding current and future trends in the journal’s fields
  • Representing WES at relevant events and conferences
  • Representing WES within the BSA.

The editors work in a highly collaborative way, meeting online monthly. New editors will be integrated into the existing team through mentoring and peer support. Typically, editors work a full day a week onWES activities.

Please find more info here.

Contact Alison Danforth with any questions regarding the application process or the roles.

Application Deadline: 17 September 2026

articles.title: Review of Social Economy: Resignation of leading editors and co-editors
articles.body_html:
Editorial note: The Newsletter office has been informed of a rupture at the Review of Social Economy, which has led to a mass resignation of the current main and associate editors. Below we share statements by the (former) RoSE editors as well as a statement from ASE as governing association of the journal. We leave it to our readers to form their own judgement on this specific incident based on the original statements below.
However, we hasten to add that the underlying tensions emerging from dominant academic publishing routines do indeed represent a key organizational challenge for heterodox institutions. Hence, in our humble view this conflict is no occasional idiosyncrasy, but represents a systemic tension in our field. At the same time, we sincerely hope RoSE will continue to play a key role as a flagship journal in heterodox discourse.

Due to the Association for Social Economics' decision to extend the cooperation with the commercial publisher Taylor & Francis, the members of Review of Social Economy's Associate Editors Board and Advisory Board stepped down and ended the collaboration with ASE. In a statement issued following their resignation on July 4 2026, the main editors of the explained their decision as follows:

“With this letter, we, the co-editors of RoSE, announce our decision to step down from this role and explain why. After having worked hard on the journal, in some cases for many years, this was not a step that came lightly, but we see it as inevitable.

RoSE is currently published by Taylor & Francis (T&F), a commercial publisher, in a subscription model. The big disadvantage of this model is that most articles are hidden behind a paywall, inaccessible for many scholars worldwide. For years, we have been in discussions about the possibility of moving to an open-access model, and we have used a considerable part of the editorial budget for "buying out" articles from behind the pay wall, especially those of young scholars or scholars from non-OECD countries.

The ASE has now decided to stay with T&F, and against the move towards a subscribe-to-open model with Stanford University Press. This decision, however, means that the future path of the journal is towards a model with author publishing fees (APFs), not subscriptions. T&F have been very clear about their estimation that the subscription model will continue to decline and will soon no longer be feasible. Having the journal run on an APF model means that the income depends on authors having funds available (which is only the case for authors in privileged countries and institutions). Editors are incentivized to publish as many articles as possible, to maximize revenue. This is not a path that we, as an editorial team, want to follow. We think it conflicts with the values of open knowledge and equity in science, especially for scholars from non-Western countries that cannot afford to pay AFPs.

The structure of ASE, with its financial dependence on the journal income, has created an unhealthy financial dependence on royalties from the journals. We have therefore never pushed for moving to models that would not generate any income. The Stanford UP model would, with high likelihood, have allowed generating a stable income, while preserving the quality and integrity of the journal. But ASE's leadership - with its short-term cycles, which make longer-term planning maybe more difficult than it would otherwise be - has decided that it does not want to take this step.

We have therefore decided to end our collaboration with the ASE and to step down as co-editors of RoSE.

As a matter of responsibility towards authors, we will continue - with ASE's consent - to handle the papers that are currently in the review process, but will not accept new submissions. We hope that ASE can soon form a new editorial board and take over the journal. "

The RoSE co-editors: Amitava Dutt, Lisa Herzog, Natascha van der Zwan, Roberto Veneziani

A large majority of the associated editors also sent a statement that supports the position of the main editors also announcing their resignation.

The Association for Social Economics (ASE) commented on the transition at the Review of Social Economy in a statement from July 22:

"The Association for Social Economics (ASE) is announcing a change in its editorial board for one of its journals, the Review of Social Economy (RoSE).

Following our recent Executive Council meeting and vote, ASE has moved forward with continuing its longstanding partnership with Taylor & Francis (T&F), a publisher that has been committed to heterodox economics books and journals for decades. RoSE publishes on a hybrid basis, meaning that it publishes both subscription and open access content. This means that it is an accessible publishing venue for all authors, whether or not they have access to open access funding.

The Executive Council considered in detail a proposal brought by the former editors of RoSE to move to a complete open access model with another press, a decision that would have major implications for ASE’s revenues and operations. After much investigation and discussion, ASE decided by a majority vote to renew its contract with T&F to ensure the continuation of its activities in line with the Association’s mission. Immediately after this decision and before the end of their contracts, the editors of RoSE resigned in unison. While the editors of RoSE insist that the journal is moving towards a model with author publishing fees (APFs), not subscriptions, this is not the case. The journal will continue to publish following its existing hybrid model as explained above.

We are grateful to all current and former editorial board members for their service to RoSE. Upcoming editorial board changes will build on their contributions while creating new opportunities for scholars from a wider range of geographical, methodological, and institutional backgrounds to participate in the journal’s future. Open calls for participation in editorial roles will be published on the ASE website, listserv, and other sites in the coming days.

ASE continues to support its mission of making knowledge and scholarly work in social economics available to everyone around the world. ASE provides free membership to scholars in least developed countries and this allows access to journal content for both RoSE and the Forum for Social Economics, also published by ASE. T&F also supports initiatives to make content in RoSE free to access for readers in least developed countries, including via its STAR initiative."

articles.title: Socio-Economic Review (SER): Call for Student Interns 2026-2027
articles.body_html:
Socio-Economic Review (SER) is inviting applications for its Board of Graduate Interns. Published by Oxford University Press, SER is the official journal of Society for the Advancement of Socio-Economics (SASE) and features contributions from around the world. SER’s primary focus is on understanding the socio-political foundations of the economy and the interplay between economy and society. Articles in SER explore how the economy is or should be governed by social relations, institutional rules, political decisions, and cultural values. The journal also emphasizes inequalities and politics. SER receives about eight hundred new article manuscripts annually, publishes four issues per year, and accepts about 13% of submissions. Its 5-year impact factor (2025) is 4.0.

Graduate interns will assist with a range of editorial and outreach activities, including identifying and evaluating potential reviewers, helping organize book symposia published in the journal, assisting with the preparation of quarterly issues, promoting recently published SER articles, and organizing the SER Café. The SER Café is an online discussion series that brings together authors of recently published SER articles and readers to discuss the research. During the internship, interns will organize and produce four SER Café events.

Interns will also participate in monthly online meetings devoted to learning about journal editing and scholarly publishing. The overall workload is comparable to that of an independent reading course.

Members of the Board of Graduate Interns will be listed by name in the journal’s masthead (impressum) in recognition of their service. Graduate interns will also receive free membership and registration for the annual SASE conference in Glasgow in 2027. The one-year internship begins on September 17, 2026.

Applicants must have successfully completed the first two years of a doctoral program in any social science discipline. Prior editorial experience or previous involvement with SASE or SER is an advantage but is not required.

This is an excellent opportunity to learn about article publishing, build professional networks, and see the latest research in the field.

To apply, send your letter of intent and a CV to Akos Rona-Tas and Alya Guseva with a subject “SER Student Interns”.

Application Deadline: 1 September 2026

issues.title: Heterodox Economics Newsletter #362
issues.editorial_html:
The craving for exactness and rigor, that characterizes so many efforts undertaken in mainstream economics, has transformed over the past decades from a focus on formal-analytical rigor towards an emphasis on ‚clean identification‘ of (allegedly) ‚causal‘ effects. And while the ghosts of formal-deductive reasoning still linger, this change had a profound impact on the discipline: in some way it changed the nature of the discipline (from more rationalist to more empiricist) and impacted prevailing methodological standards as well as dominant policy views (e.g. on the minimum wage) within the profession.

I observed this transformation not only in my role as a part-time historian of thought, but also as a real-life witness, because this transformation was quite visible in the economics department of the Johannes Kepler University, my alma mater. This department started out as a somewhat pluralist econ department in the 1970s (with Rothschild, Laszki or Riese as key figures) but had transformed into a conventional mainstream department by the time I arrived as a student some thirty years later. Over the decades I have become involved in the Linz econ department in various ways: as a student, as a lecturer, as an observer, as a colleague, as a PhD-advisor and the like…

The econ department in Linz was an interesting microcosm to observe this transition and the consequences it entailed: new priorities in the teaching canon, a change away from core econ topics towards „whatever brings good data meriting publication“ and, of course, changing standards in the evaluation of research and thereby also shifts in internal hierarchy. And while I was highly skeptical about the constraints imposed by the empirical turn on young econ researchers on very narrow, data-driven and career-instrumental paths, I could see how thinking about identification was – in some way – probably better than writing up the random, a-theoretical or all-too-simple-minded exercises that coined my (more old-school) econometrics-classes.

Aside from that, I always had the impression that there is a common denominator between the mainstream drive for identification and the heterodox notion of pluralism. Both care, albeit in different ways, about multi-causality and the complexity it brings. Research designs are employed in the hope of isolating a clear-cut relationship within a mess of causal pathways. Pluralism’s inherent contribution is to raise awareness about exactly that mess — and to insist that thinking without dogma is a necessary condition for illuminating complexity.

Just a few weeks ago, the person I considered the main architect of the empirical turn at the Linz econ department, Rudi Winter-Ebmer, retired and on this occasion I was invited to contribute to a „book of abstracts“ that collects ideas on papers that we could have written jointly with Rudi, but have never actually done so.

As you might imagine, I took this opportunity to reflect on the above intuition and contributed the short abstract shared below, which reflects on how this alleged complementarity between the key intuition behind the empirical turn and the notion of pluralism in heterodox economics could play out in practice.

Have a good time and all the best,

Jakob

Causality and Pluralism (An extended abstract)

The credibility revolution in econometrics has delivered powerful tools for causal analysis and with them a new standard of local, internally valid causal claims. Yet precision, however admirable, is not the same as understanding. A coefficient, no matter how cleanly identified, does not interpret itself; and a finding, no matter how robust, may bring quite different implications if we dare to shift our theoretical frame of reference.

In addressing this key conundrum, this paper argues that causal econometrics and pluralist economic methodology are in fact natural complements -- and that bringing them into dialogue addresses a surprisingly obvious gap in both literatures.

Drawing on a critical-rationalist epistemology, we emphasize that no single hypothesis, however well-identified, can exhaust the space of relevant explanations for complex economic phenomena. Competing and complementary hypotheses are not a nuisance, but a resource: their systematic comparison enhances external validity, internal coherence and theoretical robustness, by forcing researchers to specify the scope conditions and mechanisms that make a causal story credible in the first place. Conversely, pluralist economics gains from engaging with the demand for well-defined counterfactuals and identification strategies, which serves as a productive input when distinguishing pluralism-with-rigor from pluralism-as-anything-goes.

On this foundation, we sketch a framework in which the local precision of modern causal econometrics and the broader ambition of pluralist contextualization are treated not as rivals but as mutually reinforcing research strategies. The result, we suggest, is better economics: more honest about what a given study can and cannot establish, more attentive to the institutional and theoretical embeddedness of causal claims, and — perhaps most importantly — less likely to mistake a well-identified fragment for the whole story.

Keywords: science, foundations, causality, identification, happy retirement ;-)

JEL Codes: B41, B52, C18

articles.title: Decolonial Comparative Law Workshop (Douala, May 2027)
articles.body_html:
5-6 May, 2027 | Douala, Cameroon

Workshop theme: Decolonial Comparative Law and the Informal/Formal Economy

The exclusion of the many from access to, and the benefits of, means of production and resources has long been a colonial enterprise. Today, around 60% of the world’s labour force works in the informal economy. In legal terms, informality often translates into insecure social and economic rights – in short, precarity. At the same time, legal instruments designed to secure transactions, access to capital, and property are typically associated with the formal economy. Yet across Global South – or Global Majority – contexts, and increasingly in the Global North, participation in the formal economy does not guarantee stable economic rights.

This is paralleled by an exclusion of the informal economy within comparative law scholarship, which either ignores informality altogether or views it merely as a problem to be solved by law modelled after Global North law. This imbalance has limited the documentation of alternative legal instruments for human economies. Coloniality continues to sustain a narrow reading of how Global South and Indigenous societies structure their economic lives, including when they choose not to practise “economy” in a conventional sense. Acknowledging the heterogeneity of the informal economy requires attention to everyday legalities across both informal and formal work.

This workshop is not only interested in papers recommending or problematising formalisation initiatives. The main focus of the workshop is to take the informal economy seriously as a space of legality as such, in the context of legal pluralism. The organizers are looking for attempts to document, compare, and assess legal approaches – in formal and informal law – to the informal economy and the intersections between formal and informal economic life. The organizers welcome papers analysing how informal workers mobilise, transform, ignore, or reject state and non-state legal instruments in their economic lives, and examining how formal institutions engage with the informal sector.

Potential topics include, but are not limited to:

  • Informal cross-border trade, including commerce conducted by groups transcending state borders, regardless of their legality under state law.
  • Local and digital currencies created or used for noncolonial purposes.
  • Indigenous and customary economies, including their own value systems, exchange practices, and non-colonial monetary forms.
  • Ecofeminist, pastoralist, rural, and intentional communities (e.g. Auroville in India) as well as precolonial or other traditional modes of value creation (irrespective of the effective ancestry of the practice).
  • Labour rights in informal work, including economic dependence within and beyond the employer–employee relationship, dispute resolution practices, and collective organisation (e.g., trade unions, associations, cooperatives).
  • Microlending, alternative securities, and property rights as mechanisms for accessing capital.
  • Legal (mis)recognition of informal workers.
  • Migration and the (in)formal economy.
  • Globalisation and the informal labour serving the global supply chain.
  • Digital businesses, platform-based livelihoods (e.g. TikTok influencers, delivery and domestic workers hired online) and (in)formality.
  • State constraints on local economic sovereignty, including the spatial distribution and regulation of formal and informal economic activities.
  • Blurred lines between formal and informal economies: workers operating in both settings (e.g. civil servants’ side jobs; or ‘hustlers’, ‘débrouillards’, and ‘rebuscadores’).

If your research does not fit into any of these themes, the organizers still encourage you to submit a proposal. In general, the organizers invite papers that analyse and destabilise coloniality by examining, comparatively, the economic and legal imaginaries through which communities (typically, but not necessarily, in the Global South) define, practise, or decline to practise an economy beyond (or in spite of) coloniality.

Timeline

  • 18 March 2026 – Information meetings (2 time zones)
  • 1 September 2026 – Draft paper due
  • 1 November 2026 – Acceptance or rejection communicated
  • 14 February 2027 – Revised draft due
  • 5–6 May 2027 – Onsite workshop discussion
  • September 2027 – Informal peer-led writing workshop
  • 10 January 2028 – Final paper due for publication in 2028

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 1 September 2026

articles.title: IIPPE's The Political Economy of China’s Development Working Group: Joint Panel (Hong Kong, November 2026)
articles.body_html:
21 November, 2026 | Hong Kong, China

This is a special call for papers from the IIPPE China Working Group for a joint panel at the 2nd International Conference of Ng Teng Fong Sino Group Belt and Road Research Institute on Rethinking International Relations in an Age of Uncertainty.

The organizers invite you to submit a proposal for individual paper related to our lines of inquiry into the political economy of China’s rise and the building of a community with a shared future for humankind.

China’s rise as an economic superpower has not been deterred by the US’s containment strategy but the intensification of US militarism and financialisation destabilises the world economy and creates humanitarian crises one after another. While China shows defiance in pursuing self-strengthening strategy and calls for new global initiatives for building a community with a shared future of humankind, the ideological, political and military influence of the US remains and raises questions on how such a future will become reality. The organizers welcome contributions which address the dilemma and the evolving developments, and particularly on the following themes:

  • The impacts and possible outcomes of the US-China rivalry and/or Russia-China-Iran and Democratic Republic of Korea relations
  • Conflicts and interdependence in East Asia, ASEAN and the South China Sea
  • The political economy of China’s development and anti-imperialist struggles
  • Socialism with Chinese characteristics, Western Marxism and world socialism
  • Peculiarities of the Chinese polity and comparison with the Western models including the questions on democracy and human rights
  • China’s Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative, Global Civilisation Initiative, Global Governance Initiative and world development
  • Green transition and digital-AI transformation
  • The rise of China and its impacts on contemporary neo-imperialism and/or multipolarity

The proposal submission platform is now open until Friday 24 July 2026 (HK time). Please click on the link and follow the instruction accordingly. You will need to provide an abstract (500-1,000 words) and your biography (500 words) in the submission.

Important: If you are submitting to the IIPPE China WG panel, please ensure you select Panel 7: The political economy of China’s rise and the building of a community with a shared future for humankind on the form.

Please find more info here.

If you have any questions, please contact nsbrri.conference.3@chuhai.edu.hk or the China WG coordinator Sam-Kee Cheng.

Submission Deadline: 24 July 2026

articles.title: International Workshop: AI and its economic, financial and social impacts (London, June 2027)
articles.body_html:
17-18 June, 2027 | London, UK

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly regarded as a transformative general-purpose technology with pervasive implications across industries, institutions, and societies.

This workshop aims to contribute to ongoing research efforts by eliciting papers addressing the inherently multi-dimensional implications of AI. It aims to bring together scholars working on theoretical, empirical, and policy-oriented contributions that may fall within the following broad themes:

A. Measurement and identification issues in AI research

  • Measuring AI adoption, penetration, and use across firms, sectors, places and valuechains. Development and implementation of appropriate identification strategies for firm-,industry- and country-level research on economic implications of AI.
  • Use of AI-related journal articles for constructing task‑ or function‑specific exposuremeasures
  • AI generation, heuristics of innovators, biases and reproduction of stereotypes

B. AI and business dynamism

  • Productivity, growth, and the "AI productivity paradox".
  • AI investment and accelerated obsolescence in technologies and skills.
  • Innovation, creative destruction and obsolescence in the AI era.
  • AI and entrepreneurship.
  • Market structure, market power, and competition policy in AI ecosystems.
  • AI and the firm: Organisation, management practices, and business-model transformation.

C. AI and the labour market

  • AI and the labour market: Impacts on employment, wages and skills.
  • AI and labour relations: Worker management, surveillance, monitoring and control.
  • Algorithmic hiring and labour market sorting: Does AI improve match quality or amplify segmentation?
  • Bias, fairness, and dynamic discrimination: Long-run labour market effects of biased training data.

D. AI and finance

  • Effects of AI-based credit scoring: banking on winners or allocative efficiency?
  • Crowding and fragility from correlated AI models: Implications for pro-cyclicality and systemic risk
  • Bias, explainability, and discrimination: Long-term credit market effects of opaque scoring models.
  • AI related financial regulations and governance

E. Political economy of AI

  • AI and political economy: The role of institutions and economic policies
  • Spatial and regional dimensions of AI.
  • Sustainability, energy, and the environmental costs of AI.

Contact AI.Workshop@gre.ac.uk to receive full information on the call for papers.

Authors are invited to submit:

  • A one-page paper abstract by 1 August 2026
  • Completed papers by 1 April 2027

Selected papers will be considered for publication in a special issue of Economics of Innovation and New Technology, subject to the journal’s standard peer-review process.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 1 August 2026

articles.title: Journal of Australian Political Economy: Special Issues on "Health Inequality" and "Political Economic Challenges"
articles.body_html:
JAPE No. 99 Special Issue: The Political Economy of Health Inequality

Over the preceding two decades, mainstream public health scholarship and political discourse has accorded increasing attention to health inequalities – both their pernicious effects on population health and well-being, and the need to devise policies to redress them. Most prominently, this focus has translated into an expansive literature addressing the social determinants of health (SDH), which recognises that health outcomes stem from myriad social factors beyond healthcare alone, and are not reducible to the products of economically organised medical science. Alternatively, in seeking to discern the complex determinants of human health and inequalities therein, this tradition highlights the importance of indicators of socio-economic status (SES), such as income, wealth, and education. SDH research predominantly isolates such indicators as a means to demonstrate their causal association with negative and/or positive health outcomes, thereby implying that securing the correct balance of SES indicators would precipitate more favourable societal and/or global health consequences.

Undoubtedly, the SDH literature has heightened analytical and public awareness of in-justices surrounding health and health delivery – a fact that was plainly evident during successive COVID waves, as the relations between inequality and ill-health became increasingly stark. Without pre-existing, broad institutional acceptance of the association of SES with health status among public health institutions, researchers, hospitals, and international organisations, discussions concerning inequality and COVID would not have occurred with such potency within media and governmental circles. Nevertheless, despite this important contribution in identifying a broad nexus of social factors shaping health outcomes, the SDH literature tends to disregard the ‘upstream’ social conditions and power structures that adversely affect health. That is, the tradition largely fails to progress further up the causal chain to address how the social determinants of poor health (such as inequality) are, themselves, determined by structural factors, such as class or the systemic imperative of capitalism toward perpetual capital accumulation. Inequality or socioeconomic status here simply refers to individuals or families who are higher or lower according to a particular metric without consideration of the antagonistic social relations between these groups.

Hence, while recognising the significance of SDH research in refocusing scholarly and political attention on social factors as the fulcrum of studies of health inequality, this special issue seeks to shift how we comprehend associations between inequality and health. It places the locus of causality not so much on socio-economic status, but rather on the embodied structural forces, power, and political struggles that bring about the proximate status of SES indicators in the first place. That is, it is concerned with the political economy of health inequalities – critically analysing the historically specific nexus of structures, processes, and social relations in contemporary capitalism that constitute the material and ideological conditions in which people live and work, and thereby engender particular individual and societal patterns of health, illness, and well-being.

Contributions to this special issue may address a range of questions on this theme, including (but not limited to):

  • Conceptualising health inequality via a political economy lens
  • Financialisation, the asset economy and health inequality
  • The corporatisation of Medicare, de-universalisation and growth of out-of-pocket health expenses
  • Climate change, planetary health and health inequalities
  • Food poverty and malnutrition
  • The co-constitutive relations between class, gender, sexual, racialised and spatial health inequalities
  • Corporate power, neoliberalism and the commodification of health
  • Methodological approaches to studying health inequality that address its structural causes
  • The contemporary welfare/workfare state and entrenching of poverty
  • Contesting the primarily techno-managerial framing of health inequalities in government policy
  • Capitalism, class struggle and health
  • Case-studies of health inequalities in Australia and/or globally
  • Policy and political opportunities to promote greater social justice – from universal basic services and greater healthcare universalism to structural and systemic change

Through consideration of such themes, the special issue will showcase the cutting-edge of contemporary scholarship on the political economy of health inequality. Papers should be between 6,000-8,000 words, and formatted using the Harvard style.

Production Details

  • 1 December 2026: First drafts of papers due
  • 1 April 2027: Second drafts of papers due
  • June 2027: Special issue published as Journal of Australian Political Economy No. 99

Please direct all submissions or questions to the editors David Primrose or Edward Jegasothy.

Submission Deadline: 1 December 2026

JAPE No. 100 Special Issue: Current and Future Political Economic Challenges – and Possibilities

Volume 100 of the Journal of Australian Political Economy, due in December 2027, will be a theme issue on 'Current and Future Political Economic Challenges – and Possibilities'.

Submissions of up to 8,000 words for this special centenary issue should be sent to the coordinating editor Frank Stilwell.

Submission Deadline: 1 April 2027

articles.title: Review of Political Economy and Economia e Sociedade: Joint Symposium on "What should Central Banks do?"
articles.body_html:
What Should Central Banks Do?

Central banks were first designed to deal with financial instability and to give economic and financial support to governments by funding public debt. This was their primary raison d’être. The earliest institutions, like the Bank of England (1694), were established specifically to finance military conflicts and manage national treasuries. Later, banks like the U.S. Federal Reserve (1913) were created as “lenders of last resort” to stop bank panics and standardize currency. As time went on, however, central banks were called upon to assume additional tasks, notably the responsibility for keeping inflation ‘low and stable’ and for addressing unemployment.

Viewed from the periphery, this question cannot be separated from the hierarchical nature of the global monetary and financial system. That hierarchy shapes even central banks' ‘core’ objectives, so what is at stake is less the addition of new mandates than the degree of monetary sovereignty peripheral capitalist states possess in the first place.

Today, as research has progressed and new economic challenges have arisen, central banks are being called upon once more — from various ideological sides — to address issues of inequality and the environment, and to participate in quantitative easing for the people.

But are central banks able to address all these issues? Or, more importantly, should they? In the end, are we not asking central banks to do too much? Should central banks address income inequality? Should they address ecological problems, and, above all, should they distribute money to the general public?

It is of course one thing to recognize that monetary policy has distributive or ecological consequences, but asking central banks to address these issues is a matter of great debate. Does this fall into the mainstream trap of accepting ‘monetary policy dominance’, as coined by Rochon and Setterfield? Are central banks equipped to deal with these additional problems, or should they be relegated to fiscal policy?

Such is the question posed by this joint symposium between the Review of Political Economy and Economia e Sociedade. Our aim is to publish a total of twenty articles across the two journals, asking the important question of what central banks should do today.

Guest Editors

  • Carolina Troncoso Baltar

articles.full_text: What Should Central Banks Do? Central banks were first designed to deal with financial instability and to give economic and financial support to governments by funding public debt. This was their primary raison d’être. The earliest institutions, like the Bank of England (1694), were established specifically to finance military conflicts and manage national treasuries. Later, banks like the U.S. Federal Reserve (1913) were created as “lenders of last resort” to stop bank panics and standardize currency. As time went on, however, central banks were called upon to assume additional tasks, notably the responsibility for keeping inflation ‘low and stable’ and for addressing unemployment. Viewed from the periphery, this question cannot be separated from the hierarchical nature of the global monetary and financial system. That hierarchy shapes even central banks' ‘core’ objectives, so what is at stake is less the addition of new mandates than the degree of monetary sovereignty peripheral capitalist states possess in the first place. Today, as research has progressed and new economic challenges have arisen, central banks are being called upon once more — from various ideological sides — to address issues of inequality and the environment, and to participate in quantitative easing for the people. But are central banks able to address all these issues? Or, more importantly, should they? In the end, are we not asking central banks to do too much? Should central banks address income inequality? Should they address ecological problems, and, above all, should they distribute money to the general public? It is of course one thing to recognize that monetary policy has distributive or ecological consequences, but asking central banks to address these issues is a matter of great debate. Does this fall into the mainstream trap of accepting ‘monetary policy dominance’, as coined by Rochon and Setterfield? Are central banks equipped to deal with these additional problems, or should they be relegated to fiscal policy? Such is the question posed by this joint symposium between the Review of Political Economy and Economia e Sociedade. Our aim is to publish a total of twenty articles across the two journals, asking the important question of what central banks should do today. articles.title: Revista de Economia Critica: Special Issue on "Transformations of contemporary capitalism: neoliberalism, authoritarianism and the war economy"
articles.body_html:
The Journal of Critical Economics announces a call for papers for its semi-monographic issue for the second half of 2027 on ‘Transformations of contemporary capitalism: neoliberalism, authoritarianism and the war economy’.

Editors

  • Aurelia Mañé Estrada (UB)
  • Albert Recio Andreu (UAB)

For decades, analysis of capitalist economies has focused on neoliberalism as the emerging order that emerged from the crisis of the 1970s, centred on deregulation, financialisation and globalisation. However, this project — which has always been marked by social resistance and differing national trajectories — has shown clear limitations since the 2007 crisis, following which austerity policies reinforced inequalities and weakened the material foundations of democracy.

Neoliberalism has operated not only as an economic policy, but also as an institutional project and a rationale that reshapes the conditions of democracy, fostering processes of de-democratisation, technocratisation and authoritarianism. In this context, rising inequality, the ecological crisis and the transformations of digital capitalism are combined with the rise of the far right and a growing structural convergence between neoliberalism and new forms of fascism.

At the same time, we are witnessing significant shifts in the role of the state and in global regulation: directed reindustrialisation, a crisis of multilateralism, geopolitical tensions and the intensification of armed conflicts, and a slowdown in ecological transition policies… Within this framework, we are seeing a return to active fiscal policies and the emergence of a possible ‘war-time Keynesianism’, in which defence spending acts as a driver of demand, innovation and productive reorganisation.

Whilst inequalities continue to grow and affect the living conditions of an increasing proportion of the population, even in the dominant countries, new types of business have emerged which wield significant economic power through their control of the central networks of the new digital economy. The debate over how to characterise this new form of capitalism is ongoing, with concepts such as ‘surveillance capitalism’ or ‘techno-feudalism’ being put forward in an attempt to capture the nature of a new model that is more predatory than its predecessor. At the same time, driven by the United States, we are witnessing the dismantling of plurinational institutions and a resurgence of imperial and military tensions. A key aspect of this process is the weakening of policies designed to tackle ecological problems. Growing inequalities, the ecological crisis, imperialist conflicts and the rise of a far right that imposes policies aimed at dismantling rights paint a dramatic picture.

The aim of this special issue is to analyse these transformations, their causes and their direction, taking into account both the continuities and the breaks with historical neoliberalism.

The following lines of inquiry, amongst others, are proposed:

  • Relationships between neoliberalism, the democratic crisis, authoritarianism and fascism
  • The political economy of war: military spending, reindustrialisation and military Keynesianism
  • Transformations of the state and the global order in a context of geopolitical rivalry
  • Digital capitalism, corporate power and new forms of accumulation
  • Finance, inequality and the reconfiguration of social structures
  • The ecological crisis and the limits of the growth model
  • The role of China and new configurations of the international system
  • Elements for characterising contemporary capitalism

Theoretical and empirical contributions from critical and interdisciplinary perspectives will be welcomed.

Formal requirements:

Papers written in English or Spanish will be accepted

Abstract: 400 words maximum.

Full paper: 9,000 words maximum.

Please find more info here.

Submission Deadline: 10 October 2026

articles.title: 61st ITH Conference (Linz, September 2026)
articles.body_html:
17-19 September, 2026 | Linz, Austria

Conference theme: Working nature – exploring intersections of labour history and political ecology

The 61st ITH Conference is organized by the International Conference of Labour and Social History (ITH) and kindly supported by the Chamber of Labour of Upper Austria, the Chamber of Labour of Vienna, the Institute for Historical Social Research, the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, the Austrian Society for Political Education, and the City of Linz.

The bundle of human-made ecological crises has reached a point where most earth scientist see an actual breaching of ecological thresholds, not only in relation to climate change but also six of nine processes for which “planetary boundaries” have been defined. In this context, the interdisciplinary field of political ecology (which dates to at least the 1970s) has experienced a spectacular boom. In a certain sense, it has become the interdisciplinary critical social science of our days, a field in which both academic and political concerns converge. In the English-speaking world, political ecology has proved to be strongly inflected by historical reasoning, with several authors highlighting the entanglements between material extraction, energy carriers (particularly fossil ones), ecological over-use, capitalist economic development, and exploitation.

While the history of work and labour relations have a place in these studies, many commentators have noticed an ongoing non-communication between labour history and political ecology. Despite such (self-)critical assessments, the last decades already have seen numerous instances scholarship at the intersection of “labour” and “environmental history” as well as “political ecology”. It thus seems both timely and necessary to bring global labour history and historical political ecology into a more structured and fruitful dialogue, to assess existing research at the intersection of both and to explore further avenues of research. While open to a broad spectrum of topics and approaches – from the carbon nexus to agrarian ecologies, from toxic through contested to multispecies labour –, this conference will insist on “labour” as one major category of differentiation in past and current ecological predicaments.

Registration is available via the following form.

Please note that early bird registration ends on 24 July 2026.

articles.title: Climate Change Graz Fall School 2026 (Augustinum, October 2026)
articles.body_html:
12-16 October, 2026 | Augustinum, Austria

Overcoming Lock-Ins to Enable a Just Transition towards a Climate-Neutral and Sustainable Economy and Society

The PhD Fall School 2026 brings together doctoral researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds to explore this question in an interdisciplinary and collaborative learning environment. The programme focuses on analysing lock-ins and their interconnectedness across socio-technical systems, while developing strategies and intervention pathways for transformative change.

Participants will work in interdisciplinary teams focusing on specific production and consumption systems, including:

  • agricultural food systems,
  • industrial production and consumption,
  • transport systems,
  • and energy systems.

The Fall School combines keynote lectures, input-focused and workshop elements, collaborative research, and interdisciplinary exchange.

Throughout the week, participants will analyse lock-ins, discuss approaches for operationalisation and measurement, and collaboratively develop measures and strategies for overcoming lock-ins in the context of just sustainability transitions. Each team will be accompanied by faculty mentors throughout the week.

The Fall School is designed for doctoral researchers interested in sustainability transitions, climate neutrality, socio-technical change, and interdisciplinary research. In addition to thematic and analytical insights, participants will strengthen their interdisciplinary collaboration, critical thinking, communication, and collaborative research skills.

The programme corresponds to 4 ECTS credits and includes the collaborative development of a short interdisciplinary research paper following the Fall School. Active participation throughout the entire Fall School programme is expected.

Participation in the Fall School is free of charge. Lunch and dinner during the programme will be covered by the organisers.

Please find more info here.

Registration Deadline: 15 August 2026

articles.title: Paper Development Workshops: Special Issue of Organization on "The (Re)turn to Marx: New Readings of Marx and the Future of Organization" (November 2026)
articles.body_html:
4-late November, 2026 | London, UK (Hybrid)

Special Issue of Organization

Amidst the many crises of the 21st century, there has been a multi-stranded return to Marx across not only the critical social sciences and humanities but within broader struggles for social transformation. In different ways, these have stretched Marxian concepts and methods to examine the changing, contradictory, and uneven nature of capitalist organization and organizing against capital. This includes engagement with previously unknown or neglected texts and themes in Marx’s oeuvre, that address questions of ecology, colonialism, gender, sexuality, and more. Despite these developments, and despite the influence that Marx has had on the study of organization and organizing, direct and sustained engagement with Marxian theory remains limited within organization studies. The special issue therefore seeks to open a forum for engagement with new readings and uses of Marx, to think and struggle in the open and unknown terrain of history. We invite conceptual, methodological, and empirical contributions that critically engage with Marx, from a plurality of disciplines, traditions, geographies, and positionalities, to interrogate capitalist organization in the conjuncture and explore possibilities for organizing alternatives in and beyond capitalism.

Paper development workshops for interested authors will be held in November 2026. There will be an in-person PDW in London, UK on November 4th 2026, and an online PDW in mid- to late November 2026 for those who are unable to attend in-person. The format of the workshops will be finalized closer to the time they are held.

Please submit your abstract (max. 1000 words outlining focus, contribution, methods [if appropriate], and fit with the special issue) to returntomarxSI@gmail.com by July 30th 2026. Please also indicate whether you are interested in participating in the in-person or in the online workshop. Participation in the workshops is not a necessary condition for authors to submit a full paper to the SI.

Please find more info here.

Editors

  • Yousaf Nishat-Botero
  • Simon Barber
  • Olimpia Burchiellaro
  • Elisavet Mantzari
  • David Watson

Application Deadline: 30 July 2026

articles.title: UNU MERIT Intensive Course on Agent Based Modelling in Economics and Social Sciences (Maastricht, September 2026)
articles.body_html:
28 September - 02 October, 2026 | Maastricht, Netherlands

Agent-based models (ABM) are a powerful and increasingly essential tool in economics and across other social sciences for studying complex systems and social challenges. This summer school addresses the critical need for researchers to master not only the conceptual underpinnings of ABM but also the practical challenges of programming, adhering to robust protocols, and effectively communicating model design and results.

Building on past successful editions, this intensive, full-time course equips participants with the advanced theoretical understanding and skills to design, implement, validate, and analyse robust agent-based models, such as a PhD thesis, a high-quality academic paper, or a policy report.

In this edition the course will also evaluate the power and limitations of Large Language Models (LLM) as co-pilots in designing and coding ABMs. In an era where researchers increasingly turn to LLM to generate code, this course emphasises the critical importance of understanding model mechanics. By comparing AI-generated models with manual coding, students will appreciate the need for bridging theory and implementation.

While the methodological skills acquired are applicable across all social sciences, the primary case studies will focus on economics, innovation, development, political economy, public policy and structural change.

Upon completion, participants will be able to:

  • Understand the foundational principles and theoretical frontiers of ABMs, including their strengths and limitations in social science research.
  • Design and implement ABMs from scratch in and R, abstracting away from tedious software engineering to focus purely on modelling logic.
  • Analyse model output rigorously and apply Machine Learning methods for advanced sensitivity analysis with R.
  • Develop skills useful to produce ABMs also in other platforms/languages such as Python and NetLogo.
  • Critically compare AI-generated ABMs with expert manual coding in R and LSD, recognizing the methodological risks of treating simulation code as a black box.
  • Critically evaluate ABM methodology, navigate the pitfalls of relying on AI for model generation, and apply this learning to their own research questions.
  • Conceptualise and prototype an original ABM project, laying a strong foundation for future development and publication.

This course is designed for:

  • Ambitious graduate and PhD students in economics and other social sciences with a keen interest in advancing their research using computational methods.
  • Early-career researchers and experienced modellers looking to enhance their skills and explore new frontiers in ABMs.

Places are limited to 16 participants to ensure a high-quality learning experience and ample interaction with faculty. Interested applicants should submit a motivation letter (including detailing research interests, how this course aligns with their current or future research goals, programming experience (if any, not a requisite), and career stage) and a CV here.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 30 July 2026

articles.title: WAPE conference on 'The Wealth of Nations in the Multipolar Age' (London, August 2026)
articles.body_html:
5-7 August, 2026 | London, UK

The World Association for Political Economy (WAPE) is pleased to announce its annual forum on the theme “The Wealth of Nations in the Multipolar Age”, marking the 250th anniversary of the publication of Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations. Participants meet at the Old Royal Naval College in Greenwich, London, where the first Chinese translator of the Smith’s works and first principal of Beijing University, Yan Fu, studied.

The organizers invite scholars, researchers, activists, and practitioners to participate in the conference.

The neoclassical and neoliberal appropriation of Smith is simplistic at best and false at worst. Marx, in contrast, rightly regarded Smith as one of his most important intellectual forbears, whose ideas he both valued and criticized in arriving at his own critique of political economy.

Marx considered Smith to be among those investigating ‘the real internal framework [Zusammenhang] of bourgeois relations of production’ — in particular, through his concept of the division of labour, at once advancing the productive capacities of human labour and stunting the human personality, and his belief that labour was ‘the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities’.

Indeed, the centrality of these and other themes of Smith’s work to Marx’s indicates that many of them point beyond capitalism itself.

The Wealth of Nations also addressed, as the curtain rose on the modern capitalist world, the central issue of what makes nations rich or poor. It has formed the running thread of the study of political and geopolitical economy. Today it is central to discussions of the multipolar and pluripolar world, as socialist and other anti-imperialist countries challenge capitalist domination through the increasingly successful pursuit of development, combined with a rejection of the imperial domination that was formative of, and remains fundamental to, capitalism’s very existence.

As in previous years, WAPE will run a geopolitical economy stream to strengthen understanding of what Marx called the ‘relations of producing nations’ of the age of capital, and of the transition away from capitalism.

The organizers commemorate Smith’s The Wealth of Nations this year by inviting submissions that add to existing scholarship on Smith, particularly those that develop the radical and developmental aspects of his thought in the spirit of Marxism, those that investigate his relation to Marx and other critical thinkers since and especially those that which investigate how reconsideration of Smith’s work may contribute to understanding the political and geopolitical economy of the twenty-first century of decaying capitalism, and to advancing socialism in what Marx termed the ‘relations of producing nations’ in the age of multi- and pluripolarity.

Please register and find more information here.

Today it is central to discussions of the multipolar and pluripolar world, as socialist and other anti-imperialist countries challenge capitalist domination through the increasingly successful pursuit of development, combined with a rejection of the imperial domination that was formative of, and remains fundamental to, capitalism’s very existence. As in previous years, WAPE will run a geopolitical economy stream to strengthen understanding of what Marx called the ‘relations of producing nations’ of the age of capital, and of the transition away from capitalism. The organizers commemorate Smith’s The Wealth of Nations this year by inviting submissions that add to existing scholarship on Smith, particularly those that develop the radical and developmental aspects of his thought in the spirit of Marxism, those that investigate his relation to Marx and other critical thinkers since and especially those that which investigate how reconsideration of Smith’s work may contribute to understanding the political and geopolitical economy of the twenty-first century of decaying capitalism, and to advancing socialism in what Marx termed the ‘relations of producing nations’ in the age of multi- and pluripolarity. Please register and find more information here .

articles.title: Workshop: Researching the Industrial Policy of the Mobility Transition (Vienna, September 2026)
articles.body_html:
15-16 September, 2026 | Vienna, Austria

AK Vienna and JKU Linz (ICAE & SET Lab) invite researchers to a workshop on the industrial policy dimensions of the mobility transformation, September 15–16, 2026, in Vienna. The workshop brings together scholars working on production structures, value chains, and industrial transformation in the mobility sector, with a focus on the rail industry and publicly used vehicles (e.g. e-buses, waste collection or emergency vehicles), public procurement, and employment.

Abstract submissions (200–300 words) are welcome until July 31, 2026; early-stage scholars are explicitly encouraged to apply. Please note that the workshop itself will be conducted in German.

Registration and further details: https://veranstaltung.akwien.at/de/workshop-mobilitaetswende/registration

Submission Deadline: 31 July 2026

articles.title: Levy 40th Anniversary Conference Recordings
articles.body_html:
On May 8, 2026, the Levy Economics Institute convened its annual conference on the 40th anniversary of the Institute’s founding.

This year’s conference was held in person on the Bard College campus and featured panel discussions exploring current sources of financial instability, surveying the macro picture for the US economy, and engaging with economic policy challenges in areas such as artificial intelligence, jobs, caregiving, energy, and development finance.

Presenters included:

Sheila Bair, James K. Galbraith, Darrick Hamilton, William H. Janeway, Tom Keene, Chris Kennedy, Yan Liang, Pavlina R. Tcherneva, Isabella Weber, L. Randall Wray, and Gennaro Zezza

Recordings from the day are now available on YouTube.

articles.title: The Levy Institute Podcast Ep. 7: Discussing Wynne Godley
articles.body_html:
Levy Scholars Claudio H. Dos Santos, Gennaro Zezza, and Michalis Nikiforos sit down in this episode to discuss the life and legacy of one of the Institute's Distinguished Scholars, Wynne Godley (1926-2010).

This episode serves as part of the Levy at 40 Series. In 2026, the Levy Economics Institute marks the 40th anniversary of its founding. For four decades, the Institute has advanced independent economic research, shaped policy debates, and moved beyond the boundaries of mainstream economic thinking.

Please find a link to the episode here.

Further reading on the work of Wynne Godley:

  • "Seven Unsustainable Processes: Medium-term Prospects and Policies for the United States and the World," by Wynne Godley
  • "Debt and Lending: A Cri de Coeur," by Wynne Godley and Gennaro Zezza
  • "The US Economy amid Rising Global Uncertainty," by Dimitri B. Papadimitriou, Giuliano Toshiro Yajima, and Gennaro Zezza
  • "Monetary Economics: An Integrated Approach to Credit, Money, Income, Production and Wealth," by Wynne Godley and Marc Lavoie

articles.title: Levy Economics Institute, USA
articles.body_html:
Recruitment and Communications Coordinator

The Levy Economics Institute of Bard College, an internationally recognized policy research organization, invites applications for the position of Recruitment and Communications Coordinator. The Recruitment and Communications Coordinator will primarily be responsible for graduate recruitment and publicizing the Institute’s research activities and its innovative Master’s in Economic Theory and Policy degree programs.

Responsibilities:

  • Working with the Director of Graduate Programs on admissions strategy and outreach, including maintaining the Graduate Program web presence, arranging for applicant webinars, mailings, and recruiting schedules of the graduate program
  • The ideal candidate is motivated and charismatic, with great communication skills and the ability to cultivate applications and plan well in advance of key recruiting milestones and deadlines
  • The Coordinator is the primary contact for all incoming students and must be responsive to student requests and questions
  • Acting as the primary contact for graduate-program-related campus offices (student accounts, financial aid, international student services, etc.)
  • Traveling to regional colleges and graduate school fairs, especially during the fall recruiting season
  • Actively publicizing the Institute’s research and events through social media and an e-newsletter, including preparing synopses of new publications
  • Posting to and managing content on the Institute webpage

Qualifications:

  • The institute is seeking an individual who possesses excellent writing skills, has the ability to operate across multiple issue areas in economic theory and public policy, and can package these research ideas appropriately and communicate them clearly to a broad range of audiences. A degree in economics/public policy or experience as an economics/public policy writer are preferred. Familiarity with (or a willingness to learn) the Adobe suite (including Adobe Express for graphics) is a plus.
  • An ability to energetically articulate the Levy Graduate Program. The successful candidate must be able to speak in front of groups of potential graduate students and communicate effectively and collaboratively with various staff and faculty associated with the graduate programs, including relevant Bard College staff.
  • Previous higher education experience is valued, as is experience with admission and application software (e.g., Slate), but a willingness to learn and manage such programs is essential.
  • A bachelor’s degree (preferably in economics or a related field) is required.

To Apply:

Please provide a cover letter, resume, writing sample, and the contact information for three professional references to Interfolio by following this link.

Please find more info here.

articles.title: Lund University Centre for Sustainability Studies, Sweden
articles.body_html:
PhD position - '(Dis)orderly transitions: The financial sector's role in shaping just energy transitions'

What the project is about

In recent years the idea of an 'orderly just transition' has started to gain ground. While questions of justice have been taken up by ‘just transition’ research, the addition of 'orderly' is more recent, raising new questions around the envisioned speed, direction, and outcomes of energy transitions. In this project we want to look at this idea of 'order' in transitions more closely, identifying and analysing how (some) actors in the financial sector try to implement an orderly transition away from fossil fuels through the use of specific financial instruments and practices. By incorporating ideas from both political economy and economic sociology the project investigates how attempts at enacting order by financial actors can be understood as a process of contested temporal politics, with actors seeking to make the future knowable, trajectories towards it manageable, and outcomes controllable.

Who you will be working with

The project is a collaboration between myself (Bregje van Veelen, Lund University) and Amy Janzwood at McGill University in Canada, and will include cases in both North America and Scandinavia. The PhD candidate in Lund is expected to focus primarily on the latter, but there will be opportunity for comparative work too. The position is based at LUCSUS (Lund University Centre for Sustainability Studies) in Sweden, where you will be part of a friendly and supportive community of scholars.

What the institution is looking for in a candidate

Someone with a strong interest in critical social science approaches who is excited to explore how issues of politics and power play out in the financial sphere. The project speaks to a variety of themes and concepts, including energy transitions, sustainable finance, temporalities & future-making, and social constructions of risk. The institution does not expect anyone to be experienced with all of these, but having experience with one of these topics and an interest in some of the others is important. Most of the data collection is expected to be qualitative in nature, so experience with qualitative methods is a must. Knowledge of a Scandinavian language is a bonus, but not a requirement.

For potential applicants unfamiliar with the Swedish system

PhD positions in Sweden are fully funded for 4 years. You'll receive a regular salary, vacation days, pension contributions, etc. In addition to conducting research, you will be expected to complete 60 credits (=one year) of course work. There are also opportunities for teaching, and taking on administrative/leadership roles (such as PhD rep), for which you will receive extra time (and funding) to complete your PhD.

More details on the position and how to apply here.

Application Deadline: 28 August 2026

articles.title: University of Amsterdam, Netherlands (1)
articles.body_html:
Assistant Professor in International Relations and International Political Economy

The Department of Political Science at the University of Amsterdam invites applications for a tenure-track Assistant Professor (‘Universitair Docent’) position in Political Science. Based in the Political Economy and Transnational Governance (PETGOV) programme group, the department welcomes new members whose research (and teaching) is informed by and connected to ongoing global transformations. The ideal candidate brings an innovative research agenda, experience, and enthusiasm to complement our programme group's research and to educate our students.

For this Assistant Professor vacancy, the department seeks to strengthen its expertise on inter-state relations (diplomacy, inter-state conflict and alliances, global security) in the context of geo-political economy and combined with a rigorous methodological approach. For this position the department particularly seeks candidates who approach such questions empirically from a global perspective rather than only from a specific regional angle.  

Candidates for the position should complement PETGOV’s research community, a group interested in not just national or inter-national political relations but also non-nation-state global economic and political relations. Finally, candidates should be ready to contribute to the teaching of core courses in International Relations and/or political economy.

Core tasks

  • Teaching general and specialist courses in international relations / (International) Political Economy at both undergraduate and post-graduate levels, and involvement in post-graduate supervision;
  • Developing, conducting, and supervising high quality academic research on topics mentioned above;
  • Participating in acquiring external research funding;
  • Contributing to the research programme of the Programme Group PETGOV and the Amsterdam Institute for Social Science Research through scholarly publications and engagement in local, national, and international networks.

What do you have to offer

  • A completed and submitted doctoral thesis in Political Science – specifically in international relations / political economy, or a closely related field;
  • An innovative research programme and output that demonstrates excellence and provides potential for raising external research funding;
  • Research added value (future ambitions, and ideas about how these match or fill niches within the programme group);
  • Mastery of up-to-date research methods appropriate for your research agenda;
  • Substantial academic teaching experience – at both undergraduate and postgraduate levels– on a breadth of topics within the discipline / scope of the profile and on a variety of teaching formats such as lectures, seminars, and supervision, including (partially) independently designed courses.
  • Broad academic teaching orientation, able and willing to teach general international relations, and/or political economy courses.
  • Well-developed teaching and didactic vision showing demonstrated capacity to inspire and activate students, encourage in-class interaction, address contemporary, sensitive or topical issues, and foster bridges between academia and society.
  • The ability to work both as an independent professional and as a team player, with an appreciation for diversity and inclusion, reflected in a proven track record of good academic citizenship;
  • The ability to develop connections to practitioners/policymakers/stakeholders to the benefit of teaching and research;
  • The proven ability to develop and submit competitive research grant proposals; 
  • A capacity to teach in English and Dutch (or a willingness to acquire knowledge of Dutch within three years);
  • The basic qualification at Dutch universities in higher education (‘Basiskwalificatie Onderwijs’; BKO) certificate, or a willingness to acquire such.

If you recognize yourself in the profile and are interested in either role, the department looks forward to receiving your motivation letter outlining your potential contribution to the education and research programmes mentioned above. Please also submit your CV, including (i) past work experience and qualifications (research, teaching, and/or management), (ii) your research interest(s), and (iii) a list of publications. In addition, the department also wants to ask you for a single-page teaching statement explaining your teaching experience, ambition and vision. Make sure that your application states to which of position you are applying. As there are multiple vacancies open for the Department of Political Science and PETGOV, know that there is no obstacle or disadvantage to applying for multiple positions.

Please find more info here.

Application Deadline: 10 September 2026
